    3.3CPlotting points

    7.15.4.3Draw and identify the equations of horizontal and vertical lines, including x = 0 and y = 0.4
    7.15.4.2Plot and read coordinates in all four quadrants.2
    7.15.4.1A coordinate pair gives horizontal position then vertical position, (x, y), across all four quadrants. The origin is (0, 0), and negative coordinates lie left of it or below it. A vertical line has equation x = a, because every point on it has the same x-coordinate. A horizontal line has equation y = b, for the same reason. The y-axis is the line x = 0 and the x-axis is the line y = 0.2
    7.15.5.2Plot and read coordinates on differently scaled axes.3
    9.2.1.2Plot and read coordinates in all four quadrants and identify the equations of horizontal and vertical lines.3

    Linear graphs

    9.2.2.1A table of values generates coordinate pairs by substituting chosen x values into the equation. Each column of the table is one point on the line. Substituting a negative x value needs brackets, so that the sign stays attached to the number. Where x and y sit on the same side, the equation is rearranged to make y the subject before substituting. Three points are enough to draw a straight line, the third acting as a check on the other two.4
    9.2.2.2Draw a linear graph from a completed table of values.4
    9.2.3.2Draw linear graphs accurately, choosing a suitable scale for the axes.4
    10.3.1.1A table of values generates coordinate pairs by substituting chosen x-values into an equation - in the same way that substituting a position n into an arithmetic sequence's nth-term rule generates a term.3
    10.3.1.2Complete a table of values for a linear equation and plot the resulting points to draw a straight-line graph.4

    3.3DCoordinate geometry and midpoints

    7.15.5.3Solve coordinate problems, including finding a midpoint and completing a shape from given vertices.4
    7.15.7.3Solve mixed problems combining inequalities, coordinates, graphs and factorising.5
    10.15.1.1The midpoint of a line segment is the point halfway along it. Its coordinates are the means of the end points' coordinates: the midpoint of (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) is ((x1 + x2) / 2, (y1 + y2) / 2). Averaging the x-coordinates and the y-coordinates separately works because the segment is divided in the same ratio in each direction.3
    10.15.1.2Calculate the midpoint of a line segment from the coordinates of its two end points.3
    10.15.1.3Find the missing end point of a line segment when one end point and the midpoint are given.4
    10H.13.1.1The midpoint of a line segment is the point halfway along it. Its coordinates are the means of the end points' coordinates: the midpoint of (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) is ((x1 + x2) / 2, (y1 + y2) / 2). A line segment drawn on a coordinate grid is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle whose shorter sides are the horizontal and vertical differences between the end points. Those differences are x2 - x1 and y2 - y1, and a negative difference is used as its positive size, because a length cannot be negative. Pythagoras' theorem then gives length^2 = (x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2.5
    10H.13.1.2Find the missing end point of a line segment when one end point and the midpoint are given.4
    FM.5.1-5.2.3Derive and apply the distance formula between two coordinate points.7
    FM.5.3.1The midpoint of a line segment is the average of its endpoints' coordinates. A right angle in a coordinate problem is a statement about perpendicular gradients.6
    FM.5.3.2Find the midpoint of a line segment, including where endpoints are given algebraically.6
    FM.5.3.3Combine gradient, perpendicular gradient, distance and midpoint to solve coordinate problems.8

    3.3AInterpreting graphs

    8.13.1.1A distance-time graph shows distance from a starting point on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal. A horizontal line means stationary, since time passes but distance does not change. A steeper line means a faster speed. A line returning to the horizontal axis means travelling back to the start. Each straight section is one stage of the journey, travelled at a constant speed.4
    8.13.1.2Read and interpret distance-time graphs, describing each stage of a journey.4
    8.13.1.3Draw a distance-time graph from a described journey.4
    9.11.1.2Interpret a distance-time graph, describing each stage of a journey.4
    9.11.1.3Calculate speed from the gradient, including average speed across a whole journey.5
    9.11.1.1A distance-time graph shows distance from a starting point against time. Its gradient is the speed, in the units of the two axes. A horizontal line means stationary, since time passes but distance does not change. A steeper line means a faster speed, and a line returning to the axis means travelling back to the start. Average speed over a whole journey is total distance divided by total time, including any time spent stopped.4
    10H.13.7.3Find the equation of a linear model from two values in context, and use it to predict, saying whether the prediction can be trusted.6

    9.11.4.1A conversion graph is a straight line through the origin, because the two units are in direct proportion. It converts in both directions: read across from one axis and down to the other. Values beyond the plotted line can be found by scaling, since the relationship is proportional. A time-series graph shows a quantity measured at intervals over time, with the points joined to show the trend. Only the plotted points are measured values; the joining lines are an estimate of what happened in between.3
    9.11.4.2Use a conversion graph to convert between units in both directions.3
    9.11.4.3Interpret other time-series graphs, describing trends over time.5

Values beyond the plotted line can be found by scaling, since the relationship is proportional. A time-series graph shows a quantity measured at intervals over time, with the points joined to show the trend. Only the plotted points are measured values; the joining lines are an estimate of what happened in between.4

    3.3GGradient

    8.13.2.1Gradient measures steepness: the vertical change divided by the horizontal change. The gradient of a straight line is the same wherever along it it is measured. A positive gradient rises from left to right and a negative gradient falls. A larger size of gradient means a steeper line, whatever its sign. A horizontal line has gradient 0.5
    8.13.2.2Find the gradient of a straight line from a graph.5
    8.13.2.3Interpret the sign and size of a gradient in context.5
    8.13.3.1The gradient of a distance-time graph is the speed. Its units come from the axes: distance units divided by time units. A steeper section is a faster speed, and a horizontal section a speed of zero. Average speed over a whole journey is total distance divided by total time, including any time spent stopped. Average speed is not the average of the separate speeds, unless each stage took the same time.5
    9.2.1.1A coordinate pair gives horizontal position then vertical position, (x, y), across all four quadrants. A vertical line has equation x = a and a horizontal line y = b. Gradient measures steepness: the vertical change divided by the horizontal change. A positive gradient rises from left to right and a negative gradient falls. The gradient of a straight line is the same wherever along it it is measured.5
    9.2.1.3Find the gradient of a straight line from a graph, including negative gradients.5
    9.2.6.1In a real context both axes carry units, so the gradient carries units too: y units per x unit. On a distance-time graph the gradient is the speed. The intercept is the value when the x variable is zero, such as a fixed charge before any usage. A straight line means a constant rate of change, which is what makes the model linear.5
    10.3.2.2Find the gradient and y-intercept of a straight line from its graph, including when the gradient is negative.4
    10.3.3.3Find the gradient of a straight line drawn on a grid by reading the increase in y and the increase in x between two labelled points on it.4
    10.3.4.1A gradient can be negative (the line falls left to right) or a fraction (the line rises or falls less steeply than a whole-number gradient) - the same vertical-change-over-horizontal-change definition applies in both cases.4
    10.3.4.2Find a negative gradient by reading the two changes off a drawn line, and use it to write or sketch that line's equation.5
    10.3.4.3Find a fractional gradient by reading the two changes off a drawn line, and use it to write or sketch that line's equation.5
    10H.13.7.1In a real context both axes carry units, so the gradient carries units too: y units per x unit. On a distance-time graph the gradient is the speed. The intercept is the value when the x variable is zero, such as a fixed charge before any usage. A straight line means a constant rate of change, which is what makes the model linear.5
    FM.3.4-3.5.1To 'draw' or 'plot' a graph means calculating and plotting points accurately, whereas to 'sketch' means showing correct shape and position with axis crossings only. The gradient between two points (x1,y1) and (x2,y2) is (y2-y1)/(x2-x1); a horizontal line y = b has gradient zero and a vertical line x = a has an undefined (infinite) gradient. The gradient m and intercept c fix a line y = mx + c completely, and any linear equation can be rearranged into that form or the general form px + qy + r = 0.4
    FM.3.4-3.5.2Calculate a gradient from two points and identify a gradient as positive, negative, zero or infinite from a line's orientation.5

    3.3Hy = mx + c

    9.2.4.1In y = mx + c, m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept. The y-intercept is where the line crosses the y-axis, which is the value of y when x = 0. A line can be sketched from its equation alone: mark c on the y-axis, then step out using the gradient. Parallel lines have the same gradient, so their equations share the same m and differ only in c. A negative m gives a line falling from left to right.5
    9.2.4.2Identify the gradient and intercept from an equation and use them to sketch the line.5
    9.2.5.1The gradient and intercept can only be read off directly when the equation is in the form y = mx + c. Any linear equation can be rearranged into that form, using the same inverse operations as solving. Dividing through by the coefficient of y has to be applied to every term. A negative coefficient of x makes m negative, which is easily lost during the rearrangement.5
    9.2.5.3Interpret a pre-drawn graph, stating its gradient, intercept and equation.5
    9.2.5.2Rearrange equations such as 2y + 4x = 8 into the form y = mx + c.5
    9.2.6.3Interpret linear graphs in context, explaining what the gradient and intercept represent.6
    10.15.3.1Michaelmas topic 3 already gives a line's gradient and y-intercept from its graph and from its equation, so this lesson starts from that and adds the four things it did not cover. An equation written ax + by = c is rearranged into y = mx + c before it is drawn, using the same balancing moves as solving an equation. A horizontal line has gradient 0 and an equation of the form y = k; a vertical line x = k has no gradient at all, because its horizontal change is 0 and nothing can be divided by 0. When m is known but the line's crossing point is not on the grid, c is found by substituting the coordinates of any point on the line into y = mx + c and solving for c. A point lies on a line exactly when its coordinates satisfy the equation, and that is the check on every answer here.4
    10.15.3.2Draw the graph of a line given as ax + by = c by rearranging it into y = mx + c first, and write down the equation of a horizontal or a vertical line drawn on a grid.4
    10.15.3.3Find c by substituting the coordinates of a point on the line into y = mx + c, and test whether a further point lies on that line.5
    10.3.1.3Explain the structural link between an arithmetic sequence's nth-term rule (dn + c) and a linear equation (y = mx + c), including why both give an evenly-spaced, straight-line pattern.4
    10.3.2.1In y = mx + c, m is the gradient (steepness: vertical change divided by horizontal change) and c is the y-intercept, the value of y where the line crosses the y-axis (when x = 0).4
    10.3.2.3Identify the gradient and y-intercept directly from an equation already in the form y = mx + c, and use them to sketch the line.4
    10.3.3.1Just as an arithmetic sequence's common difference and first term give its nth-term rule directly (dn + c) without listing every term, a straight line's gradient and y-intercept give its equation directly (y = mx + c) without plotting a table of points.4
    10.3.3.2Write the equation of a straight line in the form y = mx + c directly from its gradient and y-intercept, without a table of values.4
    10H.13.2.1The gradient and intercept can only be read off directly when the equation is in the form y = mx + c. Any linear equation can be rearranged into that form, using the same inverse operations as solving. Dividing through by the coefficient of y has to be applied to every term. A negative coefficient of x makes m negative, which is easily lost during the rearrangement.5
    10H.13.2.2Rearrange equations such as 2y + 4x = 8 into the form y = mx + c.5

    10H.13.7.2Interpret linear graphs in context, explaining what the gradient and intercept represent.6

    3.3ILinear and quadratic graphs

    9.2.2.3Complete a table of values where x and y are on the same side of the equation, rearranging first.5
    9.14.8.2Use a table of values to plot quadratic and other non-linear graphs.5
    10.17.5.1A quadratic function contains an x^2 term and its graph is a smooth curve called a parabola, never a set of straight segments. A positive x^2 coefficient gives a curve shaped like a valley with a minimum; a negative one gives a hill with a maximum. A table of values gives the y for each x, and squaring a negative x gives a positive result, which is what makes the curve symmetrical.4
    10.17.5.2Complete a table of values for a quadratic function and plot its graph as a smooth curve.4
    10.17.5.3Recognise from its equation whether a quadratic graph has a minimum or a maximum, and sketch its general shape.4
    10.17.6.1The x-coordinates of the points where a curve crosses the x-axis are the solutions of y = 0, and they are called the roots. A quadratic graph may cross the x-axis twice, touch it once, or not meet it at all, which is why an equation can have two, one or no solutions. A root read off a plotted graph is an estimate limited by the scale, while a root found by factorising is exact.4
    10.17.6.2Read the solutions of a quadratic equation from its plotted graph and state the accuracy the scale allows.4
    10.17.6.3Compare the roots read from a graph with the solutions found by factorising the same equation, and account for any difference.5
    10.17.7.1A parabola is symmetrical about a vertical line through its turning point, so points at equal horizontal distances either side have equal y values. The turning point is the minimum of a valley-shaped curve or the maximum of a hill-shaped one. When the curve crosses the x-axis at two roots, the line of symmetry lies exactly halfway between them.5
    10.17.7.2Write down the coordinates of the turning point and the equation of the line of symmetry from a plotted quadratic graph.5
    10.17.7.3Use the symmetry of a quadratic curve to find a second point with a given y value once one is known.5
    10.17.8.1The solutions of f(x) = k are the x-coordinates of the points where the curve y = f(x) meets the horizontal line y = k. Drawing that horizontal line across the graph is therefore the method, and each intersection gives one solution. A solution read from a graph is an estimate, and it is quoted to the accuracy the grid supports.4
    10.17.8.2Estimate the solutions of a quadratic equation by drawing a horizontal line on a pre-drawn graph and reading the intersections.4
    10.17.8.3Use a pre-drawn graph to find the values of x for which the function is greater than, or less than, a given value.5
    FM.3.7.3Sketch a quadratic graph from this information, and match a given equation to its sketch.7

    3.3A(H)Cubic, reciprocal and trig graphs

    9.14.8.1A table of values generates points for any equation, not only for linear ones. A quadratic, highest power x^2, gives a parabola, symmetrical about a vertical line through its turning point. A cubic, highest power x^3, gives an S-shape. A reciprocal, with x in the denominator, gives a hyperbola in two separate pieces that never touch the axes. An exponential, with x in the index, rises ever more steeply and never reaches the x-axis. Non-linear points are joined with a smooth curve, never with straight segments.6
    9.14.8.3Recognise the shape of a graph from its equation.6
    11H.2.1.1y = sin x and y = cos x are waves that repeat every 360 degrees, with values from -1 to 1. y = sin x starts at 0, rises to 1 at 90 degrees, is 0 at 180 degrees, -1 at 270 degrees and 0 again at 360 degrees; y = cos x has the same shape, starting at 1. y = tan x repeats every 180 degrees, passes through 0 at 0 and 180 degrees, and is undefined at 90 and 270 degrees, where the graph has asymptotes. By the symmetry of the graphs, an equation such as sin x = 0.5 has two solutions from 0 to 360 degrees: 30 degrees and 180 - 30 = 150 degrees.7
    11H.2.1.2Sketch the graphs of y = sin x, y = cos x and y = tan x from 0 to 360 degrees, marking their key values.7
    11H.2.1.3Use the graphs and their symmetry to find every solution from 0 to 360 degrees of an equation such as sin x = 0.5 or cos x = -0.5.8

When m is known but the line's crossing point is not on the grid, c is found by substituting the coordinates of any point on the line into y = mx + c and solving for c. A point lies on a line exactly when its coordinates satisfy the equation, and that is the check on every answer here.6

    3.3J(H)Distance-time and velocity-time graphs

    8.13.3.3Solve multi-step problems involving average speed across a whole journey.6
    8.13.4.1A velocity-time graph shows velocity on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal. Its gradient is the acceleration, in velocity units per unit of time. A horizontal line means constant speed, not stationary, which is the key difference from a distance-time graph. A negative gradient is deceleration. The area beneath the graph is the distance travelled.6
    8.13.4.2Find acceleration from the gradient of a velocity-time graph.6
    8.13.4.3Interpret a velocity-time graph, describing acceleration, constant speed and deceleration.6
    9.11.2.1A velocity-time graph shows velocity against time, not distance against time. A horizontal line therefore means constant speed, not stationary. The gradient is the acceleration, in velocity units per unit of time. A negative gradient is deceleration, and a gradient of zero is constant speed. The area beneath the graph is the distance travelled.6
    9.11.2.2Interpret a velocity-time graph, describing acceleration, constant speed and deceleration.6
    9.11.2.3Find acceleration from the gradient of a velocity-time graph.6
    9.11.3.1The area under a velocity-time graph is the distance travelled. That area is found by splitting the shape into rectangles, triangles and trapeziums. A rectangle is base x height, a triangle is half base x perpendicular height, and a trapezium is half the sum of the parallel sides times the height. The area's units come from the two axes multiplied together, which is why they give a distance. Under a curve the area can only be estimated, by splitting it into strips.6
    9.11.3.3Find the distance travelled from the area under a velocity-time graph.6
    9.11.3.2Recall and use the area formulae for rectangles, triangles and trapeziums.4
    9.11.5.1What a gradient represents depends entirely on what the two axes measure: it is always the y quantity per unit of the x quantity. What an area represents depends the same way: it is the y quantity multiplied by the x quantity. So on a distance-time graph the gradient is a speed, and the area means nothing useful. On a velocity-time graph the gradient is an acceleration and the area is a distance. Reading the axis labels and their units first is what decides which applies.6
    9.11.5.2Solve multi-step problems combining distance-time and velocity-time graphs.6
    9.11.5.3Explain what gradient and area represent for a given pair of axes.6

    3.3G(H)Parallel and perpendicular lines

    9.2.3.1Every point on a line satisfies its equation, so the graph is the set of all its solutions. A point not on the line does not satisfy the equation, which is how a plotting error shows itself. The axes need a scale going up in equal steps, chosen to fit the range of values in the table. Reading up from a given x to the line and then across gives the matching y, and the reverse gives x from y. A value read off a graph is only as accurate as the scale allows.5
    9.2.4.3Write the equation of a line from its graph, and identify parallel lines from their equations.5
    10.15.4.1Two straight lines are parallel exactly when they have the same gradient. Parallel lines with different y-intercepts never meet, so the pair of equations has no common solution. y = 3x + 1 and y = 3x - 4 are therefore parallel, while y = 3x + 1 and y = 4x + 1 are not, even though they cross the y-axis at the same point.5
    10.15.4.2Decide whether two lines are parallel by comparing their gradients.5
    10.15.4.3Write the equation of the line parallel to a given line that passes through a stated point.5
    10H.13.4.1Two straight lines are parallel exactly when they have the same gradient. Parallel lines with different y-intercepts never meet, so the pair of equations has no common solution. y = 3x + 1 and y = 3x - 4 are therefore parallel, while y = 3x + 1 and y = 4x + 1 are not, even though they cross the y-axis at the same point.5
    10H.13.4.2Show whether two lines are parallel by finding both gradients, when either line is given in the form ax + by = c or through two points.6
    10H.13.4.3Write the equation of the line parallel to a given line that passes through a stated point.5
    10H.13.5.1Two lines are perpendicular when they meet at right angles. The product of their gradients is then -1, so a line perpendicular to a line of gradient m has gradient -1/m, the negative reciprocal. Turning a slope triangle through 90 degrees swaps its run and rise and changes the sign of one, which is why the reciprocal is negative. A horizontal line and a vertical line are perpendicular too, but the product rule does not apply, because a vertical line has no gradient.7
    10H.13.5.2Find the gradient of a line perpendicular to a given line, and decide whether two lines are perpendicular from their gradients.7
    10H.13.5.3Find the equation of the line perpendicular to a given line that passes through a stated point.7
    10H.13.6.1In coordinates, two sides are parallel when their gradients are equal, meet at right angles when their gradients multiply to -1, and are equal when their lengths are equal. The perpendicular bisector of AB passes through the midpoint of AB, and its gradient is the negative reciprocal of the gradient of AB. The tangent to the circle x^2 + y^2 = r^2 at a point P is perpendicular to the radius OP, where O is the origin.7
    10H.13.6.2Use gradients and lengths to show that a triangle or quadrilateral with given vertices is of a stated type.7
    10H.13.6.3Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of a line segment, or of the tangent to a circle x^2 + y^2 = r^2 at a given point on it.8
    FM.5.1-5.2.1Parallel lines have equal gradients, and perpendicular lines have gradients whose product is -1, so each is the negative reciprocal of the other. The distance between two points (x1,y1) and (x2,y2) is sqrt((x2-x1)^2 + (y2-y1)^2), from Pythagoras applied to the horizontal and vertical separation.6
    FM.5.1-5.2.2Determine whether two lines are parallel or perpendicular, and find a perpendicular gradient.6

    3.3B(H)Graph transformations

    11H.9.10.1A change inside the bracket acts on the inputs, so it moves the graph horizontally and every y-coordinate stays the same. y = f(x + a) translates the graph left by a, the opposite way to the sign, so (p, q) maps to (p - a, q) and y = f(x - 3) is the graph moved right 3. y = f(ax) stretches the graph horizontally by scale factor 1/a, so (p, q) maps to (p/a, q) and points on the y-axis stay put. y = f(-x) reflects the graph in the y-axis, so (p, q) maps to (-p, q).8
    11H.9.10.2Sketch y = f(x + a) and y = f(-x) from the graph of y = f(x), and give the image of a point.8
    11H.9.10.3Sketch y = f(ax) from the graph of y = f(x), and decide which transformation maps one given graph onto another.9
    11H.9.9.1A change outside the bracket acts on the outputs, so it moves the graph vertically and every x-coordinate stays the same. y = f(x) + a translates the graph up by a, or down when a is negative, so the point (p, q) maps to (p, q + a). y = af(x) stretches the graph vertically by scale factor a, so (p, q) maps to (p, aq) and points on the x-axis stay put. y = -f(x) reflects the graph in the x-axis, so (p, q) maps to (p, -q).8
    11H.9.9.2Sketch y = f(x) + a and y = -f(x) from the graph of y = f(x), and give the image of a point such as a turning point.8
    11H.9.9.3Sketch y = af(x) from the graph of y = f(x), and name a vertical transformation from its equation or its graph.8

    3.3D(H)Gradient of a curve

    11H.7.1.1The gradient of a curve changes from point to point, so a rate of change on a curve belongs to one instant. A tangent touches the curve at one point and has the same gradient as the curve there. The tangent's gradient is its rise divided by its run, read from the axis scales, and a large triangle gives a more accurate reading. A chord joins two points on the curve, and its gradient is the average rate of change between them, not the rate at a point.7
    11H.7.1.3Find the average rate of change between two points from the gradient of a chord, and compare it with the rate of change at a point.7

    Graphs
    • Analysing transformations

    3.3C(H)Analysing transformations

    11H.9.11.1When two transformations act in turn, a point is followed through each one in order. y = f(x + a) + b combines a horizontal and a vertical translation, so (p, q) maps to (p - a, q + b), whichever is done first. y = (x - p)^2 + q is y = x^2 translated right p and up q, so its turning point is (p, q). When a reflection or a stretch is combined with a translation, order matters: in y = -f(x) + c the reflection is done first, then the translation.9
    11H.9.11.2Find the image of a point, such as a turning point, under a combined transformation such as y = f(x - 2) + 3 or y = -f(x) + 1.9
    11H.9.11.3Describe the transformations that map y = x^2 onto a graph such as y = (x + 3)^2 - 5, and write the equation of a transformed graph.9
    Algebraic manipulation
    • Conventions and notation
    • Collecting like terms
    • Expanding a single bracket

    2.1AConventions and notation

    7.6.1.1A term is a number, a letter, or numbers and letters multiplied together; terms are separated by + and - signs. An expression is one or more terms with no equals sign: 3x + 5. An equation says two expressions are equal and is true only for particular values: 3x + 5 = 11. A formula is a rule linking two or more variables, with one of them as the subject: A = lw.3
    7.6.1.2Classify examples as expressions, equations or formulae.3
    7.6.2.1Substitution replaces each letter with a given value, then evaluates. The conventions are undone as you substitute: 3a means 3 x a, ab means a x b, a/2 means a divided by 2. The order of operations still applies once the values are in. A substituted negative keeps its sign inside brackets: with a = -4, 3a is 3 x (-4) = -12 and 5 - a is 5 - (-4) = 9.2
    7.11.1.1An equation states that two expressions are equal. Forming an equation means naming the unknown with a letter and writing the described relationship in algebra. A word equation states that relationship in words before letters are used. The equals sign means 'has the same value as', not 'here comes the answer'.3

    2.2BCollecting like terms

    7.6.4.2Multiply algebraic terms, including terms with coefficients.4
    7.6.5.1Like terms have exactly the same letters raised to exactly the same powers; only the coefficients differ. Like terms are combined by adding or subtracting the coefficients, leaving the letter part unchanged: 5x + 2x = 7x. Unlike terms (3x and 3y, or x and x^2) cannot be combined into one term. The sign in front of a term belongs to it and travels with it. A function machine shows, in order, the operations applied to an input to give an output. Multiplying powers of the same base adds the indices: x^2 x x^3 = x^5.3
    7.6.5.2Simplify expressions by collecting like terms, and represent operations with function machines.3
    7.7.1.1x and x^2 are different powers of the same letter, so they are not like terms and cannot be combined. Adding terms combines the coefficients and leaves the powers unchanged: x^2 + x^2 = 2x^2. Multiplying terms multiplies the coefficients and adds the powers: x^2 x x^2 = x^4. These two rules are easily confused because the same terms appear in both.4
    7.7.1.2Collect like terms in expressions where terms include indices.2

    2.2CExpanding a single bracket

    7.6.4.1Multiplication works in any order, so numbers and letters in a product can be gathered: 2a x 3b = 2 x 3 x a x b = 6ab. The coefficient is the number part of a term, and coefficients multiply together. A letter multiplied by itself gives an index: a x a = a^2, a x a x a = a^3. By convention the number is written first and letters in alphabetical order: 6ab, not ba6.3
    7.6.5.3Apply the addition law of indices when multiplying powers of the same base.4
    7.7.2.1Expanding a bracket multiplies every term inside by the term outside (the distributive property). 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12: the 3 reaches both terms, not just the first. A negative outside the bracket changes the sign of every term inside: -2(x - 5) = -2x + 10. A minus sign alone in front of a bracket acts as -1.3
    7.7.2.2Expand single brackets, including with algebraic terms outside.3
    7.7.2.3Expand brackets with a negative term in front, handling all sign changes correctly.4
    10.17.1.1Multiplying a bracket by a term outside it multiplies every term inside, because a(b + c) = ab + ac. The sign in front of a term travels with it, so -3(x - 4) = -3x + 12. Index notation is used when a letter multiplies itself: x times x is written x^2.3
    10.17.1.2Expand a single bracket and simplify the result by collecting like terms.3
    10.17.1.3Expand and simplify an expression containing two single brackets, including one with a negative multiplier.4

    2.3DFormulae from context

    7.11.1.2Form and use word equations to describe a situation.3

    No matching specification point

    7.11.5.1Substituting a solution back into the original equation checks it, since both sides must then give the same value. A contextual problem is solved by forming an equation, solving it, and answering in the context with units. Perimeter and angle facts give ready-made equations: sides sum to the perimeter, angles on a line sum to 180 degrees. A solution that makes no sense in context, such as a negative length, signals an error in the equation rather than the arithmetic.3

    7.7.3.3Form expressions from worded and geometric contexts (e.g. perimeters, '3 more than double n').5

    2.2ASubstitution

    7.6.2.2Substitute positive integer values into expressions and formulae.3
    7.6.2.3Substitute negative values into expressions and formulae, applying negative number rules.4
    7.6.3.1An index attaches only to the letter or bracket it follows, so 3x^2 means 3 x (x^2). (3x)^2 squares the whole term: 3x x 3x = 9x^2. Squaring a negative gives a positive, cubing gives a negative: (-2)^2 = 4, (-2)^3 = -8. Indices are evaluated before multiplication, so -x^2 with x = 2 is -4, not 4.5
    7.6.3.2Substitute values into expressions involving squares, cubes and other indices.4
    7.6.3.3Substitute into multi-term expressions and formulae combining indices, negatives and the order of operations.5
    10.8.5.2Substitute positive, negative, decimal and fractional values into a formula and evaluate it.3

    2.1C 2.1DIndices

    7.6.4.3Multiply terms producing indices, including simple powers of the same letter.4
    8.9.1.1An index says how many times the base is used as a factor: 2^5 = 2x2x2x2x2. Multiplying powers of the same base adds the indices: a^m x a^n = a^(m+n). Dividing subtracts them: a^m / a^n = a^(m-n). A power of a power multiplies them: (a^m)^n = a^(mn). Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1, since a^n / a^n is both 1 and a^0. 10^n is a place-value shift, so multiplying by 10^3 moves every digit three places to the left.4
    8.9.1.2Simplify expressions using the multiplication, division and power laws of indices.4
    10H.5.1.2Simplify expressions using the multiplication, division and power laws of indices.4

    2.2DCommon factors

    7.15.6.1Factorising is the inverse of expanding: the expression is rewritten as a product with a bracket. The factor taken outside is the highest common factor of all the terms. The bracket holds what remains when each term is divided by that factor. Fully factorised means the terms left inside the bracket share no common factor. The HCF of algebraic terms includes numbers and letters, so the HCF of 6x^2 and 9x is 3x.4
    7.15.6.2Factorise expressions by taking out a numerical or single-letter common factor.4
    7.15.6.3Factorise fully, taking out the highest common factor including coefficients and powers of a letter.5
    8.14.4.1Factorising is the inverse of expanding: the expression is rewritten as a product with a bracket. The factor taken out is the highest common factor of all the terms, letters as well as numbers. Fully factorised means the terms left inside share no common factor, so the HCF of 6x^2 and 9x is 3x. Expanding multiplies every term inside the bracket by the term outside. Multiplying the terms follows the index laws, so 3x(2x + 5) = 6x^2 + 15x.5
    8.15.3.1Algebraic fractions cancel by common factors in exactly the same way as numerical ones. Only factors cancel, never individual terms of a sum. Powers of a letter cancel by subtracting indices, so x^5 / x^2 = x^3. Multiplying algebraic fractions multiplies numerators and denominators; dividing multiplies by the reciprocal. Cancelling before multiplying keeps the expressions manageable.6
    9.7.4.1Factorising is the inverse of expanding: the expression is rewritten as a product with a bracket. The factor taken out is the highest common factor of every term, letters as well as numbers. Fully factorised means the terms left inside share no common factor, so the HCF of 6x^2 and 9x is 3x. A bracket in a factorised expression is itself a factor of the whole expression. Expanding the result checks the factorisation.4
    9.7.5.1An algebraic fraction cancels only by common factors, never by individual terms of a sum. A numerator or denominator that is a sum must be factorised before anything can cancel. Cancelling a bracket that appears in both leaves 1 in its place, not nothing. An even number is 2n and an odd number 2n + 1, so statements about factors and multiples can be proved by factorising the general expression.6
    9.8.2.3Check a factorisation by expanding it back out.4

    2.3BSimplifying

    7.7.1.3Distinguish between and correctly apply multiplication and addition of algebraic terms in mixed simplification questions.5

    2.2EExpanding double brackets

    8.14.6.1Expanding double brackets multiplies every term in the first bracket by every term in the second, giving four products before simplifying. (x + a)^2 means (x + a)(x + a), so it expands to x^2 + 2ax + a^2, not x^2 + a^2. (x + a)(x - a) gives x^2 - a^2, the difference of two squares, because the two middle terms cancel. Triple brackets are expanded two at a time, and that result is then multiplied by the third. A bracket in a factorised expression is itself a factor of the whole expression.6
    8.14.6.2Expand and simplify double brackets, including squared brackets and the difference of two squares.6
    9.7.1.1Expanding double brackets multiplies every term in the first bracket by every term in the second, giving four products before simplifying. (x + a)^2 means (x + a)(x + a), so it expands to x^2 + 2ax + a^2, not x^2 + a^2. Several single brackets are expanded one at a time, then simplified by collecting like terms. A negative outside a bracket changes the sign of every term inside it.5
    9.7.1.3Expand and simplify double brackets.5
    9.7.2.1(x + a)(x - a) gives x^2 - a^2, the difference of two squares, because the two middle terms cancel. (x + a)^2 gives x^2 + 2ax + a^2, and (x - a)^2 gives x^2 - 2ax + a^2. Recognising these forms saves expanding them term by term every time. A perimeter adds all the side lengths and an area multiplies two of them, so both give expressions to expand and simplify.5
    9.7.2.2Expand squared brackets and difference-of-two-squares expressions.5
    10.17.2.1To expand (x + a)(x + b) every term in the first bracket multiplies every term in the second, giving four products. Collecting the two x terms gives x^2 + (a + b)x + ab, so the x coefficient is the SUM of a and b and the constant is their PRODUCT. (x + a)^2 means (x + a)(x + a) and expands to x^2 + 2ax + a^2; it is not x^2 + a^2.4
    10.17.2.2Expand and simplify the product of two linear expressions.4
    10.17.2.3Expand a squared bracket and use the expansion to write down the area of a square of side (x + a).4

    2.2GExpanding multiple brackets

    7.7.3.1An expression with several brackets is expanded one bracket at a time, then like terms are collected. Subtracting a whole bracket changes the sign of every term in it: 5 - (x - 2) = 5 - x + 2. Forming an expression means naming the unknown with a letter and writing the relationship in algebra. Perimeter adds all the side lengths, and '3 more than double n' is 2n + 3.4
    7.7.3.2Expand two or more single brackets and simplify by collecting like terms.4
    8.14.4.3Expand and simplify single brackets, including in geometric contexts.5
    8.14.5.1An expression with several brackets is expanded one bracket at a time, then simplified by collecting like terms. A negative outside a bracket changes the sign of every term inside. Subtracting a whole bracket changes the sign of every term in it: 5 - (x - 2) = 5 - x + 2. A perimeter adds all the side lengths and an area multiplies two of them, so both give expressions to expand and simplify.5
    8.14.5.2Expand and simplify expressions with two or more single brackets, including with a negative outside.5
    8.14.5.3Form and simplify expressions from perimeter and area contexts.6
    9.7.1.2Expand and simplify several single brackets, including in geometric contexts.5
    9.7.2.3Form and expand expressions from area and perimeter contexts.6
    9.7.4.3Identify brackets as factors and use them to simplify expressions.5

    2.3FFormulae and rearranging

    8.2.5.1A formula is a rule relating two or more variables, with one of them as the subject. Substituting known values into a formula leaves an equation in the remaining unknown. Squaring and taking a square root are inverses, as are cubing and the cube root. An unknown inside a power is freed by rooting both sides; an unknown under a root is freed by raising both sides to that power. A square root has a positive and a negative value, so x^2 = 25 gives x = 5 or x = -5.5
    8.2.5.2Substitute into and solve one-step formulae involving powers and roots.5
    8.2.5.3Solve multi-step formulae for a given unknown.6
    8.6.3.1Changing the subject rearranges a formula so that a different variable stands alone. It uses the same inverse operations as solving an equation, but the result is a formula rather than a number. The operations are undone in the reverse of the order they were applied to the variable wanted as subject. Squaring and rooting are inverses, so a squared subject is freed by rooting both sides. A rearranged formula answers for any values, whereas substituting first answers for only one set.5
    8.6.3.2Substitute into one-step formulae involving powers and roots.5
    8.6.3.3Change the subject of a one-step formula, including where the subject is squared or under a root.6
    8.10.1.1Changing the subject rearranges a formula so that a different variable stands alone on one side. It applies the same inverse operations to both sides as solving an equation does. The operations are undone in the reverse of the order they were applied to the wanted subject. The result is a formula rather than a number, so it answers for any set of values.5
    8.10.1.2Change the subject of a one-step formula.5
    8.10.1.3Substitute into a formula after rearranging it.5
    8.10.2.1Squaring and taking a square root are inverse operations, as are cubing and the cube root. A squared subject is freed by rooting both sides; a subject under a root is freed by raising both sides to that power. The root or power applies to the whole of the other side, so that side is bracketed first. Rearranging before substituting keeps the working shorter and avoids rounding partway through.5
    8.10.2.2Change the subject of formulae involving squares, cubes and roots.5
    8.10.2.3Rearrange and then substitute into formulae involving powers and roots.6
    10.8.5.1A formula is a rule connecting quantities, with one of them written on its own as the subject. Substituting means replacing each letter by its given value and then calculating, keeping to the order of operations. Changing the subject uses the same balancing moves as solving an equation, but the answer is an expression rather than a number. A square is undone by a square root and a square root by squaring, so r can be made the subject of A = pi x r^2.5
    10.8.5.3Change the subject of a formula in which the new subject appears once, including one carrying a power or a root, such as making r the subject of A = pi x r^2 or t the subject of v = u + at.5
    10H.7.1.2Change the subject of formulae involving squares, cubes and roots.5

    2.2FFactorising quadratics

    9.8.1.1A quadratic has a squared term, and a monic quadratic is one where the coefficient of x^2 is 1. x^2 + bx + c factorises into (x + p)(x + q), where p + q = b and pq = c. This is the reverse of expanding: the middle term comes from p + q and the constant from pq. The factor pairs of c are listed first, then the pair that adds to b is chosen.5
    9.8.1.2Find the pair of numbers that add to b and multiply to c.5
    9.8.1.3Factorise monic quadratics.5
    9.8.2.1The signs of b and c together fix the signs of p and q. A positive c means p and q share a sign, and that sign is b's. A negative c means p and q have different signs, and the larger of the two takes b's sign. Expanding the factorised form back out checks both the numbers and the signs.5
    9.8.2.2Factorise monic quadratics involving negative coefficients.5
    9.8.3.1x^2 - a^2 factorises as (x + a)(x - a), because expanding it cancels the two middle terms. It is recognised by two square terms separated by a minus sign, with no x term. A common factor is always taken out before factorising any further. Removing a common factor can reveal a difference of two squares that was hidden: 2x^2 - 18 = 2(x^2 - 9) = 2(x + 3)(x - 3).5
    9.8.3.2Factorise expressions using the difference of two squares.5
    9.8.3.3Take out a common factor first, then factorise the remaining quadratic.6
    10.17.3.1Factorising reverses expanding: x^2 + bx + c factorises as (x + p)(x + q) where p + q = b and pq = c. So the two numbers are found by listing the factor pairs of c and choosing the pair that adds to b. If c is positive both numbers share the sign of b; if c is negative they have opposite signs. A common factor in every term is taken out first, because 2x^2 + 10x + 12 = 2(x^2 + 5x + 6).4
    10.17.3.2Factorise a quadratic expression of the form x^2 + bx + c into two brackets.4
    10.17.3.3Factorise a quadratic expression that first requires a common numerical factor to be taken out, and check by expanding.5

    No matching specification point

    8.2.4.1However complicated an equation looks, the method is unchanged: expand any brackets, collect the unknown onto one side, then apply inverse operations. Collecting the smaller unknown term onto the other side avoids a negative coefficient. An inequality is solved by the identical method, with one exception: multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the sign. An equation gives a single value, whereas an inequality gives a range.5

    2.2E(H)Algebraic proof

    7.4.1.1A counter-example is one case meeting a statement's conditions but not its conclusion, and it proves the statement false. One counter-example disproves a statement; no number of supporting examples proves one true. Examples can only disprove an 'always' claim or prove a 'sometimes' claim; 'always' and 'never' need an argument covering every case. Counter-examples usually sit at the edges: 0, 1, 2, negatives, fractions, and the number itself.4
    7.4.1.2Test whether a statement is always, sometimes or never true by trying examples systematically.4
    7.4.1.3Disprove a given statement by finding and presenting a counter-example.5
    8.14.1.1To verify a statement is to check that it holds for one particular case. Verifying is not proving: a statement can hold for many cases and still be false. A counter-example is a single case meeting the conditions but not the conclusion, and it disproves the statement. Proving a statement always true needs an argument covering every case, usually an algebraic one. Counter-examples usually sit at the edges: 0, 1, 2, negatives and fractions.5
    8.14.1.2Verify that a given statement holds for particular values.5
    8.14.1.3Explain why verifying cases is not a proof, and disprove a statement using a counter-example.5
    9.7.5.3Prove statements about factors and multiples using algebraic expressions.6
    11H.5.1.1To verify a statement is to check that it holds for one particular case. Verifying is not proving: a statement can hold for many cases and still be false. A counter-example is a single case meeting the conditions but not the conclusion, and it disproves the statement. Proving a statement always true needs an argument covering every case, usually an algebraic one. Counter-examples usually sit at the edges: 0, 1, 2, negatives and fractions.5
    11H.5.1.2Explain why verifying cases is not a proof, and disprove a statement using a counter-example.5
    11H.5.1.3Disprove an algebraic statement, such as (a + b)^2 = a^2 + b^2 or x^2 > x, by choosing a counter-example and working out both sides.6
    11H.5.2.1A 'show that' question gives the result, so every mark is for the working: each step is written and none is skipped. An identity is true for every value of its letters, while an equation is true only for some values; an identity is written with the symbol 'is identical to', three lines. An identity is proved by starting from one side, usually the more complicated, and expanding and simplifying until it becomes the other side. Checking with numbers can disprove an identity but can never prove it. In a geometric 'show that', each length or area is written as an expression first, then a fact about the shape gives the equation, which is rearranged into exactly the given form.6
    11H.5.2.2Prove an algebraic identity by expanding and simplifying one side until it equals the other, such as (n + 3)^2 - (n - 3)^2 = 12n.6
    11H.5.2.3Show that a given equation follows from a geometric situation, such as an area, a perimeter or Pythagoras, by forming expressions and rearranging into the given form.6
    11H.5.3.1Any integer is n, where n is an integer, and consecutive integers are n, n + 1, n + 2. An even number is 2n and an odd number is 2n + 1; consecutive even numbers are 2n and 2n + 2, and consecutive odd numbers are 2n + 1 and 2n + 3. Two unrelated numbers need two letters, such as 2m + 1 and 2n + 1, because one letter would make them equal. An expression is a multiple of k when it can be written as k x (an integer), so a proof factorises k out of every term and states that the bracket is an integer. A proof ends with a sentence saying what has been shown.6
    11H.5.3.2Prove statements about factors and multiples using algebraic expressions.6
    11H.5.3.3Prove a statement about the sum or product of consecutive integers, or of odd and even numbers, concluding in words.7
    11H.5.4.1Squaring an algebraic integer means expanding the whole bracket: (2n + 1)^2 = 4n^2 + 4n + 1, keeping the middle term. To show a result is even, write it as 2 x (an integer); to show it is odd, write it as 2 x (an integer) + 1; to show it is a multiple of k, factorise k out of every term. A difference of two squared brackets is subtracted inside a bracket, so every sign of the second square changes. A proof must hold for every integer, so it uses letters throughout and ends with a sentence stating what has been proved.8
    11H.5.4.2Prove a statement involving the squares of consecutive integers or of odd and even numbers, by expanding and factorising.8
    11H.5.4.3Construct a complete algebraic proof from a worded statement, choosing the expressions to use and concluding in words.9
    FM.1.3-1.4.3Express one variable as a percentage or fraction of another, prove a given algebraic identity, and manipulate ratios expressed with variables.7

    Algebraic fractions

    7.10.6.3Add and subtract algebraic fractions with numerical denominators (e.g. x/3 + x/4).5
    9.7.6.2Multiply and divide algebraic fractions.6
    9.12.1.1An algebraic fraction cancels by common factors in the numerator and denominator, exactly as a numerical one does. Only factors cancel, never individual terms of a sum. Powers of a letter cancel by subtracting indices, so x^5 / x^2 = x^3. Coefficients cancel by dividing both by their HCF. Different letters cancel independently of one another.5
    9.12.1.3Simplify fractions containing coefficients and several letters.5
    9.12.2.1Algebraic fractions multiply numerator by numerator and denominator by denominator. Dividing means multiplying by the reciprocal, which is that fraction inverted. Cancelling common factors before multiplying keeps the expressions small. Cancelling can be done across the two fractions, not only within one of them. The result is fully simplified only when no common factor is left.5
    9.12.2.2Multiply and divide algebraic fractions, cancelling first where possible.5
    9.12.3.3Add and subtract algebraic fractions with numerical denominators.5
    10H.7.3.1An equation with fractions is cleared by multiplying every term, on both sides, by a common multiple of the denominators, usually their LCM. A numerator with more than one term is bracketed before multiplying, so 6 x (x + 1)/3 = 2(x + 1), and a minus sign in front of a fraction then multiplies the whole bracket. An unknown in a denominator is cleared the same way, by multiplying both sides by the whole denominator: 8 / (x + 3) = 2 gives 8 = 2(x + 3). With a single fraction on each side, both denominators multiply through: 3 / (x + 1) = 2 / (x - 2) gives 3(x - 2) = 2(x + 1).5
    10H.7.3.3Solve an equation with two or more algebraic fractions, including the unknown in more than one denominator, such as (x + 1)/4 - (x - 2)/3 = 1 or 3/(x + 1) = 2/(x - 2).6
    11H.3.4.2Multiply and divide algebraic fractions.6
    11H.3.5.2Add and subtract algebraic fractions with numerical denominators.5
    11H.3.7.1An equation with fractions is cleared by multiplying every term on BOTH sides by a common denominator, usually the LCM of the denominators. A numerator that is a sum is bracketed before it is multiplied, so the multiplication reaches every term of it. A term that is not a fraction is multiplied too: it does not keep its old value. An unknown in a denominator is cleared the same way, by multiplying both sides by that whole denominator. The cleared equation is linear, is solved by the balance method, and the answer is checked in the original equation.6
    11H.3.7.3Solve equations with two or more fractions whose numerators are expressions, such as (x + 3)/4 - (x - 1)/6 = 1.6
    FM.2.4-2.5.2Solve linear equations containing algebraic fractions by clearing denominators.7

    Change the subject - advanced

    8.10.3.2Change the subject of multi-step formulae.6
    8.10.3.3Rearrange formulae containing fractions by multiplying through by the denominator.6
    8.10.3.1Multi-step rearrangement undoes operations in reverse order, exactly as when solving an equation. The operation furthest from the wanted subject is undone first. A fraction is cleared by multiplying both sides by its denominator before anything else is moved. Where the subject sits inside a bracket, the bracket is expanded or divided out before the subject is isolated.6
    8.10.4.1Where the wanted subject appears more than once, no sequence of inverse operations alone will isolate it. Every term containing the subject is collected onto one side and every other term onto the other. The subject is then factorised out, leaving it multiplied by a bracket. Dividing both sides by that bracket makes it the subject.7
    8.10.4.2Change the subject of a formula where the subject appears twice, using factorising.6
    8.10.4.3Factorise expressions with a common factor as a step within a rearrangement.6
    10H.7.1.1Changing the subject undoes the operations on the wanted letter in reverse order, doing the same to both sides each time. Squaring and taking a square root are inverses, as are cubing and taking a cube root, so from A = pi x r^2, r = the square root of (A / pi). A power or a root applies to the whole of the other side, which is treated as one bracket: from v^2 = u^2 + 2as, v = the square root of (u^2 + 2as), not u + the square root of 2as. A term added to the subject's term is removed before any root is taken.6
    10H.7.1.3Change the subject of multi-step formulae.6
    10H.7.2.2Change the subject of a formula where the subject appears twice, using factorising.6
    FM.2.2.2Rearrange a formula to make a specified letter the subject, including where a square or square root is involved.7

    No matching specification point

    8.10.5.1A geometric formula can be rearranged to make any of its variables the subject. A = pi x r^2 rearranges to r = the square root of (A / pi), dividing before rooting. Only the positive root is taken, since a length cannot be negative. The units follow the formula through the rearrangement, so an area formula still returns a length.6
    8.10.5.2Rearrange area, perimeter and volume formulae to find a missing dimension.6

    2.2C(H)Algebraic fractions

    8.15.3.2Cancel basic algebraic fractions.7
    8.15.3.3Multiply and divide algebraic fractions, cancelling common factors first.6
    9.7.5.2Cancel algebraic fractions after factorising numerator and denominator.6
    9.7.6.1Algebraic fractions multiply by multiplying numerators and denominators, exactly as numerical ones do. Dividing means multiplying by the reciprocal. Cancelling common factors before multiplying keeps the expressions manageable. Where a numerator or denominator is a sum, it is factorised first so the common factors become visible.6
    9.12.1.2Cancel basic algebraic fractions, including powers of a letter.5
    9.12.4.1A fraction whose numerator or denominator is a sum can only cancel once that sum has been factorised. Factorising turns the sum into a product, and only then are the common factors visible. A bracket appearing in both numerator and denominator cancels, leaving 1 in its place. A quadratic factorises into two brackets, either of which may be the common factor. A difference of two squares factorises as (x + a)(x - a), which is often what makes the cancelling possible.6
    9.12.4.2Factorise before cancelling an algebraic fraction.6
    9.12.4.3Simplify algebraic fractions requiring a quadratic to be factorised.7
    11H.3.3.1A fraction whose numerator or denominator is a sum can only cancel once that sum has been factorised. Factorising turns the sum into a product, and only then are the common factors visible. A bracket appearing in both numerator and denominator cancels, leaving 1 in its place. A quadratic factorises into two brackets, either of which may be the common factor. A difference of two squares factorises as (x + a)(x - a), which is often what makes the cancelling possible.6
    11H.3.3.2Factorise before cancelling an algebraic fraction.6
    11H.3.3.3Simplify algebraic fractions requiring a quadratic to be factorised.7
    11H.3.4.1Algebraic fractions multiply by multiplying numerators and denominators, exactly as numerical ones do. Dividing means multiplying by the reciprocal. Cancelling common factors before multiplying keeps the expressions manageable. Where a numerator or denominator is a sum, it is factorised first so the common factors become visible.6
    11H.3.5.3Write a sum or difference of three algebraic fractions, or of a fraction and a whole term, as a single fraction in its simplest form.6
    11H.3.6.1Fractions with algebraic denominators add and subtract exactly as numerical ones do: over a common denominator, numerators only. When two denominators share no factor, their product is the common denominator: a/(x + 1) + b/(x - 2) = (a(x - 2) + b(x + 1))/((x + 1)(x - 2)). Each numerator is multiplied by the factor its own denominator is missing, and a subtracted numerator is bracketed so that every term changes sign. A denominator that factorises is factorised first; the lowest common denominator uses each factor once, so x^2 - 9 and x + 3 give (x + 3)(x - 3). The answer is usually left with a factorised denominator and is checked for a factor that cancels.7
    11H.3.6.2Add and subtract algebraic fractions with linear denominators, writing the result as a single fraction.7
    11H.3.6.3Add and subtract algebraic fractions where a denominator must be factorised to find the lowest common denominator.8
    11H.3.8.1An equation with two algebraic denominators is cleared by multiplying every term by both denominators, whose product is the common denominator. Clearing usually leaves a quadratic, which is rearranged to = 0 and solved by factorising or by the quadratic formula. A value that makes an original denominator zero is not a solution and is rejected. Exam questions often ask to show that the equation simplifies to a given quadratic first; the working must reach that quadratic exactly.8
    11H.3.8.2Show that an equation with algebraic fractions simplifies to a given quadratic equation.8
    11H.3.8.3Solve an equation with algebraic fractions that leads to a quadratic, by factorising or by the quadratic formula.8

    FM.2.3.1An algebraic fraction cancels only by common factors of the whole numerator and denominator, so cancelling a term within a sum is invalid. Adding or subtracting requires the LCM of the denominators.7
    FM.2.3.2Simplify, multiply and divide algebraic fractions, factorising first where needed.7
    FM.2.3.3Add and subtract algebraic fractions with linear and quadratic denominators, and identify and correct illegal cancelling.8

    8.14.6.3Expand triple brackets and brackets containing three terms, and identify brackets as factors.7
    9.7.3.1Triple brackets are expanded two at a time, and that result is then multiplied by the third. Each term of the expanded pair must multiply every term of the remaining bracket. A bracket containing three terms is expanded the same way: every term by every term. The number of products to expect is the number of terms in each bracket multiplied together, which checks that none has been missed.6
    9.7.3.2Expand triple brackets.6
    9.7.3.3Expand brackets containing three terms.6
    FM.1.5.1Two linear brackets expand by multiplying each term in the first bracket by each term in the second (e.g. using a grid or FOIL), collecting like terms to give a quadratic ax^2 + bx + c. A cubed bracket is expanded by building up from the squared bracket first: square the bracket, then multiply that result by the original bracket once more.6

    Algebraic manipulation
    • Completing the square
    • Subject appearing twice

    2.2D(H)Completing the square

    FM.2.4-2.5.1Multiplying an equation through by the LCM must be applied to every term, including whole expressions in brackets. A quadratic ax^2 + bx + c completes the square to a(x + p)^2 + q; expanding a(x + p)^2 + q and comparing coefficients with ax^2 + bx + c pins down p and q, including when a is not 1.7
    FM.2.4-2.5.3Express a quadratic in completed-square form, including with a non-unit leading coefficient, by expanding and comparing coefficients.8
    FM.3.7.1The sign of a determines whether a parabola y = ax^2 + bx + c has a minimum (a > 0) or a maximum (a < 0). Completing the square to a(x - h)^2 + k gives the vertex directly as (h, k), with line of symmetry x = h.7
    FM.3.7.2Find the vertex, line of symmetry and intercepts of a quadratic by completing the square.8

    2.3A(H)Subject appearing twice

    10H.7.2.1When the wanted letter appears in more than one term, inverse operations alone cannot isolate it. Every term containing the subject is collected on one side and every other term on the other, then the subject is factorised out: ax + 2 = bx + 5 gives ax - bx = 3, so x(a - b) = 3. Dividing both sides by the whole bracket makes it the subject: x = 3/(a - b). A fraction holding the subject is cleared first, by multiplying both sides by its whole denominator: y = (x + 2)/(x - 3) gives y(x - 3) = x + 2.7
    10H.7.2.3Change the subject of a formula where the subject appears twice inside an algebraic fraction, such as y = (x + 2)/(x - 3), by clearing the fraction, collecting and factorising.7
    FM.2.2.1The new subject must end up alone on one side and absent from the other. Where the subject sits inside a square root, square both sides to remove it; where the subject itself is squared, take the square root at the end, allowing for both the positive and negative root where the context needs it. Where the subject appears twice, its terms are collected together and factorised out before dividing.7
    FM.2.2.3Rearrange a formula where the required subject appears twice, using factorising.8
    Sequences
    • Generating sequences

    3.1AGenerating sequences

    8.14.2.1A term-to-term rule gives the next term from the previous one, so earlier terms must be found first. A position-to-term rule, the nth term, gives any term directly from its position. Substituting a position number into the nth term rule generates that term. The square numbers are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36; the cube numbers are 1, 8, 27, 64, 125. The triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 are the running totals of the counting numbers, and the Fibonacci sequence adds the two previous terms.3
    8.14.2.2Generate the terms of a sequence from a term-to-term or an nth term rule.1
    8.14.2.3Recognise and continue square, cube, triangular and Fibonacci sequences.4
    7.1.5.1A sequence is a list of numbers, called terms, that follows a rule, and each term has a position: 1st, 2nd, 3rd and so on. A term-to-term rule says how to get from each term to the next, such as 'add 3' or 'multiply by 2', and it is applied to the term before, not to the position. The triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, ... count the dots in triangle patterns: each new triangle adds a row one dot longer than the last. So each triangular number is a running total of the counting numbers (10 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4), and the gaps between them grow by one: +2, +3, +4, +5.2
    7.1.5.2Generate the triangular numbers from dot patterns, continue the sequence, and recognise whether a number is triangular.2
    7.1.5.3Generate terms of a sequence from a term-to-term rule, and find and describe the term-to-term rule of a sequence to continue it.2
    Sequences
    • Sequence rules

    3.1BSequence rules

    10.2.1.1A term-to-term rule gives the next term from the previous one; a position-to-term (nth term) rule gives any term directly from its position. An arithmetic sequence changes by the same amount, its common difference, each time - found by subtracting any term from the one after it. A negative common difference means the sequence decreases.3
    10.2.1.2Generate the terms of an arithmetic sequence from a given term-to-term or nth-term rule, including sequences with a negative common difference.4
    10.2.1.3Find the common difference of a given arithmetic sequence, including a decreasing sequence, and use it to continue the sequence.4

    • nth term of a linear sequence

    3.1Cnth term of a linear sequence

    8.14.3.3Find and use the nth term rule of an arithmetic sequence, including to test whether a number is a term.5
    10.2.2.1The nth term rule of an arithmetic sequence has the form dn + c, where d is the common difference and c is found by working back one step from the first term (c = first term - d). Substituting a position number into the rule generates that term directly, without working out every term before it.4
    10.2.2.2Find and use the nth term rule of an arithmetic sequence with an integer common difference to generate any term directly from its position.4
    10.2.2.3Find and use the nth term rule of an arithmetic sequence with a non-integer (fractional or decimal) common difference.5
    10.2.3.1Substituting a term's value into the nth term rule and solving for n tests whether that value is actually a term of the sequence - it is a term only if n comes out as a positive whole number. The same equation, solved for n, gives the position of a known term.4
    10.2.3.2Test whether a given number is a term of an arithmetic sequence, using its nth term rule.4
    10.2.3.3Find the position of a given term in an arithmetic sequence (including a decreasing sequence), using its nth term rule.4
    FM.4.8.2Find terms from an nth-term formula and form an equation in n to find which term meets a given condition, rejecting invalid values of n.6
    Sequences

    3.1A(H)First term and common difference

    8.14.3.1An arithmetic sequence goes up or down by the same amount each time, its common difference. The common difference is found by subtracting any term from the one after it. The nth term takes the form dn + c, where d is the common difference. c is found by working back one step from the first term, so c = first term - d. A number is a term of the sequence only if solving dn + c for it gives a positive whole number n.5

    Linear equations
    • Simple one step equations

    Simple one step equations

    7.11.2.2Solve one-step equations involving all four operations.2
    10.8.1.2Solve a one-step equation such as x + 7 = 12 or 4x = 20, and check the answer by substituting it back.2

    No matching specification point

    7.11.2.1An equation is solved by finding the value of the unknown that makes both sides equal. Whatever is done to one side must be done to the other, keeping the equation balanced. Applying the inverse operation undoes what was done to the unknown: + and - are inverses, as are x and /. Squares and square roots are inverses, as are cubes and cube roots.2
    Linear equations
    • One- and two-step equations

    2.4COne- and two-step equations

    7.11.2.3Solve one-step equations involving squares, cubes and roots.3
    7.11.3.2Solve two-step equations, including those with negative solutions.4
    7.11.3.3Solve two-step equations with a fractional term or fractional coefficient.4
    7.11.3.1A two-step equation applies two operations to the unknown, so solving undoes them in the reverse order. The operation applied last is undone first, working outwards from the unknown. A fractional coefficient is undone by multiplying, since x/4 means x divided by 4. A solution can be negative, and a negative solution is checked the same way as a positive one.3
    10.8.1.1An equation says that two expressions are equal, and solving it means finding the value of the letter that makes that true. Whatever is done to one side of an equation must be done to the other, so that the two sides stay equal. The operations are undone in reverse order: what was done to the letter last is undone first. A solution is checked by substituting it back into the original equation.2
    10.8.1.3Solve a two-step equation such as 3x + 5 = 20, including one with a division such as x/4 - 2 = 1.3
    Linear equations
    • Equations with brackets
    • Forming linear equations

    2.4AEquations with brackets

    7.11.4.1An equation containing brackets can be solved by expanding first, or by dividing both sides by the number outside. Dividing first is quicker only when every term on the other side divides exactly. Like terms on the same side are collected before the equation is unpicked. An unknown appearing more than once on one side is still a single unknown, so its terms combine.4
    7.11.4.2Solve multi-step equations involving brackets.4
    7.11.4.3Solve multi-step equations requiring like terms to be collected before solving.4
    7.11.5.2Solve equations of mixed types fluently, checking solutions by substitution.4
    10.8.2.1A bracket in an equation is expanded first, because a(b + c) = ab + ac, and the sign in front of a term travels with it. Like terms are collected on each side before the equation is undone. An equation with the whole of one side written over a number is cleared by multiplying both sides by that number. The number multiplying the letter may be a fraction, and the equation is undone in exactly the same way.4
    10.8.2.2Solve an equation containing a bracket, such as 7(x + 3) = 42, by expanding the bracket first.4
    10.8.2.3Solve an equation with a fractional coefficient, or with a whole side written over a number, such as (4x + 5)/2 = 3.4
    FM.1.3-1.4.1An equation containing fractions is cleared by multiplying every term by the LCM of the denominators. A 'show that' question requires the algebra to arrive at the stated result, not merely verify it numerically.6
    FM.1.3-1.4.2Solve linear equations with brackets on both sides and with fractional terms, and form equations from worded contexts.6

    2.4BForming linear equations

    7.11.1.3Form algebraic equations from worded and geometric contexts.4
    7.11.5.3Form and solve equations to answer worded and geometric problems (perimeter, angle facts).5
    8.6.2.3Form and solve equations from worded and geometric contexts.5
    10.8.4.1An equation is formed by naming the unknown with a letter, writing every other quantity in terms of that letter, and then using a fact that makes two expressions equal. In a geometric diagram that fact is usually an angle sum - 180 degrees on a line or in a triangle, 360 degrees at a point or in a quadrilateral - or a perimeter given as a total, or two sides known to be equal. What the letter stands for is written down before the equation is formed, including its units. The value of the letter is not always the answer to the question, so the question is read again once the equation is solved.4
    10.8.4.2Form and solve a linear equation from a worded context, stating what the letter stands for.4
    10.8.4.3Form and solve a linear equation from a geometric diagram, such as a triangle whose angles are a, (a + 10) and (a + 20) degrees, or a rectangle whose perimeter is given as a total.5

    2.4DEquations with the unknown on both sides

    7.11.6.2Solve equations with the unknown on both sides, including with brackets.5
    7.11.6.3Substitute known values into a formula and solve the resulting equation for the remaining unknown.5
    8.2.4.2Solve multi-step equations involving brackets and an unknown on both sides.5
    8.6.1.1However complicated an equation looks, the method is unchanged: expand any brackets, collect the unknown onto one side, then apply inverse operations. Brackets on both sides are expanded before anything is collected. Collecting the smaller unknown term onto the other side avoids a negative coefficient. A solution may be negative or fractional, and is checked the same way, by substituting it back.5
    8.6.1.2Solve multi-step equations with brackets on both sides.5
    8.6.1.3Solve equations with the unknown on both sides, including negative and fractional solutions.5
    8.6.2.1An equation containing a fraction is cleared by multiplying every term by the denominator. Where there is more than one denominator, multiplying by their LCM clears them all at once. Every term must be multiplied, including any term that is not itself a fraction. An unknown in the denominator is cleared the same way, by multiplying both sides by that denominator. A worded or geometric context becomes an equation once the unknown is named and the relationship written down.5
    8.6.2.2Solve equations with fractional terms and with the unknown in the denominator.5
    10.8.3.1When the letter appears on both sides, the terms in the letter are collected onto one side and the numbers onto the other. Adding or subtracting the same term from both sides is the same balancing move as adding or subtracting a number. Moving the smaller term in the letter keeps its coefficient positive, which avoids a negative coefficient to handle at the end.4
    10.8.3.2Solve an equation with the letter on both sides, such as 5x - 4 = 2x + 11.4
    10.8.3.3Solve an equation with the letter on both sides and a bracket on one of them, such as 7(x + 3) = 5x - 8.4
    10H.7.3.2Solve equations with fractional terms and with the unknown in the denominator.5
    10H.7.4.1An equation with the unknown on both sides is solved by expanding any brackets, collecting the unknown terms on one side by doing the same to both sides, then using inverse operations. Collecting on the side with the larger coefficient keeps the coefficient positive. A worded or geometric problem becomes an equation when a letter names one unknown quantity and two expressions for the same quantity are set equal, such as two equal perimeters or two ages after the same number of years. The value of the letter is not always the answer, so the question is read again once the equation is solved.5
    10H.7.4.2Solve multi-step equations involving brackets and an unknown on both sides.5
    10H.7.4.3Form an equation from a worded or geometric context with the unknown on both sides, solve it, and use the solution to answer the question asked.6
    11H.3.7.2Solve equations with fractional terms and with the unknown in the denominator.5

    7.11.6.1When the unknown appears on both sides, the terms in the unknown are collected onto one side first. Moving the smaller unknown term avoids a negative coefficient. An unknown in a denominator is cleared by multiplying both sides by that denominator. Substituting known values into a formula leaves an equation in the remaining unknown, solved the same way.5
    Inequalities
    • Open and closed intervals

    2.8BOpen and closed intervals

    7.15.1.1The symbols compare quantities: < is less than, > is greater than, <= is less than or equal to, >= is greater than or equal to. An inequality describes a range of values, not a single one. On a number line an open circle excludes the value and a filled circle includes it. An arrow shows the range continuing without end.3
    7.15.1.2Represent an inequality on a number line and write the inequality shown by a given number line.3
    10.20.2.1On a number line an open circle marks a value that is NOT included and a filled circle one that is, and an arrow shows that the set carries on. A double-ended inequality such as 1 < x <= 5 is the region between two such marks, with the circle at each end matching its own symbol. The integers that satisfy an inequality are the whole numbers lying inside the marked region, and an end value is one of them only where the circle is filled.5
    10.20.2.2Represent an inequality, including a double-ended one, on a number line, using open and filled circles correctly.5
    10.20.2.3List the integer values that satisfy a given inequality, including a double-ended one, and say how many there are.5

    No matching specification point

    7.15.5.1Axes may be scaled in steps other than one, so each square's value is read from the scale before plotting. The two axes can carry different scales from each other. The midpoint of a line segment has coordinates halfway between the endpoints in each direction. A shape is completed from given vertices by using its properties, such as equal or parallel sides.3

    2.8AInequality symbols

    7.15.1.3List the integer values satisfying an inequality.4
    7.15.2.1A double inequality such as -2 < x <= 5 states two conditions at once. It is read from the unknown outwards: x is greater than -2 and less than or equal to 5. On a number line it is a bounded region, with the circle at each end set by its own symbol. The integers it contains lie between the bounds, and a bound itself counts only when its symbol allows it.4
    7.15.2.3List integer values satisfying a double inequality, including with negative bounds.4
    8.2.1.3List the integer values satisfying a given inequality.4
    8.2.2.1A double inequality such as -3 < x <= 4 states two conditions at once. It is read from the unknown outwards: x is greater than -3 and less than or equal to 4. On a number line it is a bounded region, with the circle at each end set by its own symbol. The integers it contains lie between the bounds, and a bound itself counts only when its symbol allows it.4
    8.2.2.3List integer values satisfying a double inequality, including with negative bounds.4
    10.20.1.1The symbols are: < is less than, > is greater than, <= is less than or equal to, and >= is greater than or equal to. An inequality is solved by the same balancing moves as an equation, but the answer is a SET of values rather than a single value. Multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the direction of the inequality sign. A solution is checked by substituting one value from inside the set and one from outside it.5

    2.8CSolving linear inequalities

    7.15.3.1An inequality is solved like an equation, by applying inverse operations to both sides. The answer is a range of values, written in inequality notation rather than as x = a single number. The sign stays the same way round when adding, subtracting, multiplying or dividing by a positive number. A solution set can be shown on a number line, or listed as the integers it contains.4
    8.2.3.1An inequality is solved like an equation, by applying inverse operations to both sides. The answer is a range of values, written in inequality notation rather than as x = a single number. The sign stays the same way round when adding, subtracting, multiplying or dividing by a positive number. Multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the sign. A solution set can be shown on a number line, or listed as the integers it contains.4
