    Quadratic equations
    • Solving quadratics by factorising

    2.7ASolving quadratics by factorising

    9.8.4.2Solve a quadratic equation given in factorised form.5
    10.17.4.1If a product of two factors is zero then at least one factor is zero, so (x + p)(x + q) = 0 gives x = -p or x = -q. A quadratic equation must therefore be rearranged so that one side is zero before it is factorised. A quadratic equation usually has two solutions, and both are stated.5
    10.17.4.2Solve a quadratic equation of the form x^2 + bx + c = 0 by factorising.5
    10.17.4.3Rearrange an equation into the form x^2 + bx + c = 0 and solve it, rejecting any solution the context makes impossible.5
    10H.9.1.1If two numbers multiply to make zero, at least one of them is zero: if ab = 0 then a = 0 or b = 0. So a product of brackets equal to zero is solved by setting each bracket equal to zero in turn: (x - 3)(x + 5) = 0 gives x = 3 or x = -5. A factor of x on its own gives the solution x = 0, so x(x - 4) = 0 gives x = 0 or x = 4. A bracket with a coefficient of x gives a fraction: 2x - 3 = 0, so x = 3/2. The principle works only for zero: (x - 1)(x - 2) = 6 does not give x - 1 = 6 or x - 2 = 6.5
    10H.9.1.2Solve a quadratic equation given in factorised form.5
    10H.9.1.3Solve an equation given as a product of factors equal to zero where a factor is x itself or a bracket has a coefficient of x other than 1, such as x(3x + 2) = 0 or (2x - 1)(3x + 4) = 0.6
    10H.9.2.1The zero-product principle needs zero on one side, so every term of a quadratic equation is collected on one side first, keeping the x^2 term positive. x^2 + bx + c = 0 is factorised as (x + p)(x + q) = 0, where p + q = b and pq = c, and each bracket is then set to zero. The solutions are the numbers in the brackets with their signs changed: (x + 3)(x - 5) = 0 gives x = -3 or x = 5. Both sides are never divided by x, because that loses the solution x = 0. Each solution can be checked by substituting it into the original equation.6
    10H.9.2.3Rearrange a quadratic equation into the form x^2 + bx + c = 0 before solving it, including equations with terms on both sides or a bracket, such as x^2 = 3x + 10 or x(x + 2) = 24.6
    Quadratic equations
    • Solving quadratics

    Solving quadratics

    9.8.4.3Factorise and then solve a quadratic equation.6
    10H.9.2.2Factorise and then solve a quadratic equation.6
    10H.9.4.1A quadratic with no constant term, ax^2 + bx = 0, factorises by taking out x and its common number: 3x^2 - 12x = 0 gives 3x(x - 4) = 0, so x = 0 or x = 4. A quadratic with no x term, ax^2 - c = 0, is solved by making x^2 stand alone and taking both square roots: 2x^2 = 50 gives x^2 = 25, so x = 5 or x = -5. Both sides are never divided by x, because that loses the solution x = 0. An equation with brackets is expanded, and one with x in a denominator is multiplied through by x, before every term is collected on one side.6
    10H.9.4.2Solve quadratic equations with no constant term or no x term, giving both solutions.6
    10H.9.4.3Rearrange and solve quadratic equations that start with brackets, terms on both sides or x in a denominator, such as (x + 3)(x - 1) = 21 or x + 12/x = 7.7
    Quadratic equations
    • Harder quadratic factorising
    • Formula and completing the square

    2.7A(H)Harder quadratic factorising

    10H.9.3.1A non-monic quadratic ax^2 + bx + c, with a not 1, factorises as (px + q)(rx + s), so numbers that simply add to b and multiply to c no longer work. Splitting the middle term finds two numbers that multiply to a x c and add to b, rewrites bx as their sum, then factorises in pairs: 2x^2 + 7x + 3 = 2x^2 + 6x + x + 3 = 2x(x + 3) + 1(x + 3) = (2x + 1)(x + 3). Any common factor of all three terms is taken out first. Expanding the brackets checks the factorisation. Each bracket is then set to zero, and a bracket such as 2x + 1 gives a fractional solution, x = -1/2.7
    10H.9.3.3Solve quadratic equations of the form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 by factorising, rearranging first where needed and giving fractional solutions exactly.7

    2.7B(H)Formula and completing the square

    10H.9.5.1Any quadratic equation ax^2 + bx + c = 0 is solved by the formula x = (-b plus or minus the square root of (b^2 - 4ac)) / 2a, which is given in the exam. The equation is rearranged so that one side is zero first, and a, b and c are read with their signs: for 2x^2 - 3x - 4 = 0, a = 2, b = -3 and c = -4. The plus and the minus give the two solutions, and the whole numerator is divided by 2a. A negative b makes -b positive, and b^2 is never negative; the calculator needs brackets round a negative b. The formula is used when a quadratic does not factorise, and the solutions are rounded only at the end. If b^2 - 4ac is negative the equation has no real solutions.6
    10H.9.5.2Solve a quadratic equation using the quadratic formula, giving solutions to a stated accuracy.6
    10H.9.5.3Rearrange an equation into the form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 and solve it with the formula, deciding when factorising is quicker and recognising when there are no real solutions.7
    FM.4.1.1A quadratic has two roots, which may be equal. It can be solved by factorising, by completing the square, or using the quadratic formula x = (-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / (2a), which is itself derived by completing the square on the general form ax^2 + bx + c = 0.7
    FM.4.1.2Solve a quadratic by rearranging to zero and factorising, and by completing the square including with a non-unit leading coefficient.8
    FM.4.1.3Solve a quadratic using the formula, giving answers in exact surd form or rounded, and form and solve quadratics from context.8
    Quadratic equations
    • Quadratics from context

    2.7C(H)Quadratics from context

    10H.9.6.1A worded or geometric problem becomes a quadratic equation when a letter names the unknown length or number and two expressions for one quantity, such as an area, are set equal. The equation is rearranged so that one side is zero and solved by factorising or by the formula. A solution that is impossible in the context, such as a negative length, is rejected with a reason; a negative number the context allows is kept. The value of the letter is not always the answer, so it is substituted back to find the quantity the question asks for.6
    10H.9.6.2Form a quadratic equation from an area, number or geometric context and solve it.6
    10H.9.6.3Solve a quadratic problem in context, rejecting any impossible solution with a reason and using the valid one to answer the question asked.7
    Quadratic equations
    • Linear and quadratic simultaneously

    2.7D(H)Linear and quadratic simultaneously

    9.8.4.1If a product equals zero then at least one of its factors must be zero, which is the zero-product principle. So (x + p)(x + q) = 0 gives x = -p or x = -q. A quadratic must have zero on one side before it is factorised, so every term is collected there first. A quadratic equation usually has two solutions, and both are stated.6
    11H.3.2.1When one equation is linear and the other is quadratic, the linear one is rearranged to make x or y the subject and that expression is substituted, in a bracket, into the quadratic one. The result is a quadratic equation in one unknown: it is rearranged to = 0 and solved by factorising or by the formula. It can have two, one or no real solutions, matching a line that crosses a curve twice, touches it once, or misses it. Each value is substituted into the LINEAR equation to find its partner, and the solutions are given as pairs. x^2 + y^2 = r^2 is a circle centred on the origin with radius r, so a line and this circle are solved the same way.9
    11H.3.2.2Solve a linear and a quadratic equation simultaneously by substitution, giving the solutions as pairs.9
    11H.3.2.3Find the points where a straight line meets the circle x^2 + y^2 = r^2.9
    FM.4.2.1Simultaneous equations describe the intersection of two graphs. A linear-quadratic pair generally gives two solution pairs, and x and y values must be correctly paired.8
    FM.4.2.3Solve linear-quadratic simultaneous equations by substitution, pairing the solutions correctly.8
    Simultaneous linear equations
    • Simultaneous equations
    • Graphical solutions

    2.6ASimultaneous equations

    9.14.3.1Adding or subtracting two true equations produces a third equation that is also true. If a variable has the same coefficient in both, subtracting removes it; if the coefficients are equal but opposite, adding removes it. Removing one variable leaves a single equation in the other, which solves as usual. The value found is substituted back into either original equation to give the second unknown. Same signs subtract, different signs add.5
    9.14.3.2Solve simultaneous equations by elimination where the coefficients already match.5
    9.14.3.3Decide whether to add or subtract the equations based on the signs.5
    9.14.4.1Multiplying an entire equation by any number keeps it true, since both sides change equally. So one or both equations can be scaled until a variable's coefficients match. Every term must be multiplied, including the constant on the right-hand side. The LCM of the two coefficients gives the smallest numbers to work with. Substituting the answer into both original equations checks it, since it has to satisfy both.6
    9.14.4.2Multiply one or both equations to match coefficients, then eliminate.6
    9.14.4.3Solve and check the answer by substituting into both original equations.6
    9.14.5.1Either variable may be eliminated, and choosing the one with the easier coefficients reduces the arithmetic. A solution can be negative or fractional, and is checked in exactly the same way. A worded problem gives two conditions, and each condition becomes one equation. The two unknowns are named explicitly before either equation is written.6
    9.14.6.1Where one equation already gives a variable on its own, that expression can replace the variable in the other equation. The result is a single equation in one unknown. The substituted expression is bracketed, so that any multiplication reaches all of it. Substitution suits a pair where one equation is already rearranged; elimination suits a pair where neither is.6
    9.14.6.2Solve simultaneous equations by substitution.6
    9.14.6.3Choose between elimination and substitution for a given pair of equations.6
    9.14.7.1Two unknowns need two independent equations, which a worded problem supplies as two separate conditions. Two equations are independent only if neither is a rearrangement or a multiple of the other. Costs and totals give the commonest pair: one equation for the quantities, one for the money. The answer is interpreted back in context, with units, and checked for sense.6
    11H.3.1.1Where one equation already gives a variable on its own, that expression can replace the variable in the other equation. The result is a single equation in one unknown. The substituted expression is bracketed, so that any multiplication reaches all of it. Substitution suits a pair where one equation is already rearranged; elimination suits a pair where neither is.6
    11H.3.1.2Solve simultaneous equations by substitution.6
    11H.3.1.3Choose between elimination and substitution for a given pair of equations.6

    Graphical solutions

    9.14.1.1Simultaneous equations are two equations in two unknowns that must both hold at once. Every point on a line satisfies that line's own equation, so the point where two lines cross satisfies both. That crossing point is therefore the solution, read off as a coordinate pair. A line can only be drawn once its equation gives y from x, so an equation with x and y on the same side is rearranged first.5
    9.14.1.2Draw two linear graphs and read off their point of intersection.5
    9.14.1.3Rearrange an equation with x and y on the same side before drawing it.6
    9.14.2.2Solve simultaneous equations graphically, giving the solution as a coordinate pair.5

    No matching specification point

    Simultaneous linear equations
    • Harder simultaneous equations
    • Advanced graphical solutions

    2.6A(H)Harder simultaneous equations

    9.14.5.2Solve simultaneous equations with negative and fractional solutions.6
    9.14.5.3Form and solve simultaneous equations from worded problems.6
    9.14.7.2Form simultaneous equations from contexts such as costs and totals.6
    9.14.7.3Solve them and interpret the answer back in context.6
    FM.4.2.2Solve linear-linear simultaneous equations by elimination and by substitution.6

    2.6B(H)Advanced graphical solutions

    9.14.2.1The solution is written as a coordinate pair, or as separate x = and y = values. Parallel lines never meet, so a pair of equations with equal gradients has no solution. Two equations describing the same line meet everywhere, so they have infinitely many solutions. In a real context the axes carry meaning, so the intersection is where the two situations give the same value. A graphical solution is only as accurate as the scale allows, so it may need reading to the nearest half square.6
    9.14.2.3Interpret what the point of intersection means in a real context.6

    No matching specification point

    9.14.9.1x^2 + y^2 = r^2 is a circle centred on the origin with radius r. It follows from Pythagoras, since every point on the circle is r away from the origin. The radius is the square root of the number on the right, not that number itself. Three unknowns need three independent equations, eliminated one variable at a time down to a pair.7
    9.14.9.2Recognise and sketch the graph of x^2 + y^2 = r^2.7
    9.14.9.3Solve three simultaneous equations in three unknowns.7
    Function notation
    • Function notation

    3.2B(H)Function notation

    11H.9.1.1A function is a rule that gives exactly one output for each input, like a function machine. f(x) = 3x + 2 names the rule f, and f(4) is the output when the input is 4: f(4) = 3 x 4 + 2 = 14. The same rule may be written f: x -> 3x + 2. The x in the rule is a placeholder, so f(-2), f(a) and f(2x) replace every x with that input, in a bracket. f(x) = k is an equation asking which input gives the output k, so it is solved for x, not substituted into.6
    11H.9.1.2Evaluate a function for a numerical or algebraic input, such as f(-3) or f(2a).6
    11H.9.1.3Solve equations written in function notation, such as f(x) = 17 or f(x) = g(x).6
    FM.3.1-3.2.2Evaluate a function for numeric and algebraic inputs, and solve f(x) = k.6
    Function notation
    • Functions as mappings
    • Domain and range

    3.2A(H)Functions as mappings

    11H.9.8.1The graph of y = f(x) plots each input x against its output f(x), so f(a) = b means the point (a, b) lies on the graph. f(x) = k is solved by reading the x-values where the line y = k meets the graph, and the roots of f(x) = 0 are where the graph crosses the x-axis. The domain is the span of x-values the graph covers, and the range is the span of its heights. The graph of y = f^-1(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x, because the inverse swaps each point (a, b) to (b, a).7
    11H.9.8.2Read values of f(x), and solve equations such as f(x) = k, from the graph of a function.7
    11H.9.8.3Find values of an inverse function from a graph, and sketch y = f^-1(x) by reflecting y = f(x) in the line y = x.8

    3.2C(H)Domain and range

    11H.9.2.1The domain of a function is the set of inputs it may take, and the range is the set of outputs it produces. An input is excluded from the domain when the rule cannot use it: a denominator cannot be 0, and a square root cannot take a negative number. So f(x) = 1/(x - 2) has domain x not equal to 2, and g(x) = the square root of (x - 3) has domain x >= 3. The range comes from the outputs: a square is never negative, so x^2 + 1 has range f(x) >= 1. The domain is written as an inequality in x, and the range as an inequality in f(x).7
    11H.9.2.2Find the values that must be excluded from the domain of a function with a denominator or a square root.7
    11H.9.2.3Find the range of a function built from a square or a square root, such as x^2 - 4 or 5 + the square root of x.7
    11H.9.3.1A function can be defined on a limited domain, such as f(x) = 2x + 1 for 0 <= x <= 5, and its range then comes only from those inputs. A linear function's range runs between its outputs at the two ends of the domain: here 1 <= f(x) <= 11. A decreasing function has its least output at the right-hand end, and the range is still written smallest first. A quadratic's least or greatest output is at its turning point when that lies inside the domain, so its range is not found from the ends alone. A strict end of the domain, <, gives a strict end of the range.7
    11H.9.3.2Find the range of a linear function on a given limited domain, including a decreasing function.7
    11H.9.3.3Find the range of a quadratic function on a limited domain, using its turning point when it lies inside the domain.8
    11H.9.4.1A piecewise function uses different rules on different parts of its domain, each rule written with its own interval. To evaluate it, first find the interval the input lies in, then use that rule only. At a boundary the inequality signs say which rule owns the point: x < 3 excludes 3, and x >= 3 includes it. Its graph is drawn piece by piece, each rule over its own interval only, with an open circle at an excluded end. f(x) = k is solved rule by rule, and a solution is kept only if it lies in that rule's interval.8
    11H.9.4.2Evaluate a piecewise function and sketch its graph from linear and quadratic pieces.8
    11H.9.4.3Solve f(x) = k for a piecewise function, rejecting any solution outside its own interval.8
    FM.3.1-3.2.1A function assigns exactly one output to each input. The domain is the set of permitted inputs and the range the set of outputs it produces, so excluded values such as division by zero restrict the domain.6
    FM.3.1-3.2.3State the domain and range of a function, reading them from a sketch graph where helpful.7
    Function notation
    • Composite and inverse functions

    3.2D(H)Composite and inverse functions

    11H.9.5.1A composite function applies one function to the output of another. fg(x) means f(g(x)): g acts first and f second, because the function written next to x acts first. fg(x) and gf(x) are usually different, and ff(x) means f(f(x)), not f(x) squared. fg(x) is found algebraically by putting the whole of g(x), in a bracket, in place of every x in f(x).7
    11H.9.5.2Evaluate a composite function such as fg(3) or ff(-1), working from the inside out.6
    11H.9.5.3Find a composite function such as fg(x) algebraically, and solve an equation such as fg(x) = 7.7
    11H.9.6.1The inverse function f^-1 reverses f: if f(3) = 11, then f^-1(11) = 3. It undoes the steps of f in reverse order, like a function machine run backwards. To find f^-1(x), write y = f(x), make x the subject, then write the result with x as the input. f^-1(x) is not 1/f(x): the -1 names the inverse, not a reciprocal. Applying a function and then its inverse returns the input: f^-1(f(x)) = x.7
    11H.9.6.2Find the inverse of a linear function, such as f(x) = 3x - 5 or f(x) = (x + 4)/2, and evaluate it.6
    11H.9.6.3Find the inverse of a function involving a power, a root or a reciprocal, such as f(x) = 2x^3 + 1 or f(x) = 6/(x - 1).7
    11H.9.7.1When x appears twice in y = f(x), as in y = (2x + 1)/(x - 3), the denominator is cleared, the x terms are collected on one side and x is factorised out, as in changing the subject. The domain of f^-1 is the range of f, and the range of f^-1 is the domain of f. A function has an inverse only when each output comes from one input, so a quadratic needs a limited domain, such as x >= 0, first. An equation such as f^-1(x) = 4 is solved most simply as x = f(4).8
    11H.9.7.2Find the inverse of a function where x appears twice, such as f(x) = (2x + 1)/(x - 3), by collecting the x terms and factorising.8
    11H.9.7.3Solve equations involving inverse and composite functions, such as f^-1(x) = 4 or f^-1(x) = g(x).8
    FM.3.3.1In the composite fg(x) the inner function g is applied first. Composition is different from adding, multiplying or dividing functions, and is not generally commutative.8
    FM.3.3.2Form and evaluate composite functions, including fgh(x) and f^2(x).8
    FM.3.3.3Combine functions by addition, multiplication and division, distinguishing these from composition.7
    FM.3.8-3.9.1An inverse function undoes the original, so it exists only where the function is one-to-one over its domain. An exponential graph y = a^x passes through (0,1), and replacing x by -x reflects it in the y-axis.8
    FM.3.8-3.9.2Find an inverse function by reversing the operations, or algebraically by interchanging x and y and rearranging.7
    Proportion
    • Direct and inverse proportion

    2.5A(H)Direct and inverse proportion

    Calculus
    • Variable rate of change
    • Differentiating powers of x
    • Maxima and minima

    3.4A(H)Variable rate of change

    3.4B(H)Differentiating powers of x

    11H.7.2.1The gradient function dy/dx gives the gradient of a curve at every point. For y = x^n, dy/dx = n x^(n - 1): the power multiplies, then drops by one; so y = a x^n gives dy/dx = a n x^(n - 1). A term in x differentiates to its coefficient, and a constant differentiates to 0, because its graph is flat. A sum or difference is differentiated term by term. The gradient at a point is found by substituting its x-value into dy/dx, not into y.8
    11H.7.2.2Differentiate expressions of the form a x^n for positive integer n, term by term, including x terms and constants.8
    11H.7.2.3Find the gradient of a curve at a given point by differentiating and substituting the x-value.8
    11H.7.3.1The rule differentiates one power of x at a time, so an expression is rewritten as a sum of powers of x first. Brackets are expanded before differentiating, never differentiated factor by factor. A fraction with a single term underneath splits into separate terms: (x^3 + 2x)/x = x^2 + 2. A power of x underneath becomes a negative power: 1/x = x^(-1) and 4/x^2 = 4x^(-2). The same rule works for negative integer powers: the power multiplies and drops by one, so x^(-2) gives -2x^(-3).8
    11H.7.3.2Differentiate expressions that need expanding first, such as (x + 3)(2x - 1) or (2x - 5)^2.8
    11H.7.3.3Differentiate expressions with negative integer powers of x, such as 4/x^2 or (x^3 + 2)/x, by rewriting them first.9
    11H.7.5.1The tangent at a point has the same gradient as the curve there, so m is found by substituting the x-value into dy/dx. The tangent passes through the point itself, so substituting the point into y = mx + c gives c. When only x is given, the y-coordinate of the point is found from the equation of the curve first. The point where the gradient takes a given value is found by setting dy/dx equal to that value and solving; a tangent parallel to a line has that line's gradient.8
    11H.7.5.2Find the equation of the tangent to a curve at a given point.8
    11H.7.5.3Find the point or points on a curve where the gradient takes a given value, including where a tangent is parallel to a given line.9

    3.4D(H)Maxima and minima

    Calculus
    • Stationary and turning points
    • Kinematics

    3.4C(H)Stationary and turning points

    11H.7.4.1At a stationary point the tangent is horizontal, so the gradient is zero: stationary points are found by solving dy/dx = 0. Solving gives the x-coordinate; substituting it into the equation of the curve gives the y-coordinate. A maximum has a positive gradient just before it and a negative gradient just after; a minimum is the other way round. A function is increasing where dy/dx > 0 and decreasing where dy/dx < 0.8
    11H.7.4.2Find the coordinates of the stationary points of a quadratic or cubic curve by solving dy/dx = 0.8
    11H.7.4.3Decide whether a stationary point is a maximum or a minimum from the gradient either side, and find where a function is increasing or decreasing.9

    3.4E(H)Kinematics

    11H.7.6.1For displacement s as a function of time t, velocity is the rate of change of displacement, v = ds/dt, and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, a = dv/dt. The velocity at a time is found by substituting t into v, not into s. A particle is momentarily at rest when v = 0, so the times are found by solving v = 0, rejecting any negative time. The units follow the chain: s in m, v in m/s, a in m/s^2.8
    11H.7.6.2Find the velocity and acceleration of a particle at a given time by differentiating its displacement.8
    11H.7.6.3Find when a particle is at rest, and its displacement or acceleration at that time.9
    NumberArithmetic, ratio and proportion
    Integers
    • Positive, negative and zero
    • Ordering integers
    • Place value

    1.1APositive, negative and zero

    1.1DOrdering integers

    10.1.1.2Order a set of positive and negative integers and decimals.2

    1.1BPlace value

    7.5.1.1A digit's value depends on its place: in 3407 the 4 is 4 hundreds. Only digits of the same place value combine directly, which is why columns line up by place. Ten of any place is worth one of the place to its left, so carrying trades ten ones for one ten. Exchange in subtraction is that trade in reverse. Addition works in any order; subtraction does not, since 7 - 3 and 3 - 7 differ. Multiplication is repeated addition and works in any order. Grid and column methods split a number by place value, multiply each part, then add the parts.1
    10.1.1.1A digit's value comes from its place-value column, not just which digit it is. To compare two numbers, line up place values and compare digit by digit from the most significant place - the first place that differs decides which number is larger; for negative numbers, the value further from zero is the smaller one. Multiplying by 10 shifts every digit one place-value column to the left; dividing by 10 shifts every digit one column to the right - the decimal point doesn't move, the digits move around it.1
    Integers
    • Categorising integers
    • The four operations
    • Directed number

    1.1GCategorising integers

    7.1.1.1A factor divides into a number exactly; factors come in pairs that multiply to the number. A multiple is a number multiplied by a positive integer. Even numbers are multiples of 2; odd numbers are not. A prime has exactly two factors, 1 and itself, so 1 is not prime and 2 is the only even prime. In index notation 3^4 means 3x3x3x3: the base is multiplied by itself, the index says how often.2
    7.1.1.2Identify odd/even numbers, and list factors (including factor pairs) and multiples of a given number.2

    1.1EThe four operations

    7.5.1.2Add and subtract integers without a calculator, including with carrying and exchange/borrowing.1
    7.5.1.3Multiply integers without a calculator (column/grid method).2
    7.5.2.2Divide integers without a calculator (short division).2
    7.5.4.3Evaluate mixed calculations involving all four operations with negatives, including powers of negative numbers.4
    8.1.3.2Derive related multiplication and division facts from a given calculation.4

    1.1CDirected number

    7.5.3.1On a number line, adding moves right and subtracting moves left, whatever the signs. Adding a negative subtracts: 5 + (-3) = 5 - 3 = 2. Subtracting a negative adds: 5 - (-3) = 5 + 3 = 8. Two adjacent signs combine: '+ -' and '- +' give minus, '- -' gives plus. A difference is the distance between two values, so it is never negative: from -4 to 3 is 7.2
    7.5.3.2Add and subtract with negative numbers, including using a number line.2
    7.5.3.3Solve calculations and worded problems involving directed number addition and subtraction (e.g. temperature change).3
    7.5.4.1Two numbers with the same sign multiply or divide to a positive. Two numbers with different signs give a negative. In a longer product, an odd number of negative factors gives a negative result, an even number a positive. Even powers of a negative are positive, odd powers negative: (-2)^2 = 4, (-2)^3 = -8.3
    7.5.4.2Multiply and divide with negative numbers.3
    10.1.2.1Adding a positive number moves right on a number line and adding a negative number moves left; subtracting works the opposite way, so subtracting a negative has the same effect as adding a positive. When multiplying or dividing directed numbers, work out the size of the answer first, then decide its sign separately: same signs (both positive or both negative) give a positive answer, different signs give a negative answer.2
    10.1.2.2Add and subtract directed numbers.2
    10.1.2.3Multiply and divide directed numbers.3
    Integers
    • Squares, cubes and roots
    • Priority of operations
    • Factors and multiples
    • Prime factorisation

    1.4ASquares, cubes and roots

    7.5.2.1Division is the inverse of multiplication and does not work in any order, since 12 / 3 and 3 / 12 differ. Short division works through a number one place at a time from the left, carrying any remainder into the next place. n-squared is n x n; n-cubed is n x n x n. A root is the inverse of a power: square-root-25 = 5 because 5^2 = 25, and cube-root-8 = 2 because 2^3 = 8. Squares to know: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, 121, 144. Cubes: 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 1000.3
    7.5.2.3Evaluate squares, cubes, square roots and cube roots of common values without a calculator.3

    1.1FPriority of operations

    7.5.5.1Operations run in a fixed order: Brackets, Indices, Multiplication and Division, Addition and Subtraction. Multiplication and division rank equally, as do addition and subtraction; equal ranks work left to right. A fraction bar and a root sign group everything inside them, acting as invisible brackets. Brackets override the default order, which is why inserting them changes the answer.3
    7.5.5.2Evaluate multi-operation calculations using the correct order of operations.3
    7.5.5.3Insert brackets to make a calculation true and identify errors in worked calculations that break the order of operations.4
    10.1.5.1The order of operations convention is: brackets first, then indices, then multiplication and division left to right, then addition and subtraction left to right. A negative sign directly in front of a power with no brackets applies after the power is evaluated, not to the base - so -2^2 means -(2^2) = -4, not (-2)^2 = 4.2
    10.1.5.2Evaluate expressions involving brackets and indices using the correct order of operations.3
    10.1.5.3Evaluate expressions involving all four operations, indices and negative numbers using the correct order of operations.3

    1.1HFactors and multiples

    7.1.2.1Divisible means dividing exactly, with no remainder, so 'divisible by n' and 'has n as a factor' mean the same. By 2: the last digit is even. By 4: the last two digits form a multiple of 4. By 8: the last three digits form a multiple of 8. By 5: the last digit is 0 or 5. By 10: the last digit is 0. By 3: the digits add to a multiple of 3. By 9: the digits add to a multiple of 9. By 6: divisible by both 2 and 3. Factors come in pairs, so testing divisors up to the square root finds every factor.3
    7.1.2.2Apply the divisibility rules for 2, 3, 5, 9 and 10 to test a number and to find all the factors of a 2- or 3-digit number efficiently.3
    7.1.2.3Apply the divisibility rules for 4, 6 and 8 to test a number and to find all the factors of a 2- or 3-digit number efficiently.3
    7.1.3.1Common factors are the factors two numbers share; the HCF is the largest. Common multiples are the multiples they share; the LCM is the smallest. The HCF is at least 1; the LCM is at most the two numbers multiplied. Splitting or grouping into equal parts needs the HCF; two repeating events coinciding needs the LCM.3
    7.1.3.2Find the HCF and LCM of two numbers by listing factors/multiples and identifying those in common.3
    7.1.3.3Recognise whether a worded problem requires the HCF or the LCM and solve it.4
    9.1.3.3Recognise whether a worded problem requires the HCF or the LCM, and solve it.4
    10.1.3.1A factor of a number divides into it exactly, with no remainder. A multiple of a number is what you get by multiplying it by a whole number. A prime number has exactly two factors, 1 and itself - so 1 is not prime, because it only has one factor. Every whole number greater than 1 breaks down into a unique product of prime numbers (its prime factorisation); a factor tree finds this by repeatedly splitting a number into a factor pair and continuing to split any factor that isn't yet prime.1
    10.1.3.2List all the factors of a number and the first several multiples of a number, and identify prime numbers up to 100.2
    10.1.4.2Find the HCF and LCM of two numbers by listing factors and multiples.3

    1.4DPrime factorisation

    7.1.1.3Identify prime numbers and interpret index (power) notation as repeated multiplication.3
    8.1.1.1Every whole number above 1 is prime, or a product of primes in exactly one way. A factor tree splits a number until every branch ends in a prime, and the primes are the same whichever pair is split first. Index form collects the repeats: 360 = 2^3 x 3^2 x 5. The HCF takes the lower power of each prime the two numbers share; the LCM takes the higher power of every prime appearing in either. In a Venn of the two factorisations, the HCF is the product of the intersection and the LCM the product of the whole diagram.3
    8.1.1.2Express a number as a product of its prime factors using a factor tree, writing the answer in index form.3
    9.1.1.1Every whole number above 1 is prime, or a product of primes in exactly one way. A factor tree splits a number until every branch ends in a prime, and the primes are the same whichever pair is split first. Index form collects the repeats: 360 = 2^3 x 3^2 x 5. A calculator's FACT function returns the prime factorisation directly, which matters for numbers too large to tree by hand.3
    9.1.1.2Express a number as a product of its prime factors using a factor tree, in index form.3
    10.1.3.3Express a number as a product of its prime factors using a factor tree.3

    No matching specification point

    7.5.6.1An index says how many times the base is used as a factor: 2^5 = 2x2x2x2x2. Multiplying powers of the same base adds the indices: a^m x a^n = a^(m+n). Dividing subtracts them: a^m / a^n = a^(m-n). Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1, since a^n / a^n is both 1 and a^0. A power outside a bracket applies to every factor inside: (2a)^3 = 2^3 x a^3 = 8a^3. The laws need the same base, so 2^3 x 3^2 cannot be combined.4
    Integers
    • HCF and LCM by prime factorisation

    1.4EHCF and LCM by prime factorisation

    7.1.4.1Every whole number above 1 is prime, or a product of primes in exactly one way. A factor tree splits a number until every branch ends in a prime, and the primes are the same whichever pair is split first. Index form collects the repeats: 60 = 2x2x3x5 = 2^2 x 3 x 5. In a prime-factor Venn, the HCF is the product of the intersection and the LCM the product of the whole diagram.4
    7.1.4.3Use a Venn diagram of prime factors to find the HCF and LCM of two numbers.5
    8.1.1.3Use prime factor decomposition to find the HCF and LCM of two numbers.4
    8.1.2.3Use the calculator's FACT function to decompose large numbers, and find the HCF and LCM of three numbers.4
    9.1.3.1The HCF is the product of the primes the two numbers share, each taken to the lower of its two powers. The LCM is the product of every prime appearing in either number, each taken to the higher power. In a Venn of the two factorisations, the HCF is the product of the intersection and the LCM the product of the whole diagram. Listing gives the same answers, but becomes impractical as the numbers grow. Splitting or grouping into equal parts needs the HCF; two repeating events coinciding needs the LCM.4
    9.1.3.2Find the HCF and LCM by listing, and by prime factorisation using a Venn diagram.4
    10.1.4.1The Highest Common Factor (HCF) of two numbers is the largest number that divides into both exactly; the Lowest Common Multiple (LCM) is the smallest number that both numbers divide into exactly. Using prime factorisation, the HCF is the product of the primes common to both numbers, each raised to the lower of the two powers; the LCM is the product of every prime appearing in either number, each raised to the higher of the two powers.2
    10.1.4.3Find the HCF and LCM of two numbers using prime factorisation, and use them to solve a simple context problem.4

    No matching specification point

    8.1.5.1Time is measured in base 60: 60 seconds make a minute and 60 minutes an hour. Decimal time and clock time are different, so 1.5 hours is 1 hour 30 minutes, not 1 hour 50 minutes. A decimal fraction of an hour converts to minutes by multiplying by 60, and minutes convert back by dividing by 60. The calculator's DMS key converts between the two forms directly. A rate given per hour applies to decimal time, so a duration must be converted before multiplying.4
    8.1.5.2Convert between decimal time and hours/minutes/seconds using the calculator's DMS function.4
    7.1.4.2Find the prime factor decomposition of a number using a factor tree (index and non-index form).4
    8.1.3.1A known calculation generates a family of related facts without any recalculation. Scaling one number by a power of ten scales the answer by that same power. Scaling one number up and the other down by the same factor leaves the product unchanged. Multiplication and division are inverses, so 24 x 15 = 360 also gives 360 / 15 = 24 and 360 / 24 = 15. A decimal calculation is the whole-number one rescaled, so 2.4 x 1.5 = 3.6 follows from 24 x 15 = 360.4
    Integers
    • Advanced prime factorisation

    Advanced prime factorisation

    8.1.2.1A square number has only even powers in its prime factorisation, because squaring doubles every power. A cube number has only powers that are multiples of three, for the same reason. The smallest multiplier making a number square is the product of the primes whose powers are odd. For three numbers, the HCF takes the lowest power of each prime shared by all three and the LCM the highest power of every prime appearing in any of them. A calculator's FACT function gives a prime factorisation directly, which matters for numbers too large to tree by hand.5
    8.1.2.2Use prime factor decomposition to determine whether a number is a square or a cube, and find the smallest multiplier that makes it one.5
    9.1.2.1A square number has only even powers in its prime factorisation, because squaring doubles every power. A cube number has only powers that are multiples of three, for the same reason. The smallest multiplier making a number square is the product of the primes whose powers are odd. The smallest multiplier making it a cube brings every power up to the next multiple of three.5
    9.1.2.2Determine from its prime factorisation whether a number is a square or a cube.5
    9.1.2.3Find the smallest multiplier that makes a number a square or a cube.5
    9.1.4.2Solve worded problems requiring the HCF or LCM, including with three numbers.5

    No matching specification point

    8.1.5.3Solve problems involving durations, timetables and rates expressed in time.5
    Integers
    • Algebraic HCF / LCM

    1.4GAlgebraic HCF / LCM

    9.1.4.1With three numbers the HCF takes the lowest power of each prime shared by all three, and the LCM the highest power of every prime appearing in any of them. Algebraic terms work the same way, treating each letter as a prime factor. The HCF of algebraic terms takes the lowest power of each shared letter, so the HCF of 12x^3y and 18x^2 is 6x^2. The LCM takes the highest power of every letter appearing, so the LCM of those two terms is 36x^3y.6
    9.1.4.3Find the HCF and LCM of algebraic terms.6
    Powers and roots
    • Index laws, integer powers

    1.4CIndex laws, integer powers

    7.5.6.2Simplify numerical expressions using the multiplication and division laws of indices, including the power of 0.5
    10.10.1.3Rewrite a power with a different base using the power law, for example writing 8^4 as 2^12.4
    10.6.1.1An index says how many times the base is used as a factor (e.g. 2 to the power 5 = 2x2x2x2x2); multiplying powers of the same base adds the indices (a^m x a^n = a^(m+n)) and dividing subtracts them (a^m / a^n = a^(m-n)). Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1.3
    10.6.1.2Simplify numerical expressions using the multiplication and division laws of indices, including the power of 0.4
    10.6.1.3Recognise square and cube numbers in index form and apply the multiplication/division laws to expressions involving them.4
    10.6.2.1A negative index means a reciprocal, for any base, not only base 10: a^-n = 1/a^n. This extends the same pattern already met for 10^-n = 1/10^n to any number.4
    10.6.2.2Evaluate and simplify expressions with a negative index for any base (not only base 10), including combining with the multiplication and division laws.4
    10.6.2.3Simplify expressions combining positive, negative and zero indices of the same base.4
    10H.5.1.1An index says how many times the base is used as a factor: 2^5 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2. Multiplying powers of the same base adds the indices, a^m x a^n = a^(m+n); dividing subtracts them, a^m / a^n = a^(m-n); a power of a power multiplies them, (a^m)^n = a^(mn). Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1, since a^n / a^n is both 1 and a^0. A power outside a bracket applies to every factor inside, coefficients included: (ab)^n = a^n x b^n, so (3x^2)^3 = 27x^6. The laws need the same base, so 2^3 x 3^2 cannot be combined into one power.4
    10H.5.1.3Raise a bracket containing multiple items to a power, applying the power to every factor inside.5
    10H.6.1.1A base that is itself a power can be rewritten: 8 = 2^3, so 8^4 = (2^3)^4 = 2^12 by the power law. A reciprocal or a root of the base is a power of it too: 1/8 = 2^-3 and the square root of 2 = 2^(1/2). Once every part is written over one base, a product or a quotient becomes a single power: 4^3 x 8 = 2^6 x 2^3 = 2^9. Two powers of the same base are equal only when their indices are equal, so 2^x = 2^9 means x = 9.6
    10H.6.1.2Rewrite a power with a different base using the power law, for example writing 8^4 as 2^12.4
    10H.6.1.3Write a product or quotient of powers as a single power of one base, and solve an equation with the unknown in the index by writing both sides as powers of the same base, such as 4^x = 8^3 or 3^(x + 1) = 1/27.7

    Powers and roots
    • Surds

    1.4A(H)Surds

    11H.1.1.1A surd is a square root that cannot be written exactly as a whole number or a fraction, such as the square root of 2; the square root of 9 = 3 is not a surd. The square root of (ab) = the square root of a x the square root of b, so the square root of 12 = the square root of 4 x the square root of 3 = 2 x the square root of 3. A surd is simplified by taking out the largest square factor of the number inside. The square root of a x the square root of a = a, and the square root of a / the square root of b = the square root of (a/b). The square root of (a + b) is not the square root of a + the square root of b.6
    11H.1.1.2Simplify a surd by taking out the largest square factor, such as the square root of 72 = 6 x the square root of 2.6
    11H.1.1.3Multiply and divide surds, simplifying the answer, such as 2 x the square root of 6 x the square root of 3.7
    11H.1.2.1Like surds collect like terms: 3 x the square root of 2 + 5 x the square root of 2 = 8 x the square root of 2, but the square root of 2 + the square root of 3 cannot be simplified. Surds with different numbers inside may become like surds once simplified: the square root of 8 + the square root of 18 = 2 x the square root of 2 + 3 x the square root of 2 = 5 x the square root of 2. Brackets containing surds expand as in algebra, every term times every term, using the square root of a x the square root of a = a. (a + the square root of b)(a - the square root of b) = a^2 - b, a whole number, because the surd terms cancel.7
    11H.1.2.2Add and subtract surds, simplifying them first to find like surds.7
    11H.1.2.3Expand and simplify brackets containing surds, such as (3 + the square root of 2)(1 - the square root of 2) or (2 + the square root of 5)^2.8
    FM.1.7.1A surd simplifies by extracting the largest square factor. Multiplying a two-term surd expression by its conjugate eliminates the surd, which is what makes rationalising a two-term denominator possible.7
    FM.1.7.2Simplify, multiply and add surds, and expand brackets containing surds.7
    Powers and roots
    • Fractional and negative indices

    1.4C(H)Fractional and negative indices

    10H.5.2.1A negative index means a reciprocal: a^-n = 1/a^n for any non-zero base, which follows from the division law, since a^2 / a^5 = a^(2-5) = a^-3 and also 1/a^3. A negative index makes a value smaller, never negative: 2^-3 = 1/8, not -8. A fraction raised to a negative power is turned over and the power made positive: (a/b)^-n = (b/a)^n, so (2/3)^-2 = 9/4. The index laws hold unchanged for negative indices.5
    10H.5.2.2Evaluate and simplify expressions with a negative index for any base (not only base 10), including combining with the multiplication and division laws.4
    10H.5.2.3Evaluate a negative power of a fraction or a decimal by turning it over, and find an unknown index such as x in 2^x = 1/8.6
    10H.5.3.1A power of 1/n means the nth root: a^(1/2) is the square root of a and a^(1/3) is the cube root, because (a^(1/n))^n = a^(n/n) = a^1 = a. So 25^(1/2) = 5, 8^(1/3) = 2 and 81^(1/4) = 3: the denominator of the index names the root. The root of a fraction is the root of its numerator over the root of its denominator: (4/9)^(1/2) = 2/3. A root can be written as a power: the cube root of x is x^(1/3).6
    10H.5.3.2Evaluate a whole number raised to a power 1/n by taking the nth root.6
    10H.5.3.3Evaluate a fraction or a decimal raised to a power 1/n, and write a root as a power, such as the cube root of x = x^(1/3).7
    10H.5.4.1A power of m/n is a root and a power: a^(m/n) is the nth root of a, raised to the power m, which is also the nth root of a^m. Taking the root first keeps the numbers small: 8^(2/3) = 2^2 = 4. A negative fractional index adds a reciprocal: a^(-m/n) = 1/a^(m/n), so 8^(-2/3) = 1/4; the minus sign never makes the value negative. A fraction base with a negative index is turned over first: (27/8)^(-2/3) = (8/27)^(2/3) = 4/9.7
    10H.5.4.2Evaluate a number raised to a positive fractional index m/n, taking the root and then the power.7
    10H.5.4.3Evaluate a number or a fraction raised to a negative fractional index, such as (27/8)^(-2/3).7
    FM.4.6.1The three index laws extend to zero, negative and fractional indices: a^0 = 1, a^-m is the reciprocal of a^m, and a^(1/n) is the nth root of a.7
    FM.4.6.2Simplify compound expressions using the index laws with negative and fractional indices.7
    FM.4.6.3Solve equations where the unknown is in the base or the index, including disguised quadratics.8
    Powers and roots
    • Rationalising a denominator

    1.4B(H)Rationalising a denominator

    11H.1.3.1Rationalising a denominator rewrites a fraction so that no surd is left in its denominator. Multiplying the numerator and the denominator by the same number leaves the value of the fraction unchanged. For a / the square root of b, multiplying top and bottom by the square root of b gives (a x the square root of b) / b, since the square root of b x the square root of b = b. The answer is then simplified, cancelling any common factor of the whole numbers outside the roots.7
    11H.1.3.2Rationalise a denominator of the form the square root of b, such as 6 / the square root of 3 = 2 x the square root of 3.7
    11H.1.3.3Rationalise a denominator of the form c x the square root of b, or one that needs simplifying first, such as 10 / (3 x the square root of 5).8
    11H.1.4.1A denominator such as a + the square root of b is rationalised by multiplying top and bottom by a - the square root of b, which changes only the sign between the terms. The product (a + the square root of b)(a - the square root of b) = a^2 - b is a whole number, because the surd terms cancel. The numerator is expanded fully, every term times every term. The result is simplified by cancelling a factor common to every term of the numerator and the denominator.8
    11H.1.4.2Rationalise a denominator of the form a + the square root of b or a - the square root of b, such as 4 / (3 - the square root of 5).8
    11H.1.4.3Rationalise and simplify a fraction where both the numerator and the denominator contain surds, such as (2 + the square root of 3) / (2 - the square root of 3).8
    FM.1.7.3Rationalise a denominator, including two-term denominators using the conjugate.8

    1.11ACalculator use

    8.1.4.1The calculator has dedicated keys for fractions, powers, roots and brackets, and entering a calculation as written preserves the order of operations. Brackets are needed wherever the written layout groups terms that the keystroke order would not, such as everything above a fraction bar. The Ans key reuses the previous full result rather than a rounded copy of it. Memory keys store an exact value, so rounding only once at the end stops errors compounding.3

    • Decimal notation

    1.3ADecimal notation

    Decimals
    • Decimal place value
    • Ordering decimals
    • Decimal to fraction or percentage
    • Terminating decimals as fractions

    1.3BDecimal place value

    7.16.1.1Each place to the right of the decimal point is worth a tenth of the one before: tenths, hundredths, thousandths. Decimals are compared place by place from the left, so 0.45 is smaller than 0.5. Trailing zeros after the decimal point do not change a value, so 0.5 = 0.50. Rounding to a given number of decimal places is decided by the next digit, rounding up at 5 or above.2
    7.16.2.1Only digits of the same place value can be added or subtracted, which is why the decimal points are lined up. Empty places can be filled with zeros without changing the value. The decimal point in the answer sits directly below the points above it. Money is written to two decimal places, and measures to the precision the question states.2
    10.1.1.3Multiply and divide numbers by 10, 100 and 1000, and by 0.1 and 0.01, using place value.2

    1.3COrdering decimals

    7.16.1.2Order and compare decimals by comparing place value digit by digit.2

    1.3DDecimal to fraction or percentage

    7.16.5.1A decimal converts to a fraction by reading its place value, so 0.7 is 7/10 and 0.25 is 25/100. A fraction converts to a decimal by dividing the numerator by the denominator. Multiplying a decimal by 100 gives a percentage, and dividing a percentage by 100 gives a decimal. A percentage converts to a fraction by writing it over 100 and simplifying. The key equivalents are 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%, 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%, 1/5 = 0.2 = 20%, 1/10 = 0.1 = 10%, 3/4 = 0.75 = 75%. A denominator that is not a factor of a power of ten gives a recurring decimal, shown with a dot.3

    1.3ETerminating decimals as fractions

    10.13.6.1A terminating decimal stops; a recurring decimal repeats the same block of digits for ever. The recurring block is marked with a dot over its first digit and a dot over its last, so 0.4444... is 0.4 dotted and 0.323232... is 0.32 dotted at both ends. A fraction in its simplest form terminates exactly when the only prime factors of its denominator are 2 and 5; otherwise it recurs. Every terminating decimal is itself a fraction: 0.65 = 65/100 = 13/20.4
    10.13.6.2Convert a fraction to a decimal on a calculator and state whether it terminates or recurs, writing any recurring block in dot notation.3
    10.13.6.3Predict from the prime factors of its denominator whether a fraction in its simplest form terminates or recurs, and check the prediction.4

    7.16.2.3Solve worded problems involving addition and subtraction of decimals, including money and measures.3
    7.16.3.2Multiply decimals without a calculator, using an equivalent whole-number calculation.3
    7.16.4.1The order of operations applies to decimals exactly as it does to integers. A decimal answer can be checked for plausibility by estimating with rounded values first. Multiplying by a number less than 1 makes a quantity smaller, and dividing by one makes it larger. In a worded problem the operations are identified before any calculation is started.3
    10.13.1.1To add or subtract decimals the digits are aligned by place value, so the decimal points line up. To multiply decimals, multiply as if there were no points and then place the point so that the answer has as many decimal places as the two numbers together. To divide by a decimal, multiply both numbers by the same power of 10 until the divisor is a whole number; the quotient is unchanged.3
    10.13.1.2Add, subtract, multiply and divide decimals, checking each answer by estimating with values rounded to 1 significant figure.3

    • Recurring decimals to fractions

    1.3A(H)Recurring decimals to fractions

    7.16.5.2Convert between decimals, fractions and percentages in all six directions.2
    7.16.5.3Convert fractions with awkward denominators to decimals by division, including recurring decimals.2
    7.16.6.3Solve problems requiring conversion between fractions, decimals and percentages in context.4
    10H.11.4.1A recurring decimal repeats one block of digits for ever, and a dot over the first and the last digit of the block marks it, so 0.272727... is written 0.27 with dots over the 2 and the 7. Every recurring decimal is a fraction. To find it, call the decimal x and multiply by 10 for a one-digit block, 100 for a two-digit block and 1000 for a three-digit block, so that the digits after the point line up. Subtracting x then removes the part that recurs, leaving a whole number: 9x, 99x or 999x equals it. So a block of n digits gives a denominator of n nines before simplifying: 0.272727... = 27/99 = 3/11.6
    10H.11.4.2Convert a recurring decimal whose repeating block of one or two digits starts straight after the point, such as 0.777... or 0.363636..., into a fraction in its simplest form, using the algebraic method.6
    10H.11.4.3Convert a recurring decimal with a repeating block of three digits, or with a whole-number part, such as 0.216216... or 2.454545..., into a fraction or a mixed number in its simplest form.7
    10H.11.5.1When digits that do not recur come before the repeating block, two multiples of x are needed: one power of ten moves the point to the start of the block, and another moves it to the end of the first block. Subtracting the smaller from the larger removes the recurring part, so for x = 0.1666..., 100x - 10x = 16.666... - 1.666..., giving 90x = 15 and x = 1/6. The denominator before simplifying is one 9 for each recurring digit followed by one 0 for each non-recurring digit after the point. A 'show that' answer writes both equations, the subtraction and the simplifying, ending at the fraction given. Recurring decimals are added, subtracted, multiplied or divided exactly by writing each as a fraction first.7
    10H.11.5.2Convert a recurring decimal with one or more non-recurring digits before the repeating block, such as 0.1666... or 0.2454545..., into a fraction in its simplest form.7
    10H.11.5.3Show that a recurring decimal is equal to a given fraction, and calculate exactly with recurring decimals, such as 0.333... + 0.454545..., by writing each as a fraction.8

      • Percentage, fraction, decimal
      • One number as a percentage of another

      1.6APercentage of an amount

      7.10.7.1Per cent means per hundred, so a percentage is a fraction out of 100. 50% is found by dividing by 2, 25% by dividing by 4, 10% by dividing by 10, and 1% by dividing by 100. Any percentage can be built by adding or scaling these blocks, so 35% is 25% + 10%. An increase adds the percentage to the original amount; a decrease subtracts it.3
      7.10.7.2Find simple percentages of an amount without a calculator (50%, 25%, 10%, 1%).3
      7.10.7.3Build any percentage of an amount from these blocks, and increase or decrease an amount by a percentage.4
      10.13.3.1A percentage is a number of parts per 100, so 15% of an amount is (15 / 100) x that amount. An increase of p% multiplies by (100 + p) / 100 and a decrease of p% multiplies by (100 - p) / 100; that factor is the multiplier. Percentage change = (change / original amount) x 100, and the original amount is always the denominator. In a reverse percentage the amount given is the amount AFTER the change, so the original is found by dividing by the multiplier.4

      1.6CPercentage, fraction, decimal

      10.13.5.1A fraction, a decimal and a percentage are three ways of writing the same proportion, so a problem may be worked in whichever form is easiest and converted at the end. A ratio a : b describes a whole of a + b parts, so the first share is a / (a + b) of the whole. Two proportions can only be compared in a common form: either over a common denominator, or both written as percentages.4
      10.13.5.2Convert between fractions, decimals, percentages and ratios in order to compare two proportions.4

      1.6BOne number as a percentage of another

      1.6DPercentage multipliers

      8.5.6.2Find a percentage of an amount using a multiplier.3

      1.6EPercentage increase and decrease

      8.5.6.1A percentage multiplier turns a percentage change into a single multiplication. p% of an amount is a multiplication by p/100, so 35% of an amount is x0.35. An increase of p% is a multiplication by (1 + p/100), so a 12% rise is x1.12. A decrease of p% is a multiplication by (1 - p/100), so a 12% fall is x0.88. Successive changes multiply their multipliers together, and the result is not the same as adding the percentages.4
      8.5.6.3Increase and decrease amounts using multipliers, including successive changes.5
      9.5.1.1Per cent means per hundred, so p% of an amount is a multiplication by p/100. 35% of an amount is therefore a multiplication by 0.35. An increase of p% is a multiplication by (1 + p/100), so a 12% rise is x1.12. A decrease of p% is a multiplication by (1 - p/100), so a 12% fall is x0.88. A multiplier above 1 always increases an amount and one below 1 always decreases it.4
      9.5.1.3Increase and decrease an amount using a multiplier.4
      9.5.2.3Solve contextual problems involving percentage increase and decrease.5
      9.5.4.2Solve reverse percentage problems, including VAT and sale prices.5
      10.13.3.2Increase or decrease an amount by a percentage using a multiplier, and express a change as a percentage of the original amount.3

      1.6FReverse percentages

      9.5.3.3Find the original amount given the value after a percentage change.5
      9.5.4.1In a reverse percentage problem the amount given is the result of the change, not the original. The original is found by dividing by the multiplier, never by applying the percentage to the amount given. A price including 20% VAT is 120% of the pre-VAT price, so dividing by 1.2 recovers it. A sale price after a 30% reduction is 70% of the original, so dividing by 0.7 recovers it. The wording tells which is which: 'before' or 'original' signals a reverse problem, 'after' an ordinary one.5
      9.5.4.3Distinguish a reverse percentage problem from an ordinary percentage change.6
      10.13.3.3Find the original amount when a quantity and the percentage change that produced it are given.4

      1.6GCompound interest and depreciation

      9.5.2.1Successive percentage changes multiply their multipliers together. Two changes therefore combine into a single multiplier, applied once. The combined effect is not the sum of the percentages: a 10% rise then a 10% fall is x1.1 x 0.9 = x0.99, not a return to the original. The order the changes are applied in does not matter, since multiplication can be done in any order.5
      9.5.5.1Simple interest adds the same amount each period, always calculated on the original. Over n periods simple interest totals n times the interest for one period. Compound interest applies the multiplier to the running total, so each period earns interest on the interest already added. After n periods the compound amount is the original x multiplier^n. Compound growth therefore accelerates, and beyond the first period always exceeds simple interest at the same rate.5
      9.5.5.2Calculate simple interest over a number of years.4
      9.5.5.3Calculate compound interest using repeated multipliers.5
      10.13.4.1Compound interest is calculated on the amount at the start of each period, including interest already added, so the multiplier is applied once per period. After n periods at r% per period, amount = starting amount x ((100 + r) / 100)^n. Depreciation is the same calculation with a decrease, so the multiplier is (100 - r) / 100. Simple interest, by contrast, adds the same amount each period and is not compounded.4
      10.13.4.2Calculate the value of an investment or of a depreciating asset after a given number of periods using a repeated multiplier.4
      10.13.4.3Compare two savings or borrowing offers by calculating the total amount each produces over the same period.5

      Percentage change

      9.5.3.1Percentage change is the change divided by the original amount, then multiplied by 100. The original is always the denominator, which is why a rise and the matching fall are different percentages. Profit and loss are percentage changes on the cost price, not on the selling price. A multiplier turns the original into the new amount, so dividing the new amount by that multiplier recovers the original.5
      9.5.3.2Calculate percentage change, including profit and loss.5

      9.5.7.1Percentage problems differ by what is unknown: the change, the original amount, or the final amount. An unknown final amount multiplies by the multiplier; an unknown original divides by it. An unknown percentage comes from comparing the change with the original. Fractions, decimals, percentages and ratios all express the same multiplicative relationships, so a problem can be converted into whichever form is easiest.5

      1.6B(H)Compound interest problems

      9.5.6.1Depreciation is repeated percentage decrease, so its multiplier is below 1. After n periods the value is the original x multiplier^n, exactly as for growth. Where the rate differs between periods, the multipliers are multiplied in sequence rather than raised to a power. The number of periods needed to reach a given value is found by applying the multiplier repeatedly and counting.6

      1.2AEquivalent fractions

      7.10.1.1The denominator names how many equal parts the whole is split into; the numerator counts how many are taken. Multiplying or dividing both by the same number gives an equivalent fraction, because the value is unchanged. A fraction is in its lowest terms when the only common factor of numerator and denominator is 1. Dividing both by their HCF simplifies a fraction in one step. Fractions can only be compared directly when they share a denominator.2
      7.10.1.2Generate equivalent fractions and simplify a fraction to its lowest terms using the highest common factor.3
      7.10.4.2Multiply fractions, cancelling common factors before multiplying where possible.3
      8.15.1.2Simplify fractions by cancelling, and multiply fractions cancelling common factors first.4

      1.2DOrdering fractions; fraction of a quantity

      7.10.1.3Compare and order fractions by converting to a common denominator.3
      10.13.2.3Calculate exactly with fractions in context, finding a fraction of a quantity and expressing one quantity as a fraction of another.4

      1.2CCommon denominators

      7.10.3.1Fractions can only be added or subtracted when they share a denominator, since only equal-sized parts combine. A common denominator is any common multiple of the denominators, and the LCM gives the smallest. Where one denominator is a multiple of the other, only one fraction needs changing. Where they share no factor, multiplying the denominators always gives a common one. Only the numerators are added; the denominator names the part size and stays the same.3
      9.12.3.1Fractions can only be added or subtracted once they share a denominator, since only equal-sized parts combine. A common denominator is a common multiple of the denominators, and the LCM gives the smallest. Each numerator is multiplied by whatever its own denominator was multiplied by. Only the numerators are then added; the denominator names the part size and stays as it is. With an algebraic numerator the whole numerator is bracketed before subtracting, so that every term changes sign.5
      11H.3.5.1Fractions can only be added or subtracted once they share a denominator, since only equal-sized parts combine. A common denominator is a common multiple of the denominators, and the LCM gives the smallest. Each numerator is multiplied by whatever its own denominator was multiplied by. Only the numerators are then added; the denominator names the part size and stays as it is. With an algebraic numerator the whole numerator is bracketed before subtracting, so that every term changes sign.5

      1.2FAdding and subtracting fractions

      7.10.3.2Add and subtract fractions with related denominators, where one denominator is a multiple of the other.3
      7.10.3.3Add and subtract fractions with different denominators, both where the denominators share a common factor and where they do not.4
      9.12.3.2Add and subtract simple numerical fractions.4
      10.13.2.1Fractions are added or subtracted only over a common denominator; the numerators are then added or subtracted and the denominator is unchanged. To multiply fractions, multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators. To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal, because a unit fraction is a multiplicative inverse: 3 / (1/5) = 3 x 5. A mixed number is converted to an improper fraction before multiplying or dividing.3

      7.16.6.1Quantities written in different forms can only be compared once converted to a common form. Decimals are usually the easiest common form, since they compare place by place. A percentage of one amount cannot be compared with a percentage of a different amount. The form an answer is given in should match the form the question uses.3

      Fractions
      • Reciprocals

      1.2HReciprocals

      7.10.2.1A mixed number is a whole number and a proper fraction together. An improper (top-heavy) fraction has a numerator at least as large as its denominator. A mixed number converts to an improper fraction because each whole is one denominator's worth of parts. The reciprocal of a fraction is that fraction inverted, and a number multiplied by its reciprocal gives 1. A whole number n is n/1, so its reciprocal is 1/n.3
      7.10.2.3State the reciprocal of a fraction, whole number or mixed number.4
      7.10.5.2Divide a fraction by a fraction and by an integer using the reciprocal.4

      1.2IMultiplying and dividing fractions

      7.10.4.1Multiplying fractions multiplies the numerators and the denominators separately. 'of' means multiply, so 3/4 of 20 is 3/4 x 20. A whole number is written over 1 before multiplying. Cancelling a common factor from a numerator and a denominator before multiplying gives the same answer with smaller numbers. Multiplying by a fraction less than 1 makes a quantity smaller.3
      7.10.5.1Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal. This works because dividing asks how many of the divisor fit into the dividend. Dividing by a fraction less than 1 gives a larger answer. A whole number is written over 1 before dividing.4
      7.10.6.1Mixed numbers are converted to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing. Adding and subtracting mixed numbers can be done either by converting, or by handling the wholes and the parts separately. Algebraic fractions with numerical denominators follow the same rules as numerical ones, so x/3 + x/4 needs a common denominator of 12. The order of operations applies to fractions exactly as it does to integers.4
      7.10.6.2Add, subtract, multiply and divide mixed numbers, converting to improper fractions where needed.4
      8.15.1.1A fraction is simplified by dividing numerator and denominator by a common factor. Dividing both by their HCF simplifies it in one step. Cancelling before multiplying gives the same answer with smaller numbers to handle. Multiplying fractions multiplies the numerators and the denominators separately. Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal.4
      8.15.1.3Divide fractions by multiplying by the reciprocal, cancelling before multiplying.4
      8.15.2.1Mixed numbers are converted to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing. Multiplying the whole parts and the fraction parts separately does not work, because it ignores the bracket the mixed number stands for. Each whole is one denominator's worth of parts, which is what makes the conversion work. The answer is converted back to a mixed number where the context calls for it. 'of' means multiply, so a fraction of a mixed-number quantity is a multiplication.4
      8.15.2.2Multiply and divide mixed numbers.4

      10.13.2.2Add, subtract, multiply and divide fractions and mixed numbers, giving each answer in its simplest form.3
      10H.11.2.1Mixed numbers are converted to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing. Adding and subtracting mixed numbers can be done either by converting, or by handling the wholes and the parts separately. Algebraic fractions with numerical denominators follow the same rules as numerical ones, so x/3 + x/4 needs a common denominator of 12. The order of operations applies to fractions exactly as it does to integers.4

      1.8BDecimal places

      7.16.1.3Round decimals to a given number of decimal places.3
      10.1.6.1To round to a given decimal place or significant figure, look only at the single digit immediately after the place you're rounding to: 5 or more rounds the target digit up, less than 5 leaves it as it is; every digit after the rounding point is then removed, or replaced with zeros for significant figures before the decimal point. To estimate a calculation, round every value involved to 1 significant figure first, then carry out the simplified calculation - a calculator answer wildly different from this estimate signals a mis-pressed button, not a wrong estimate.2
      10.1.6.2Round numbers to a given number of decimal places and significant figures.2
      Degree of accuracy
      • Significant figures

      Significant figures

      8.9.5.1Significant figures are counted from the first non-zero digit. Leading zeros are never significant; zeros sitting between other digits always are. Rounding to a given number of significant figures is decided by the next digit, rounding up at 5 or above. Estimating rounds every value in a calculation to 1 significant figure first. An estimate checks whether an answer is plausible, so it is written with an 'approximately equals' sign rather than an equals sign.4
      8.9.5.2Round numbers to a given number of significant figures.4
      9.9.1.1Significant figures are counted from the first non-zero digit. Leading zeros are never significant; zeros sitting between other digits always are. Rounding to a given number of significant figures is decided by the next digit, rounding up at 5 or above. Estimating rounds every value in a calculation to 1 significant figure first. An estimate is written with an 'approximately equals' sign rather than an equals sign.4

      No matching specification point

      9.9.2.1The point of an estimate is a calculation that can be done mentally, so values are rounded to convenient figures rather than strictly the nearest ones. A root is easiest to estimate by rounding to the nearest square number. Rounding the numerator up, or the denominator down, makes the estimate too large. Rounding the numerator down, or the denominator up, makes it too small. Knowing which way each value was rounded is what makes an over- or under-estimate explainable.5

      Degree of accuracy
      • Upper and lower bounds

      1.8CUpper and lower bounds

      9.9.3.2Find the upper and lower bounds of a rounded value.6
      9.9.3.3Write an error interval using inequality notation.6
      9.9.3.1A rounded value stands for an interval of possible true values, not a single one. The bounds lie half a rounding unit either side, so 24 to the nearest whole number has bounds 23.5 and 24.5. The lower bound is included and the upper bound excluded, since 24.5 would itself round up. The interval is written as an error interval in inequality notation: 23.5 <= x < 24.5. The rounding unit sets the half: to the nearest 10 the bounds are 5 either side, and to 1 decimal place 0.05.5
      10.13.7.1A rounded value stands for every value that would round to it, so it has a lower bound and an upper bound. A value given to the nearest u has lower bound = value - u/2 and upper bound = value + u/2. The lower bound is reachable and the upper bound is not, so the error interval is written 12.5 <= x < 13.5 for 13 to the nearest whole number.5
      10.13.7.2Write down the upper and lower bounds of a value rounded to the nearest whole number, to a given number of decimal places, or to a given number of significant figures.5
      10.13.7.3Write the error interval of a rounded measurement in inequality notation and decide whether a stated value is consistent with it.5
      10H.11.6.1A rounded value stands for an interval of possible true values, not a single one. The bounds lie half a rounding unit either side, so 24 to the nearest whole number has bounds 23.5 and 24.5. The lower bound is included and the upper bound excluded, since 24.5 would itself round up. The interval is written as an error interval in inequality notation: 23.5 <= x < 24.5. The rounding unit sets the half: to the nearest 10 the bounds are 5 either side, and to 1 decimal place 0.05.5

      Degree of accuracy
      • Calculating with bounds

      1.8A(H)Calculating with bounds

      10H.11.7.1For a sum or a product, the upper bound uses both upper bounds and the lower bound uses both lower bounds. For a difference a - b, the upper bound is the upper bound of a minus the lower bound of b, and the lower bound is the lower bound of a minus the upper bound of b. For a quotient a / b, the upper bound is the upper bound of a divided by the lower bound of b, and the lower bound is the lower bound of a divided by the upper bound of b. A result is given to a suitable degree of accuracy by rounding both of its bounds: the answer is the most accurate rounding on which the two bounds agree.7

      1.7BDividing in a ratio

      8.5.1.3Express each part of a ratio as a fraction of the other part and of the whole, using a ratio table to show equivalent ratios.5
      8.5.5.2Divide a quantity into a given ratio with two or three parts.4
      8.5.7.1When a quantity is added to or taken from one share, the ratio changes but the other share often stays fixed. That fixed share is the way into the problem, since it must represent the same amount in both ratios. Scaling both ratios so the fixed share carries the same number of parts makes them directly comparable. Fractions, decimals, percentages and ratios all express the same multiplicative relationships, so a problem can be converted into whichever form is easiest.6
      9.15.1.1A ratio records a multiplicative relationship between quantities. In the ratio a:b the first part is a/b of the second and a/(a+b) of the whole. A ratio simplifies by dividing both parts by their HCF, with both parts in the same unit first. In the form 1:n, n comes from dividing both parts by the first part. Fractions, decimals, percentages and ratios all express the same relationships, so any one converts into any other.4
      9.15.2.1A ratio can be read as a total number of equal parts to be shared out. The total divided by the number of parts gives the value of one part. Each share is then that part value multiplied by its own number of parts. The difference between two shares in a:b is (a - b) parts, so a given difference also gives the value of one part.4
      9.15.2.2Divide a quantity into a given ratio with two or three parts.4
      9.15.5.1When a quantity is added to or taken from one share the ratio changes, but the other share often stays fixed. That fixed share is the way in, since it must represent the same amount in both ratios. Scaling both ratios so the fixed share carries the same number of parts makes them comparable. Two ratios sharing a common element combine into one three-part ratio by scaling both until the shared element matches.5
      10.6.4.1A ratio can be read as a total number of equal parts to be shared out: the total divided by the number of parts gives the value of one part, and each share is that part value multiplied by its own number of parts.4

      1.7DDirect proportion and the unitary method

      8.5.2.1Two quantities are in direct proportion when multiplying one multiplies the other by the same factor. Their ratio therefore stays constant, so doubling one doubles the other. The unitary method finds the value of one unit first, then scales up to the amount wanted. A unit cost makes different pack sizes comparable, so the best buy is the lowest cost per unit. An exchange rate is a direct proportion, so it works the same way in both directions.3
      8.5.2.2Solve direct proportion problems using the unitary method.4

      10.21.1.1Two quantities are in direct proportion when doubling one doubles the other, so their ratio stays the same. The unitary method finds the value of one item first, by dividing, and then multiplies to reach the quantity wanted. Because the ratio is constant, a / b is the same for every matching pair, which is the check on an answer.2
