      1.7CProportionality

      7.13.1.3Read values from a scale whose divisions are not single units, and use a simple scale (e.g. 1 cm : 2 m) to find real distances.3
      8.5.1.1Any two quantities can be linked multiplicatively, not only obvious pairs such as 3 and 6 but any pair such as 3 and 5. A ratio a:b records that relationship, and multiplying or dividing both parts by the same number gives an equivalent ratio. A ratio is simplified by dividing both parts by their HCF, and both parts must be in the same unit before that is done. In the form 1:n, n is found by dividing both parts by the first part. In the ratio a:b, the first part is a/b of the second and a/(a+b) of the whole.4
      8.5.3.1A map scale is a ratio of distance on the map to the matching real distance. Both parts of the scale must be in the same unit before it is used. A scale written 1:n means one unit on the map represents n of the same units in reality. Map to real multiplies by the scale, and real to map divides by it. A scale drawing preserves angles and shape, so only the lengths change.4
      8.5.3.2Use a map scale to convert between map distance and real distance.4
      8.5.3.3Interpret and produce scale drawings, converting units as required.5
      9.15.3.1A map scale is a ratio of distance on the map to the matching real distance. Both parts must be in the same unit before the scale is used. A scale written 1:n means one unit on the map represents n of the same units in reality. Map to real multiplies by the scale, and real to map divides by it. A scale drawing preserves angles and shape, so only the lengths change.4

      10.22.1.1Quantities in direct proportion satisfy y = kx for a fixed number k, so y / x is the same for every pair. The graph of a direct proportion is a straight line through the origin, and k is its gradient. A straight line that does NOT pass through the origin is not a direct proportion, however regular it looks.4

      10.22.3.1Direct proportion graphs as a straight line through the origin; inverse proportion graphs as a curve that falls steeply and then flattens, approaching but never meeting either axis. A conversion graph is a direct proportion graph used as a calculator: a value is read across to the line and down to the other axis. A reading taken from a graph is an estimate limited by the scale.4

      1.7ERatio and proportion problems

      8.5.5.3Solve problems where the difference between shares, or the value of one share, is given rather than the total, using the multiplier between shares.5
      9.15.2.3Solve problems where the difference between two shares is given.5
      9.15.4.3Solve problems where the difference between two shares is given rather than the total.5

      9.15.4.1Knowing the value of one share gives the value of one part, by dividing by that share's number of parts. Every other share, and the total, then follow from that one part value. This is the multiplicative reading of a ratio, and it is what solves problems where the total is unknown. A given difference between two shares works the same way, over (a - b) parts instead of one share's parts.5
      9.15.5.2Solve changing ratio problems.5

      Inverse proportion

      8.5.4.1Two quantities are in inverse proportion when multiplying one divides the other by the same factor. Their product therefore stays constant, so one known pair of values gives that constant for every other pair. Doubling one halves the other, which is the opposite of direct proportion. More of one meaning less of the other, such as workers and time taken, signals inverse proportion; more meaning more signals direct.5
      8.5.4.2Solve basic inverse proportion problems.5
      9.15.6.1A unit cost makes different pack sizes comparable, so the best buy is the lowest cost per unit. An exchange rate is a direct proportion, so it works the same way in both directions. In direct proportion, multiplying one quantity multiplies the other by the same factor, so their ratio stays constant. In inverse proportion, multiplying one divides the other by the same factor, so their product stays constant. More of one meaning less of the other signals inverse proportion; more meaning more signals direct.5
      10.22.2.1Two quantities are in inverse proportion when doubling one halves the other, so their PRODUCT stays the same rather than their ratio. Six workers taking 10 days and twelve workers taking 5 days is inverse proportion, because 6 x 10 = 12 x 5. The constant product is found from one complete pair and then used to find any missing value.5
      10.22.2.2Decide from a table or a context whether two quantities are in direct or in inverse proportion, giving a reason.5
      10.22.2.3Find a missing value in an inverse proportion by using the constant product.5

      No matching specification point

      8.5.5.1A ratio can be read additively, as a total number of equal parts to be shared out. It can also be read multiplicatively, as each share being a fixed fraction of the total. The additive view solves problems where the total is known: the total divided by the number of parts gives the value of one part. The multiplicative view solves problems where only one share, or the difference between shares, is given. In the ratio a:b the difference between the shares is (a - b) parts, which gives the value of one part directly.5

      Standard form
      • Writing in standard form

      Writing in standard form

      8.9.2.1Standard form writes a number as A x 10^n, where 1 <= A < 10 and n is an integer. A positive index means a large number, and n counts how many places the digits shift left. 10^n is 1 followed by n zeros, so 3.6 x 10^4 = 36000. Standard form exists so that very large numbers can be written and compared without counting zeros. A calculator shows standard form on its display and takes it in through the x10^x key, not by typing the power out.4
      8.9.2.2Write large numbers in standard form and convert back to ordinary form.4
      8.9.3.2Write small numbers in standard form and convert back to ordinary form.5
      Standard form
      • Standard form

      1.9AStandard form

      8.9.3.1A negative index means a reciprocal: 10^-n = 1/10^n. So multiplying by 10^-n divides, shifting the digits n places to the right. A negative index in standard form therefore represents a number smaller than 1. The index counts place shifts, not zeros, so 4.2 x 10^-3 = 0.0042. A stays between 1 and 10 whatever the sign of the index.5
      8.9.3.3Convert fluently between standard form and ordinary form with both positive and negative indices.5
      8.9.4.1Numbers in standard form are ordered first by index, and only by A when the indices are equal. A larger index always means a larger number, whatever the A values are. A negative index is always smaller than a positive one. A number is not in standard form unless 1 <= A < 10. Adjusting A back into range changes the index to compensate: 34 x 10^5 = 3.4 x 10^6, and 0.7 x 10^-3 = 7 x 10^-4.5
      8.9.4.2Order numbers written in standard form, including a mix of positive and negative indices.5
      8.9.4.3Rewrite numbers such as 34 x 10^5 or 0.7 x 10^-3 in correct standard form.6
      8.9.6.1Multiplying in standard form multiplies the A values and adds the indices. Dividing divides the A values and subtracts the indices. The result is then adjusted if its A falls outside 1 <= A < 10. Adding and subtracting need a common index first, because only matching powers of ten combine. Alternatively both numbers can be written in ordinary form, added or subtracted, and converted back.5
      8.9.6.2Multiply and divide numbers in standard form without a calculator.5
      10.10.1.1A number is in standard form when it is written as a x 10^n, where a is at least 1 and less than 10, and n is a whole number. A positive power of 10 makes the number larger and a negative power makes it smaller, so 1.5 x 10^8 = 150,000,000 and 1.5 x 10^-3 = 0.0015. The power counts the places the decimal point moves, not the number of zeros written. A power can also be rewritten with a different base, because (a^m)^n = a^(m x n).4
      10.10.1.2Write an ordinary number in standard form, and write a number given in standard form as an ordinary number, for both positive and negative powers.4
      10.10.2.1Two numbers in standard form are compared by their powers of 10 first, and only by the value of a when the powers are equal. A number such as 34 x 10^5 is not in standard form, because 34 is not less than 10; it is rewritten as 3.4 x 10^6. The power goes up by one for each place the decimal point moves left, and down by one for each place it moves right, so 0.62 x 10^4 = 6.2 x 10^3.4
      10.10.2.2Rewrite a number given as a x 10^n, where a is not between 1 and 10, into correct standard form.4
      10.10.2.3Order a list of numbers written in standard form, including negative powers, from smallest to largest.4
      10.10.3.1Multiplying two numbers in standard form multiplies the values of a and adds the powers of 10; dividing divides the values of a and subtracts the powers. The answer is rewritten afterwards if a is no longer between 1 and 10. Adding or subtracting needs both numbers written with the SAME power of 10 first, or written out in full. Both papers allow a calculator, which has a standard-form key, and its display may show an answer in standard form without writing the x 10 out.4
      10.10.3.2Multiply and divide numbers written in standard form, giving the answer in standard form.4
      10.10.3.3Add and subtract numbers in standard form, and solve a problem in context whose answer must be rewritten into standard form.5
      10H.6.2.1A number is in standard form when it is written as A x 10^n, where 1 <= A < 10 and n is an integer. Moving the decimal point of A one place left raises n by one, and one place right lowers it by one, so the value is unchanged: 34 x 10^5 = 3.4 x 10^6 and 0.62 x 10^-3 = 6.2 x 10^-4. Only numbers with the same power of 10 can be added or subtracted directly, because only matching place values combine: 4.2 x 10^5 + 3 x 10^4 = 4.2 x 10^5 + 0.3 x 10^5 = 4.5 x 10^5. The powers of 10 are never added when the numbers are added; the answer is rewritten if A has left 1 <= A < 10.5
      10H.6.2.2Rewrite a number given as a x 10^n, where a is not between 1 and 10, into correct standard form.4
      10H.6.3.1Multiplying in standard form multiplies the A values and adds the powers of 10, because the factors can be taken in any order: (3 x 10^4) x (5 x 10^6) = 15 x 10^10 = 1.5 x 10^11. Dividing divides the A values and subtracts the powers: (2 x 10^3) / (8 x 10^-2) = 0.25 x 10^5 = 2.5 x 10^4. A power of a number in standard form raises both parts: (3 x 10^4)^2 = 9 x 10^8; to take a square root, first make the power of 10 even: 1.6 x 10^9 = 16 x 10^8, whose square root is 4 x 10^4. The answer is rewritten at the end if A has left 1 <= A < 10.5
      10H.6.3.2Multiply and divide numbers written in standard form, giving the answer in standard form.4

A side is drawn with a ruler to the nearest millimetre, an angle is set with a protractor to the nearest degree, and a length from a point is marked with compasses as an arc.       8.16.7.2Construct the locus of points around a point and around a shape.5
      8.16.7.1The locus of points a fixed distance d from a point is a circle of radius d. From a straight line it is a pair of parallel lines, one either side, each d away. From a line segment it is a racetrack: two parallel segments joined by a semicircle of radius d at each end. From a polygon it is the outline with its corners rounded into arcs of radius d. An exact distance defines a locus, whereas an inequality ('at least', 'within', 'closer to') defines a region bounded by it. Where several conditions hold at once, the answer is the region where they all overlap.5

      Construction
      • Standard constructions and loci

      4.5DStandard constructions and loci

      7.3.1.1A locus is the set of all points satisfying a given rule. Equidistant means the same distance from. A circle is the locus of points a fixed distance (the radius) from a point, which is what compasses draw. Constructions use compasses and a straight edge only, never measurement. Equal arcs from each end of a line segment form a rhombus, whose diagonals cross at right angles and bisect each other.4
      7.3.1.3Construct the perpendicular bisector of a line segment, identifying the rhombus that the construction creates.5
      7.3.2.1To bisect is to cut exactly in half. The perpendicular bisector of AB is the locus of points equidistant from A and B. An angle bisector is the locus of points equidistant from the two lines forming the angle. Both constructions build a rhombus: its diagonals bisect each other at right angles, and each bisects the angles it passes through.5
      7.3.2.2Construct a perpendicular line through a given point on a line, and from a point off the line.4
      7.3.2.3Construct the bisector of a given angle using a straight edge and compasses.4
      7.3.3.1A fixed distance d from a point gives a circle of radius d. From a straight line, a pair of parallel lines, one either side, each d away. From a line segment, a racetrack: two parallel segments joined by a semicircle of radius d at each end. From a polygon, its outline with corners rounded into arcs of radius d.5
      7.3.3.2Construct the locus of points at a fixed distance from a point, from a straight line, and around a shape.4
      7.3.3.3Construct a line parallel to a given line at a fixed distance using the equidistant principle.5
      8.16.1.1A locus is the set of all points satisfying a given rule. Equidistant means the same distance from. A circle is the locus of points a fixed distance (the radius) from a point, which is what a pair of compasses draws. Constructions therefore work by geometrical property, never by measurement with a ruler or protractor. Two intersecting arcs locate the one point that is a set distance from each of two others.4
      8.16.1.3Construct the perpendicular bisector of a line segment, identifying the rhombus that the construction creates.5
      8.16.2.1To bisect is to cut exactly in half. The perpendicular bisector of AB is the locus of points equidistant from A and B. An angle bisector is the locus of points equidistant from the two lines forming the angle. Both constructions build a rhombus, which is itself two congruent isosceles triangles. A rhombus's diagonals bisect each other at right angles, and each diagonal bisects the angles it passes through.5
      8.16.2.2Construct a perpendicular through a point on a line, and from a point off a line, locating the rhombus in each.5
      8.16.2.3Construct the bisector of a given angle, explaining which rhombus property makes it work.5
      8.16.3.2Construct a line parallel to a given line at a fixed distance.5
      8.16.3.3Combine two or more constructions accurately within a single diagram, identifying the circles and rhombuses used.5
      8.16.3.1Two lines are parallel when every point on one is the same perpendicular distance from the other. So a parallel line at a fixed distance is constructed by erecting perpendiculars and marking that distance along them. The perpendicular distance is measured at right angles to the line, not in any other direction. Constructions combine within one diagram because each only needs the circles and rhombuses it creates, which stay visible.5
      8.16.6.3Construct the incircle and circumcircle of a triangle using angle and perpendicular bisectors.6
      10.16.2.1The perpendicular bisector of a line segment is the line that cuts it in half at right angles. Every point on it is the same distance from both end points, which is why it is drawn with two arcs of equal radius centred on those end points. The radius must be more than half the length of the segment or the arcs do not cross.3
      10.16.2.2Construct the perpendicular bisector of a line segment using a straight edge and compasses only.3
      10.16.2.3Use a perpendicular bisector to find the set of points equidistant from two given points.4
      10.16.3.1The bisector of an angle is the line that divides it into two equal angles. Every point on it is the same distance from both arms of the angle, which is why it is drawn from an arc centred on the vertex and then two equal arcs from where that arc meets the arms. The construction works for any angle and needs no protractor.3
      10.16.3.2Construct the bisector of a given angle using a straight edge and compasses only.3
      10.16.3.3Use an angle bisector to find the set of points equidistant from two given lines.4

      7.3.4.1An exact distance ('exactly 3 cm from A') defines a locus: a line or curve. An inequality ('at least', 'no more than', 'within', 'closer to') defines a region bounded by that locus. 'Closer to A than B' is the region on A's side of the perpendicular bisector of AB. 'Closer to one line than another' is the region on that line's side of the angle bisector. Several conditions at once give the region where they all overlap.5

      7.3.5.1Three side lengths fix a triangle completely (SSS): the third vertex is where two arcs cross. The arcs cross twice, giving mirror images of the same triangle. A triangle exists only if the two shorter sides add to more than the longest. Equal arc radii construct an isosceles triangle.5
      Angles, lines and triangles
      • Types of angle

      4.1ATypes of angle

      7.9.1.3Name angles using three-letter notation and classify them by type.3
      7.9.1.2Measure and draw angles to the nearest degree using a protractor, estimating first.2
      7.9.1.1An angle measures turn, in degrees, and a full turn is 360 degrees. Acute is under 90 degrees, right is exactly 90, obtuse is between 90 and 180, and reflex is over 180. Angle ABC means the angle at vertex B, turning from A to C. A protractor carries two scales, and the one to read is the one starting at zero on a line of the angle.2
      10.7.1.1An acute angle is less than 90 degrees, a right angle is exactly 90 degrees, an obtuse angle is between 90 and 180 degrees, and a reflex angle is more than 180 degrees. Angles on a straight line add to 180 degrees and angles around a point add to 360 degrees. When two straight lines cross, the angles opposite each other are equal; these are the vertically opposite angles.2

      No matching specification point

      7.9.2.1Angles around a point sum to 360 degrees. Angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees. Vertically opposite angles are equal. Angles that sum to a known total can be written as an equation: 2x + (x + 30) = 180.2

      8.3.1.2Find missing angles using point, line, triangle and vertically opposite facts, stating the reason each time.3

Every step in an angle calculation is justified by naming the fact used, not by the answer alone.3
      9.4.1.2Find missing angles using point, line, triangle and vertically opposite facts, stating the reason each time.3
      10.7.3.1The three angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees and the four angles of a quadrilateral add to 360 degrees. An isosceles triangle has two equal sides, and the two angles opposite those sides are equal; an equilateral triangle has three equal sides and three angles of 60 degrees; a right-angled triangle has one angle of 90 degrees, so its other two add to 90 degrees. The exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior angles not next to it.3

      11H.6.3.1Angles around a point sum to 360 degrees. Angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees. Angles in a triangle sum to 180 degrees. Vertically opposite angles are equal.       9.10.1.1A compound measure combines two other measures into a single one. Its units state the relationship: km/h is kilometres divided by hours, so speed = distance / time. Rearranging gives distance = speed x time and time = distance / speed. Density is mass divided by volume, in g/cm3 or kg/m3, and rearranges the same way. The units are the check: if they do not come out right, the operation was the wrong one.4

      9.10.2.1A compound unit converts by converting each of its parts in turn. m/s to km/h multiplies by 3600 to turn seconds into hours and divides by 1000 to turn metres into kilometres, so overall it multiplies by 3.6. The unit on the bottom converts the opposite way round to the one on top. Every quantity must be in the units the answer is wanted in before any calculation starts.5

Any 'per' quantity works this way: a rate is one measure divided by another. A multi-step problem finds an intermediate quantity first, keeping it exact until the end.5

The gradient of a tangent drawn at that point gives the rate of change at that instant.6

      4.2ANaming polygons

      9.3.1.2Name polygons up to a decagon and distinguish regular from irregular ones.3
      10.7.4.1A polygon is a closed shape made of straight sides, named by how many it has: triangle, quadrilateral, pentagon, hexagon, heptagon, octagon. The interior angles of a polygon with n sides add to 180 x (n - 2) degrees, which the specification also writes as (2n - 4) right angles. The exterior angles of any polygon add to 360 degrees, and each interior angle and the exterior angle beside it add to 180 degrees. A regular polygon has all its sides and all its angles equal, so each of its exterior angles is 360/n degrees.4

      4.2CProperties of quadrilaterals

      8.3.4.1A quadrilateral is classified by its sides, angles, diagonals and symmetry. A square has four equal sides and four right angles; a rectangle has four right angles with opposite sides equal. A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides and equal opposite angles; a rhombus is a parallelogram with four equal sides. A trapezium has exactly one pair of parallel sides; a kite has two pairs of adjacent equal sides. The diagonals separate them further: those of a square and rhombus cross at right angles, those of a square and rectangle are equal, and a kite's longer diagonal is a line of symmetry.3
      8.3.4.2Identify and classify quadrilaterals from their properties.3
      8.3.4.3Reason about the diagonal and symmetry properties of a quadrilateral to justify its classification.5
      10.15.5.2Name a quadrilateral from its side, angle, diagonal and symmetry properties.2

      4.2BAngles in a quadrilateral

      8.3.5.1Angles in a quadrilateral sum to 360 degrees. This follows from splitting any quadrilateral into two triangles, each summing to 180 degrees. A quadrilateral's own properties give further facts: opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, and co-interior angles between its parallel sides sum to 180 degrees. An angle written as an algebraic expression turns the angle sum into an equation to solve.4
      8.3.5.2Find missing angles in quadrilaterals, including using their side and angle properties.4
      8.3.5.3Solve multi-step problems combining parallel lines, triangles and quadrilaterals, including angles expressed algebraically.5
      10.15.5.1The angles of any quadrilateral sum to 360 degrees. A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides, equal opposite sides and equal opposite angles; a rhombus is a parallelogram with all four sides equal. A rectangle is a parallelogram with four right angles, and a square is both a rectangle and a rhombus. A kite has two pairs of adjacent equal sides and one pair of equal opposite angles; a trapezium has exactly one pair of parallel sides.4
      10.15.5.3Calculate missing angles in a quadrilateral, giving a reason drawn from its properties.4
      Polygons
      • Regular polygon angles

      4.2DRegular polygon angles

      9.3.1.1A polygon is a closed shape with straight sides, named by how many it has: pentagon 5, hexagon 6, heptagon 7, octagon 8, nonagon 9, decagon 10. A regular polygon has all sides equal and all angles equal; an irregular one does not. The exterior angles of any polygon sum to 360 degrees, because walking once round the shape is one full turn. In a regular polygon every exterior angle is the same, so each one is 360 / n. The number of sides follows from a given exterior angle, as n = 360 / exterior angle.3
      9.3.1.3Find the exterior angle of a regular polygon, and the number of sides from a given exterior angle.4
      9.3.2.1Any polygon splits into (n - 2) triangles by drawing diagonals from a single vertex. Each of those triangles contributes 180 degrees, so the interior angles sum to (n - 2) x 180 degrees. This holds for irregular polygons just as much as regular ones. A missing interior angle is found by subtracting the known angles from that sum.4
      9.3.2.2Calculate the interior angle sum of a polygon with any number of sides.4
      9.3.2.3Find a missing interior angle in a polygon.4
      9.3.3.1In a regular polygon all interior angles are equal, so each one is (n - 2) x 180 / n. At every vertex the interior and exterior angles lie on a straight line, so they sum to 180 degrees. Each interior angle can therefore be found more quickly as 180 - (360 / n). The number of sides follows from a given interior angle by finding the exterior angle first.4
      10.7.4.2Calculate the interior angle sum of a polygon, and the size of one interior and one exterior angle of a regular polygon.4
      11H.6.1.1A polygon is a closed shape with straight sides, named by how many it has: pentagon 5, hexagon 6, heptagon 7, octagon 8, nonagon 9, decagon 10. A regular polygon has all sides equal and all angles equal; an irregular one does not. The exterior angles of any polygon sum to 360 degrees, because walking once round the shape is one full turn. In a regular polygon every exterior angle is the same, so each one is 360 / n. The number of sides follows from a given exterior angle, as n = 360 / exterior angle.3
      11H.6.1.2Find the exterior angle of a regular polygon, and the number of sides from a given exterior angle.4
      11H.6.2.1In a regular polygon all interior angles are equal, so each one is (n - 2) x 180 / n. The number of sides follows from a given interior angle by finding the exterior angle first.4

      4.2GCongruent polygons

      9.4.4.1Congruent shapes are identical in both size and shape, whereas similar shapes share angles but not size. Two triangles are congruent if they satisfy SSS, SAS (the angle between the two sides), ASA or RHS. AAA proves similarity only, because equal angles fix a shape's proportions but not its size. SSA is not a condition, since two different triangles can share two sides and a non-included angle. Corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal, which is what makes congruence a tool for proving lengths and angles equal.5

      Symmetry
      • Line and rotational symmetry

      4.3ALine and rotational symmetry

      7.18.1.1The order of rotational symmetry is how many times a shape looks identical during one full turn about its centre. Every shape has order at least 1, since a full turn always returns it to its starting position. The centre of rotation is the point the shape turns about, usually its centre. Order of rotational symmetry and number of lines of symmetry are separate properties and need not match.3
      7.18.1.2Find the order of rotational symmetry of a given shape.3

      7.18.3.2Identify lines of symmetry in 2D shapes.2
      8.18.2.2Identify lines of symmetry and the order of rotational symmetry of a shape.4
      10.14.6.1A line of symmetry is a line about which a shape reflects onto itself. The order of rotational symmetry is the number of positions, within one full turn, in which a shape looks the same; every shape has order at least 1. A parallelogram has no lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order 2, so the two kinds of symmetry are independent of each other.3

      Symmetry on graphs

      7.15.7.1The lines x = a and y = b can act as mirror lines. Reflecting in a vertical line x = a leaves y-coordinates unchanged and moves each point to the same distance the other side of the line. Reflecting in a horizontal line y = b leaves x-coordinates unchanged. A point lying on the mirror line does not move.5

      4.10ANaming solids

      7.19.1.2Name common 3D shapes (cube, cuboid, prism, pyramid, cylinder, cone, sphere).2
      9.13.1.2Draw and identify the nets of cuboids and other solids.3
      10.11.1.1A solid is named by its shape: cube, cuboid, prism, pyramid, cylinder, sphere and cone; a face is a flat surface, an edge is where two faces meet and a vertex is a corner. A prism has the same cross-section all the way along its length. The surface area of a solid is the total area of all its faces, found by adding the areas of the rectangles and triangles of its net. A cylinder's curved surface area is 2 x pi x r x h and its two ends are circles, so its total surface area is 2 x pi x r x h + 2 x pi x r^2. Surface area is measured in square units.4

      4.10BFaces, edges and vertices

      7.19.1.1A face is a flat surface, an edge is where two faces meet, and a vertex is where edges meet. A prism has the same cross-section along its whole length, and is named after that cross-section. A pyramid narrows from a base to a single vertex. A cylinder, cone and sphere have curved surfaces, so they are neither prisms nor pyramids.2

      7.19.4.1A net is the 2D shape that folds up to form a solid. Surface area is the total area of all the faces, so it is measured in square units, not cubic ones. A cuboid has three pairs of identical faces, so its surface area is 2(lw + lh + wh). Isometric paper shows a 3D shape by drawing its edges along three fixed directions.3

A solid can have several different valid nets, since its faces can be arranged in more than one way. A cuboid has three pairs of identical faces, so its surface area is 2(lw + lh + wh).3

Its surface area is not the sum of the parts' surface areas, because the joining faces are hidden inside.3

      4.10FUnits of volume

      7.19.2.1Volume is the space a solid occupies, measured in cubic units such as cm3. The volume of a cuboid is length x width x height. All three dimensions must be in the same unit before multiplying. A missing dimension is found by dividing the volume by the product of the other two.3
      7.19.2.2Calculate the volume of a cube or cuboid, working in consistent units.3
      7.19.3.1Converting a length unit changes a volume unit by the cube of that factor: 1 cm3 = 1000 mm3 and 1 m3 = 1000000 cm3. This is because all three dimensions are converted, not just one. 1 cm3 holds 1 ml, so 1000 cm3 is 1 litre. A compound solid is split into cuboids whose volumes are added.5
      7.19.3.2Convert between units of volume and capacity.5
      8.19.2.1A prism has the same cross-section along its whole length. The volume of any prism is cross-sectional area x length. A cylinder is a prism with a circular cross-section, so its volume is pi x r^2 x h. All dimensions must be in the same unit before multiplying, and a volume unit converts by the cube of the length factor: 1 m^3 = 1000000 cm^3. A missing dimension is found by dividing the volume by the rest of the formula.5
      9.13.3.1Converting a length unit changes a volume unit by the cube of that factor: 1 m^3 = 1000000 cm^3 and 1 cm^3 = 1000 mm^3. This is because all three dimensions are converted, not just one. An area unit converts by the square of the factor, for the same reason. 1 cm^3 holds 1 ml, so 1000 cm^3 is 1 litre. A missing dimension is found by dividing the volume, or by rearranging the surface area formula, before solving.5

      10H.10.4.11 cm = 10 mm, 1 m = 100 cm and 1 km = 1000 m. Area has two length dimensions, so the conversion factor is squared: 1 cm2 = 10^2 mm2 = 100 mm2 and 1 m2 = 100^2 cm2 = 10000 cm2. Volume has three, so it is cubed: 1 cm3 = 10^3 mm3 = 1000 mm3 and 1 m3 = 100^3 cm3 = 1000000 cm3. 1 litre = 1000 cm3.5

      4.10A(H)Advanced surface area and volume

      8.19.3.1A cylinder's net is two circles and one rectangle. The curved surface unrolls into a rectangle whose width is the circumference, 2 x pi x r, and whose height is h. So the curved surface area is 2 x pi x r x h, and the total surface area is 2 x pi x r^2 + 2 x pi x r x h. Surface area is in square units and volume in cubic units, which is what decides which a context needs. An irregular solid can be approximated by breaking it into prisms and cylinders.6
      8.19.3.3Solve contextual problems involving volume and surface area, including the human body volume project.6
      9.13.4.3Solve contextual problems involving the volume of prisms.6
      9.13.5.1A cylinder's net is two circles and a rectangle whose width is the circumference, 2 x pi x r. So its total surface area is 2 x pi x r^2 + 2 x pi x r x h. A prism's surface area is its two cross-sections plus the rectangle formed by the perimeter x length. The sphere, hemisphere, cone and pyramid formulae are given in the exam, so what matters is choosing the right one and identifying the correct radius or height. A hemisphere's surface area includes its flat circular face as well as the curved half.6
      9.13.5.2Calculate the surface area of prisms and cylinders.6
      9.13.5.3Calculate the volume and surface area of spheres, hemispheres and pyramids.6
      10H.8.1.1A sphere of radius r has volume (4/3) x pi x r^3 and surface area 4 x pi x r^2; both formulae are given in the exam, and the radius is half the diameter. The radius is cubed or squared first, before it is multiplied by 4/3 or 4 and by pi. A hemisphere is half a sphere, so its volume is (2/3) x pi x r^3 and its curved surface area is 2 x pi x r^2. A solid hemisphere also has a flat circular face of area pi x r^2, so its total surface area is 3 x pi x r^2. An answer in terms of pi keeps pi as a symbol, such as 36pi cm3; a rounded answer evaluates pi at the end.6
      10H.8.1.2Calculate the volume and surface area of a sphere, giving answers in terms of pi or to a stated accuracy.6
      10H.8.1.3Calculate the volume and total surface area of a hemisphere, including its flat circular face.6
      10H.8.2.1A pyramid's volume is (1/3) x base area x perpendicular height: one third of the prism on the same base with the same height. A cone is a pyramid on a circular base, so its volume is (1/3) x pi x r^2 x h, and its curved surface area is pi x r x l, where l is the slant height; both cone formulae are given in the exam. The perpendicular height h, the radius r and the slant height l form a right-angled triangle, so l^2 = r^2 + h^2. A compound solid's volume is the sum of its parts' volumes, minus any part cut away; a frustum is a large cone minus the small cone cut from its top. A compound solid's surface area counts only the faces on the outside, leaving out any face where two parts join.6

      10H.8.3.1A formula with every value but one known becomes an equation: the values are substituted and the equation is solved, so (4/3) x pi x r^3 = 36pi gives r^3 = 27 and r = 3. Everything multiplying the unknown power is undone first; a cubed length is then found with a cube root and a squared length with a square root. When a solid is melted and recast, or a liquid poured from one container into another, its volume stays the same, so the two volume expressions are set equal. When pi appears in every term on both sides it cancels, so the answer is exact with no pi in it. With letters for the lengths, the same equation gives one length in terms of another.6

      Circle properties
      • Parts of a circle

      4.6AParts of a circle

      8.8.1.1The radius runs from the centre to the edge and the diameter right across through the centre, so the diameter is twice the radius. The circumference is the distance all the way around the circle. A chord joins two points on the circle, and a tangent touches it at exactly one point. An arc is part of the circumference; a sector is bounded by two radii and an arc; a segment is bounded by a chord and an arc. The circumference is C = pi x d, so from a radius the diameter is found first.3
      8.8.1.2Label the parts of a circle correctly and convert between radius and diameter.3
      10.16.4.1The centre is the point every point of the circle is equidistant from, and that distance is the radius; a diameter is a chord through the centre and is twice the radius. A chord is a straight line joining two points on the circle, and it divides the circle into two segments. A tangent is a straight line that touches the circle at exactly one point. An arc is part of the circumference, and a sector is the region between an arc and two radii.2
      10.16.4.2Name the centre, radius, chord, diameter, circumference, tangent, arc, sector and segment on a circle diagram.2
      10.16.4.3Draw a circle of given radius and mark on it a chord, a tangent, an arc, a sector and a segment.3

      4.6C(H)Circle theorems

      9.17.1.1Every radius of a circle is the same length. So any triangle formed by two radii is isosceles, and its base angles are equal. The angle in a semicircle is a right angle: an angle at the circumference standing on a diameter is 90 degrees. Each circle theorem is a named fact, and that name is the reason quoted in the working.5
      9.17.1.3Apply the angle in a semicircle theorem.5
      9.17.1.2Use the isosceles property of two radii to find missing angles.5
      9.17.2.1The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference when both stand on the same arc. Angles in the same segment are equal: two angles at the circumference standing on the same arc are equal to each other. That follows from the first theorem, since each is half of the same angle at the centre. The arc both angles stand on is what has to be identified first, not the shape they appear to make.6
      9.17.2.2Apply the angle at the centre theorem.6
      9.17.2.3Apply the angles in the same segment theorem.6
      9.17.4.1A tangent touches the circle at exactly one point. A tangent meets the radius at that point at a right angle. Two tangents drawn from the same external point are equal in length. Those two tangents and the two radii form a kite, symmetrical about the line to the centre. The isosceles triangle made by the two equal tangents gives further equal angles.6
      9.17.4.2Apply the tangent and radius theorem to find missing angles.6
      9.17.4.3Use equal tangents to find missing lengths and angles.6
      9.17.5.3Identify which circle theorem applies in a given diagram.6
      FM.6.1-6.3-6.4.1The circle theorems are: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc. The angle in a semicircle is 90 degrees. Angles in the same segment are equal. Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180 degrees. A tangent meets a radius at 90 degrees, and two tangents from a point are equal. The alternate segment theorem: the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment.7
      FM.6.1-6.3-6.4.2Apply the circle theorems to find missing angles, including reflex cases, stating a reason at each step.7

      4.6B(H)Cyclic quadrilaterals

      9.17.3.1A cyclic quadrilateral has all four of its vertices on the circumference. Its opposite angles sum to 180 degrees. A chord is a line joining two points on the circumference. The perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the centre, so a radius drawn perpendicular to a chord bisects it. That creates a right-angled triangle, so Pythagoras finds a missing length.6
      9.17.3.2Find missing angles in a cyclic quadrilateral.6
      9.17.3.3Use the chord bisector property to find missing lengths and angles.6

      4.6BChord and tangent properties

      10.16.5.1A tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact, so the angle between them is 90 degrees. The two tangents drawn to a circle from a point outside it are equal in length. Those two tangents, the two radii to their points of contact and the line from the centre to the external point form a pair of congruent right-angled triangles, symmetric about that line.4
      10.16.5.2Calculate a missing angle or length in a diagram containing a tangent and a radius.4
      10.16.5.3Solve a problem about two tangents from an external point, using the equal lengths and the right angles at the points of contact.5
      10.16.6.1The line from the centre of a circle that is perpendicular to a chord bisects that chord, and the converse also holds: the line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to it. The perpendicular bisector of any chord therefore passes through the centre. A radius, half the chord and the perpendicular distance from the centre to the chord form a right-angled triangle.4
      10.16.6.2Calculate the length of a chord, or the distance of a chord from the centre, using the right-angled triangle the perpendicular from the centre creates.4
      10.16.6.3Locate the centre of a circle by constructing the perpendicular bisectors of two chords.5
      10.16.7.1A geometrical reason names the property being used, not the arithmetic: 'the tangent is perpendicular to the radius' rather than '90 take away 40'. Circle work also uses the angle facts already established: angles in a triangle sum to 180 degrees, base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal, and any two radii of the same circle are equal, which makes many triangles in a circle isosceles. A chain of reasoning states each step and the reason for it, in order.5
      10.16.7.2Calculate missing angles in a circle diagram combining tangent, chord and radius properties with triangle angle facts.5

      Circle properties
      • Harder circle theorems

      Harder circle theorems

      9.17.5.1A chord drawn from the point where a tangent touches divides the circle into two segments. The angle between the tangent and that chord equals the angle in the alternate segment, the one on the other side of the chord. The alternate segment is identified from the chord, not from how the diagram happens to look. Which theorem applies is decided by what the diagram contains: a diameter, the centre, a cyclic quadrilateral, a tangent, or two angles on one arc.7
      9.17.5.2Apply the alternate segment theorem.7
      9.17.6.1A multi-step problem chains several theorems, each step feeding the next. Every step needs its reason stated by name, since the reasoning is what carries the marks. Circle theorems combine with the ordinary angle facts: triangles, straight lines, isosceles triangles and parallel lines. On a goal-free diagram every angle that can be found is found, and the route to the target emerges from that.7

      • Area and perimeter of rectangles

      Area and perimeter of rectangles

      7.13.3.1Perimeter is the distance around a shape, measured in units of length. Area is the space a shape covers, measured in square units. The area of a rectangle is length x width, and its perimeter is twice the length plus twice the width. All lengths must be in the same unit before either is calculated. A compound rectangular shape is split into rectangles whose areas are added.2
      7.13.3.2Calculate the area and perimeter of squares and rectangles, working in consistent units.2
      Mensuration of 2D shapes

      4.9AConverting metric units

      7.13.2.1Metric units convert by powers of ten: 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, 1000 m = 1 km, 1000 ml = 1 l, 1000 g = 1 kg, 1000 kg = 1 t. Converting to a smaller unit multiplies; converting to a larger unit divides. Common imperial equivalents: 1 inch is about 2.5 cm, 1 kg is about 2.2 lb, 1 litre is about 1.75 pints. An imperial conversion is only approximate, so answers are rounded sensibly.3
      7.13.2.2Convert between metric units of length, mass and capacity.3
      7.13.2.3Convert between metric and imperial units using a given conversion fact.4
      10.12.3.11 cm = 10 mm, 1 m = 100 cm and 1 km = 1000 m. Area has two length dimensions, so the conversion factor is squared: 1 cm2 = 10^2 mm2 = 100 mm2 and 1 m2 = 100^2 cm2 = 10000 cm2. Volume has three, so it is cubed: 1 cm3 = 10^3 mm3 = 1000 mm3 and 1 m3 = 100^3 cm3 = 1000000 cm3. 1 litre = 1000 cm3.5
      10.5.3.3Solve an area or perimeter problem requiring a unit conversion (e.g. between cm squared and m squared) before or after the calculation.5

      4.9CArea of triangles

      7.14.1.1The area of a triangle is half the base times the perpendicular height. The height must be perpendicular to the chosen base, so a slant side is not the height. Any side may be taken as the base, provided the matching perpendicular height is used. The perpendicular height can fall outside the triangle, and the formula still holds.3

      7.14.1.3Calculate the area of a triangle where the perpendicular height falls outside the triangle, or where units must be converted first.4

      7.14.3.1A compound shape is split into rectangles and triangles whose areas are added. It can instead be treated as a surrounding rectangle with a missing piece subtracted. Perimeter adds the outside lengths only, and missing lengths are deduced from the ones given. Algebraic side lengths give an expression for area or perimeter, which becomes an equation once its value is stated.4

Converting an area between units squares the conversion factor, so 1 m squared = 10,000 cm squared, not 100 cm squared.4

      4.9DParallelograms and trapezia

      7.14.2.1An area formula can be applied backwards, using inverse operations to find a missing length. For a triangle, base = 2 x area / height. For a rectangle, a missing side is the area divided by the known side. Where the missing length appears more than once, the situation is written as an equation and solved.4
      8.12.1.1The area of a parallelogram is base x perpendicular height. This follows from cutting a triangle off one end and moving it to the other, which makes a rectangle. The area of a trapezium is half the sum of the parallel sides times the perpendicular height: 1/2 x (a + b) x h. The height is always perpendicular to the parallel sides, never a slant side. A missing length is found by rearranging the formula and dividing.4

      8.12.1.3Find a missing length given the area of a parallelogram or trapezium.5
      10.5.1.1The area of a triangle is half the base times the perpendicular height; the area of a parallelogram is base times perpendicular height; the area of a trapezium is half the sum of the parallel sides times the height. In each case the height used must be perpendicular to the chosen base, not a slant side.3

      4.9ECircles and semicircles

      8.8.1.3Calculate the circumference of a circle using C = pi x d, given the radius or the diameter.4
      8.8.2.1pi is the ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter, and is the same for every circle. So C = pi x d, which is the same as C = 2 x pi x r. The diameter is found from the circumference by dividing by pi, and the radius by dividing by 2 x pi. Leaving an answer in terms of pi keeps it exact, whereas a decimal answer has been rounded. One full revolution of a wheel covers one circumference.4
      8.8.2.2Find the radius or diameter given the circumference, and give answers exactly in terms of pi.5
      8.8.3.1The area of a circle is A = pi x r^2. The radius is squared first and then multiplied by pi, since the index applies only to r. Given the diameter, the radius is halved before the formula is used. The radius is found from the area by dividing by pi and then taking the square root. Area is measured in square units and circumference in units of length, which is why the two formulas cannot be swapped.4
      8.8.3.2Calculate the area of a circle given the radius or the diameter.4
      8.8.3.3Find the radius given the area, and give answers in terms of pi or to a stated accuracy.5
      8.8.4.1A semicircle is half a circle and a quarter circle a quarter, so their areas are the whole circle's area halved or quartered. Their perimeters are not a simple fraction of the circumference, because the straight edges must be added. A semicircle's perimeter is half the circumference plus the diameter; a quarter circle's is a quarter of the circumference plus two radii. A compound shape is split into circles, rectangles and triangles whose areas are added, or subtracted where a piece has been removed. Only the outside edges count towards a compound shape's perimeter.5
      8.8.4.2Find the area and perimeter of semicircles and quarter circles.5
      10.5.2.1The circumference of a circle is C = pi x d (or C = 2 x pi x r) and its area is A = pi x r squared; the radius is squared before multiplying by pi, since the index applies only to r. A semicircle's area is half the full circle's area, but its perimeter is half the circumference plus the diameter - the straight edge must be added separately.4

      4.9A(H)Sectors

      10H.4.2.1A sector is the region between two radii and the arc joining them; an angle of theta at the centre makes it theta/360 of the whole circle, so its area is theta/360 x pi x r^2. The two radii cut the circle into a minor sector and a major sector, whose angles add to 360 degrees, so the major sector's angle is 360 - theta. A segment is the region between a chord and its arc; its area is the sector's area minus the area of the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord.6
      10H.4.2.2Calculate the area of a sector given its radius and angle, exactly in terms of pi or to a stated accuracy, including a major sector.6
      10H.4.2.3Calculate the area of a segment by subtracting the triangle from its sector, where the triangle is right-angled at the centre or its base and height are given.7
      10H.4.3.1An arc is part of a circle's circumference; an arc whose angle at the centre is theta is theta/360 of the circumference, so its length is theta/360 x pi x d, the same as theta/360 x 2 x pi x r. A sector's perimeter is its arc length plus the two radii, since the sector is closed by two straight edges. Arc length is a length, measured in units such as cm, while a sector's area is in square units.6
      10H.4.3.2Calculate the length of an arc given the radius and the angle at the centre, exactly in terms of pi or to a stated accuracy.6
      10H.4.3.3Calculate the perimeter of a sector, adding both radii to the arc length, including for a major sector.6
      10H.4.4.1The sector formulas can be used backwards: given an arc length or an area together with the radius or the angle, the missing quantity is found by forming an equation and solving it. From theta/360 x 2 x pi x r = arc length, the angle is theta = 360 x arc length / (2 x pi x r). From theta/360 x pi x r^2 = area, r^2 is found first and the radius is its positive square root. A region between two sectors with the same centre has an area of the larger sector minus the smaller, and a perimeter of both arcs plus two straight edges, each the difference of the radii.7
      10H.4.4.2Find the angle or the radius of a sector given its arc length or its area.7

      5.2GTranslation

      7.18.2.1A translation slides a shape without turning, reflecting or resizing it, so the image is identical to the original. A column vector gives the movement: right or left on top, up or down below. A negative top number means left, and a negative bottom number means down. Every point of the shape moves by the same vector.3
      7.18.2.2Translate a shape by a given column vector.3
      7.18.2.3Write the column vector describing a given translation, including negative components.4
      8.18.1.2Translate a shape by a column vector and write the vector describing a given translation.4
      10.14.1.2Translate a shape by a given column vector and write down the column vector of a translation shown on a grid.3

      5.2FSpecifying a translation

      10.14.1.1A translation is specified by a distance and a direction and is written as a column vector with the horizontal movement above the vertical. A positive top number moves right and a negative one left; a positive bottom number moves up and a negative one down. A translation preserves length and angle, so the image is congruent to the object and points the same way.3
      10H.12.1.1A translation is specified by a distance and a direction and is written as a column vector with the horizontal movement above the vertical. A positive top number moves right and a negative one left; a positive bottom number moves up and a negative one down. A translation preserves length and angle, so the image is congruent to the object and points the same way. A line of symmetry is a line about which a shape reflects onto itself. The order of rotational symmetry is the number of positions, within one full turn, in which a shape looks the same; every shape has order at least 1.3

      Describing transformations

      7.18.5.1A transformation is fully described only when all its defining information is given. A translation needs its column vector, a reflection needs its mirror line, and a rotation needs centre, angle and direction. One transformation is named, not several, unless the question asks for a combination. The transformation can be identified from what has changed: position, orientation, or the direction the shape faces.4
      7.18.5.2Describe a single transformation fully, giving all required information.4
      8.18.5.1A transformation is fully described only when all its defining information is given. A translation needs its column vector, and a reflection needs its mirror line. A rotation needs a centre, an angle and a direction; an enlargement needs a centre and a scale factor. One transformation is named, not several, unless a combination is what the question asks for. Two transformations applied in turn can often be described as a single one, and the order they are applied in can change the result.5
      8.18.5.2Describe a single transformation fully, giving all required information.4
      10.14.7.1A complete description names the transformation and gives everything that specifies it: a translation needs its column vector, a reflection its mirror line, a rotation its centre, angle and direction, and an enlargement its centre and scale factor. Translations, reflections and rotations preserve length and angle, so they produce a congruent image; an enlargement with k not equal to 1 does not. Two transformations performed one after the other can often be described as a single transformation.4
      10.14.7.2Give a complete description of a single transformation shown on a grid.4
      10H.12.5.1A complete description names the transformation and gives everything that specifies it: a translation needs its column vector, a reflection its mirror line, a rotation its centre, angle and direction, and an enlargement its centre and scale factor. Translations, reflections and rotations preserve length and angle, so they produce a congruent image; an enlargement with k not equal to 1 does not. A mirror line is halfway between each point and its image, a centre of rotation is as far from each point as from its image, and a centre of enlargement is where lines through matching points meet.5
      10H.12.5.2Give a complete description of a single transformation shown on a grid.4
      10H.12.5.3Give a complete description of a rotation about a centre other than the origin, or of an enlargement with a fractional or negative scale factor, finding the centre first.6

      5.2ARotation

      7.18.4.1A rotation is fully defined by three things: a centre, an angle and a direction. Every point stays the same distance from the centre as it turns. Clockwise and anticlockwise turns of the same angle give different images, except for 180 degrees. The centre may lie on the shape, inside it, or outside it.4
      7.18.4.2Rotate a shape about a given centre through 90, 180 or 270 degrees, clockwise or anticlockwise.4
      7.18.4.3Rotate a shape about a centre lying on or outside the shape, using tracing paper to check.4
      8.18.2.1A rotation is fully defined by a centre, an angle and a direction. Every point stays the same distance from the centre as it turns. Clockwise and anticlockwise turns of the same angle give different images, except for 180 degrees. A line of symmetry divides a shape into two mirror halves. The order of rotational symmetry is how many times a shape looks identical during one full turn, and is always at least 1.5
      8.18.2.3Rotate a shape about a given centre through 90, 180 or 270 degrees, clockwise or anticlockwise.4
      10.14.3.1A rotation is specified by a centre, an angle and a direction. An anticlockwise rotation is a positive angle and a clockwise rotation is a negative angle. Every point of the image is the same distance from the centre as its object point, and the centre itself does not move. A rotation preserves length and angle, so the image is congruent to the object.4

      5.2EReflection

      7.18.3.1A line of symmetry divides a shape into two halves that are mirror images of each other. In a reflection every point moves to the same perpendicular distance on the other side of the mirror line. A point lying on the mirror line does not move. The mirror line may be given as an equation: x = a, y = b, or y = x.2
      7.18.3.3Reflect a shape in a given mirror line, including the lines x = a, y = b and y = x.4
      8.18.1.1A translation slides a shape without turning or resizing it, so the image is identical to the original. A column vector gives the movement: right or left on top, up or down below, with negatives for left and down. In a reflection every point moves to the same perpendicular distance on the other side of the mirror line. A point lying on the mirror line does not move. Reflecting in y = x swaps a point's coordinates; reflecting in y = -x swaps them and changes both signs.4
      8.18.1.3Reflect a shape in the lines x = a, y = b, y = x and y = -x.5
      10.14.2.1A reflection is specified by a mirror line, and every point of the image is the same perpendicular distance from that line as its object point, on the opposite side. A point on the mirror line does not move. Mirror lines are given as equations such as x = 1, y = 2, y = x and y = -x. A reflection preserves length and angle, so the image is congruent to the object, but the sense is reversed.3
      10.14.2.2Reflect a shape in a given mirror line, including the lines y = x and y = -x.3
      10H.12.2.1A reflection is specified by a mirror line, and every point of the image is the same perpendicular distance from that line as its object point, on the opposite side. Mirror lines are given as equations such as x = 1, y = 2, y = x and y = -x. A rotation is specified by a centre, an angle and a direction. An anticlockwise rotation is a positive angle and a clockwise rotation is a negative angle. Every point of the image is the same distance from the centre as its object point, and the centre itself does not move. Reflections and rotations preserve length and angle, so the image is congruent to the object; a reflection reverses the sense and a rotation does not.4

      8.18.3.1An enlargement changes a shape's size but not its shape, so corresponding angles stay equal and the two shapes are similar. The scale factor multiplies every length. The centre of enlargement fixes where the image sits, and rays drawn from it through each vertex locate the image points. The distance from the centre to an image point is the scale factor times the distance to the matching object point. The scale factor is found by dividing an image length by the matching object length.5

Every length on the image is k times the matching length on the object, and the distance from the centre to an image point is k times the distance from the centre to its object point. An enlargement preserves angles but not lengths, so the image is similar to the object and not congruent to it.4

An enlargement preserves angles but not lengths, so the image is similar to the object and not congruent to it.4

      Enlargement - negative / fractional scale factor

      8.18.4.1A scale factor between 0 and 1 makes the image smaller, though it is still called an enlargement. The rules are unchanged: every length, and every distance from the centre, is multiplied by the scale factor. A negative scale factor places the image on the opposite side of the centre. It also turns the image upside down, so it is equivalent to a positive enlargement followed by a 180 degree rotation about the centre. An invariant point does not move under a transformation, and the centre of enlargement is always invariant.7
      8.18.4.2Enlarge a shape by a fractional scale factor.5
      8.18.4.3Enlarge a shape by a negative scale factor.7
      10.14.5.1A scale factor between 0 and 1 produces an image smaller than the object, and it is still called an enlargement. The rule is unchanged: each distance from the centre is multiplied by k, so k = 1/2 halves every distance from the centre. The image is still similar to the object, and the enlargement with scale factor 1/k about the same centre undoes it.4

It also turns the image upside down, so it is equivalent to a positive enlargement followed by a 180 degree rotation about the centre. An invariant point does not move under a transformation, and the centre of enlargement is always invariant.7

      Similarity
      • Similar figures
      • Congruence
      • Maps and scale drawings

      4.11ASimilar figures

      8.4.1.1Similar shapes have equal corresponding angles and corresponding sides in the same ratio. The scale factor is the ratio of a length on one shape to the matching length on the other. A scale factor above 1 enlarges and one below 1 reduces. A missing length is found by multiplying the corresponding length by the scale factor. Corresponding sides are matched by their position in the shape, not by how they look on the page.4
      8.4.1.2Identify similar shapes and calculate the scale factor between them.4
      8.4.1.3Find missing lengths in a pair of similar shapes using the scale factor.5
      8.4.2.1Triangles formed between a pair of parallel lines are similar, because alternate and corresponding angles make their angles equal. Two triangles with all three angles equal are similar whatever their size. In the hourglass and arrowhead arrangements it is the equal angles that identify which sides correspond.6
      8.4.2.2Identify triangles formed between a pair of parallel lines as similar, and use the equal angles to match corresponding sides in the hourglass and arrowhead arrangements.5
      8.4.2.3Find missing lengths in a pair of similar triangles formed between parallel lines, using the scale factor between corresponding sides.6
      8.16.5.1Proving two triangles congruent establishes that every pair of corresponding sides and angles is equal. That is what makes congruence a tool for proving two lengths or angles equal, rather than an end in itself. Corresponding parts are matched by the order the vertices are named, so ABC congruent to DEF means AB = DE. A structured proof states each fact with its reason, then the condition satisfied, then the conclusion drawn.6
      10.12.1.1Two shapes are similar when one is an enlargement of the other: corresponding angles are equal and corresponding lengths are all in the same ratio. That ratio is the scale factor k, found by dividing a length on the image by the length it corresponds to on the object. A length on the image = k x the matching length on the object, so k > 1 enlarges and k < 1 reduces.4
      10.12.1.2Identify the corresponding sides and angles of a pair of similar shapes and calculate the scale factor between them.4
      10.12.1.3Calculate an unknown length in a pair of similar shapes, including two triangles that share an angle.5
      10H.10.1.1Similar shapes have equal corresponding angles and corresponding sides in the same ratio. The length scale factor k is a length on one shape divided by the matching length on the other, and every length on the second shape, its perimeter included, is k times its partner. Corresponding sides are matched by the equal angles they sit opposite, not by where they sit on the page. Going from the larger shape back to the smaller, each length is divided by k. When one triangle sits inside another, sharing an angle, with the third sides parallel, the two triangles are similar, and the scale factor uses the whole sides, never only the parts.5
      10H.10.1.3Find a missing length in two similar triangles where one sits inside the other and shares an angle with it, including a length that is only part of a side, found by subtraction.6

      Congruence

      8.4.3.1Congruent shapes are identical in both size and shape, whereas similar shapes share angles but not size. Two triangles are congruent if they satisfy SSS (three sides), SAS (two sides and the angle between them), ASA (two angles and a corresponding side) or RHS (right angle, hypotenuse and one other side). AAA proves similarity only, because equal angles fix a shape's proportions but not its size. SSA is not a condition, since two different triangles can share two sides and a non-included angle. Corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal, which is what makes congruence useful for proving two lengths or angles equal.5
      8.4.3.3Prove that two triangles are congruent, stating the condition used, and use congruence to justify that two lengths or angles are equal.6
      8.16.5.2Use congruence to prove that two lengths or angles in a diagram are equal.6

      4.11BMaps and scale drawings

      10.12.2.1A scale of 1 : n means that 1 unit on the drawing stands for n of the same units in real life. A map scale of 1 : 25000 means 1 cm on the map is 25000 cm, which is 250 m, in real life. Real length = drawing length x n, and drawing length = real length / n, so the two are inverse operations.3
      10.12.2.2Use a given scale to convert between a length on a map or scale drawing and the real length it stands for.3
      10.12.2.3Produce a scale drawing to a stated scale and use it to answer a question about a real distance.4

      No matching specification point

      8.16.4.1Congruent shapes are identical in both size and shape, whereas similar shapes share angles but not size. Two triangles are congruent if they satisfy SSS, SAS (the angle between the two sides), ASA or RHS. AAA proves similarity only, because equal angles fix a shape's proportions but not its size. SSA is not a condition, since two different triangles can share two sides and a non-included angle. A congruence proof names the condition and gives a reason for each equal side or angle used.5
      8.16.4.2Identify congruent shapes and state the condition satisfied.5
      8.4.3.2Identify congruent triangles and state which condition they satisfy.5
      8.16.4.3Prove that two triangles are congruent, giving the condition and reasons.6
      8.16.6.1Three sides (SSS), two sides and the angle between them (SAS), or two angles and the side between them (ASA) each fix a triangle uniquely. SSA does not: two sides and a non-included angle can produce two different triangles, which is the ambiguous case. The incircle touches all three sides, so its centre is where the three angle bisectors meet. The circumcircle passes through all three vertices, so its centre is where the three perpendicular bisectors meet. Both follow from the loci: equidistant from the sides gives the incircle, equidistant from the vertices the circumcircle.6
      Similarity
      • Areas of similar figures

      4.11A(H)Areas of similar figures

      10H.10.2.1When every length of a shape is multiplied by the scale factor k, every area is multiplied by k^2, because area has two length dimensions. So a length scale factor of 3 gives an area scale factor of 9, and this holds for any area: a face, a cross-section or a whole surface. In reverse, the length scale factor is the square root of the area scale factor, so areas in the ratio 25 : 4 come from lengths in the ratio 5 : 2. The area scale factor is the ratio of two areas, so an area is never divided by a length to find it.6
      10H.10.2.2Find the area of a shape similar to one of known area, given a pair of corresponding lengths.6
      10H.10.2.3Find a missing length given the areas of two similar shapes and one of their lengths, by square-rooting the area scale factor.7

      No matching specification point

      8.16.5.3Construct a structured congruence proof, stating each fact with its reason.7
      Similarity
      • Volumes of similar figures
      • Similarity problems

      4.11B(H)Volumes of similar figures

      10H.10.3.1When every length of a solid is multiplied by the scale factor k, its volume is multiplied by k^3, because volume has three length dimensions, while its surface area is multiplied by k^2. So a length scale factor of 2 gives an area scale factor of 4 and a volume scale factor of 8. In reverse, the length scale factor is the cube root of the volume scale factor and the square root of the area scale factor. To go between areas and volumes, the length scale factor is found first: surface areas in the ratio 4 : 9 come from lengths in the ratio 2 : 3, so the volumes are in the ratio 8 : 27. The masses and capacities of similar solids made of the same material scale like their volumes.6
      10H.10.3.2Find the volume of a solid similar to one of known volume, given a pair of corresponding lengths.6
      10H.10.3.3Find a length, a surface area or a volume of a similar solid given the ratio of two other quantities, such as a volume from two surface areas, by finding the length scale factor first.7

      2D Pythagoras bsaics

      8.11.1.1In a right-angled triangle, a^2 + b^2 = c^2. The hypotenuse c is the longest side and always lies opposite the right angle. The theorem holds only for right-angled triangles. The hypotenuse is found by adding the squares of the two shorter sides and taking the square root. A Pythagorean triple is a set of three whole numbers fitting the theorem: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, and any multiple of these.4
      8.11.1.2Find the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle.4
      9.6.1.1The hypotenuse is the longest side and always lies opposite the right angle. The opposite and adjacent sides are named relative to the angle in use, so the same side changes label when the angle changes. The three ratios are sin = opp/hyp, cos = adj/hyp and tan = opp/adj. The ratio to use is decided by which two sides the question involves. A ratio depends only on the angle and not on the size of the triangle, which is why a calculator can return it.4
      9.6.1.2Label the sides of a right-angled triangle relative to a given angle.4

      8.11.1.3Recognise Pythagorean triples and use them to find lengths without a calculator.5
      8.11.2.1The same theorem finds a shorter side, rearranged to a^2 = c^2 - b^2. Finding a shorter side subtracts, whereas finding the hypotenuse adds. Identifying the hypotenuse first is what decides which of the two applies. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is always the largest of the three values. A shorter side coming out larger than the hypotenuse signals the subtraction was done the wrong way round.5
      8.11.2.2Find a shorter side of a right-angled triangle.5
      8.11.2.3Decide whether to add or subtract by identifying the hypotenuse first.5
      9.6.1.3Choose the correct ratio by identifying which two sides are involved, and evaluate sin, cos and tan of an angle on a calculator.5
      9.6.2.1With the unknown on the numerator, the ratio is an equation solved in one step: multiply both sides by the denominator. sin(x) = opp/hyp with the hypotenuse known therefore gives opp = hyp x sin(x). The working is set out as a labelled equation before any numbers are substituted. The calculator must be in degrees mode or every ratio will be wrong. Rounding is done once, at the end, to the accuracy the question states.5
      9.6.3.1With the unknown on the denominator, the ratio takes two steps: multiply both sides by the unknown, then divide. sin(x) = opp/hyp with the opposite known therefore gives hyp = opp / sin(x). The unknown sits on the denominator when finding the hypotenuse with sin or cos, or the adjacent with tan. Which case applies is decided from the labelled diagram before any calculation starts. The hypotenuse must come out larger than either other side, which checks the answer.5
      10.15.2.1A line segment drawn on a coordinate grid is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle whose shorter sides are the horizontal and vertical differences between the end points. Those differences are x2 - x1 and y2 - y1, and a negative difference is used as its positive size, because a length cannot be negative. Pythagoras' theorem then gives length^2 = (x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2.5
      10.15.2.2Calculate the length of a line segment from the coordinates of its end points, giving the answer to a stated accuracy.5
      10.15.2.3Decide whether two line segments on a grid are equal in length by calculating both.5
      10.9.1.1A right-angled triangle has one angle of exactly 90 degrees, and the side opposite that angle is the hypotenuse, which is always its longest side. Pythagoras' theorem says the square drawn on the hypotenuse has the same area as the squares on the two shorter sides added together: a^2 + b^2 = c^2, where c is the hypotenuse. The theorem is true only for right-angled triangles, so the right angle is found in the diagram before the theorem is used. A length is never negative, so only the positive square root is taken.5
      10.9.1.2Calculate the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle from its two shorter sides, giving the answer to a stated accuracy.5
      10.9.1.3Explain why a^2 + b^2 = c^2 by comparing the areas of the three squares drawn on the sides of a right-angled triangle.5
      10.9.2.1Rearranging a^2 + b^2 = c^2 for a shorter side gives a^2 = c^2 - b^2, so the two squares are SUBTRACTED, not added. Which of the two operations is needed is decided by whether the unknown side is the hypotenuse or one of the shorter sides. A shorter side must come out smaller than the hypotenuse, and that is the check on the answer.5
      10.9.2.2Calculate a shorter side of a right-angled triangle from the hypotenuse and the other shorter side.5
      10.9.2.3Decide whether a triangle with three given side lengths is right-angled by testing whether a^2 + b^2 = c^2.5

      4.8A2D Pythagoras - multi-step

      8.11.3.1A multi-step problem chains two applications of the theorem, the first result becoming an input to the second. Rounding an intermediate value carries that error into the final answer, so exact values are kept until the end. The calculator's store function holds an exact intermediate value for reuse. On a coordinate grid the horizontal and vertical differences between two points are the two shorter sides, so their distance apart follows from the theorem. Inside a 2D shape a right-angled triangle must first be found or constructed before the theorem applies.6
      8.11.3.2Solve multi-step problems using Pythagoras, using the calculator's store function.6
      8.11.3.3Apply Pythagoras in context, including on coordinate grids and within 2D shapes.6
      8.11.4.1The perpendicular from the apex of an isosceles triangle bisects its base. It therefore splits the triangle into two congruent right-angled triangles. Each has half the base as one shorter side and an equal side as the hypotenuse, so Pythagoras gives the perpendicular height. The area is then half the base times that perpendicular height.6
      8.11.4.2Find the perpendicular height of an isosceles triangle using Pythagoras.6
      8.11.4.3Find the area of isosceles triangles and of compound shapes requiring Pythagoras first.6
      10.9.3.1A context question rarely draws the right-angled triangle, so it is sketched first, with the right angle marked and the three sides labelled. A ladder against a wall, a diagonal across a rectangle, and the straight-line distance between two points on a grid are all right-angled triangles. The answer is rounded only at the end, and its units are the units of the lengths given.5
      10.9.3.2Solve a practical problem by identifying a right-angled triangle within it and applying Pythagoras' theorem.5
      10.9.3.3Calculate the diagonal of a rectangle, and the distance between two points on a coordinate grid, using Pythagoras' theorem.5

      4.8B(H)Elevation and depression

      9.6.5.1An angle of elevation is measured upward from the horizontal, and an angle of depression downward from it. The elevation and depression between the same two points are equal, because the two horizontals are parallel. A worded problem is turned into a labelled right-angled triangle before any ratio is chosen. In a three-dimensional solid the problem is solved by finding a right-angled triangle inside it and redrawing that triangle on its own. A multi-step problem may need Pythagoras for one length and trigonometry for another, with exact values kept between the steps.6
