      4.8A(H)Trig ratios of obtuse angles

      4.8C(H)Sine and cosine rules

      11H.2.2.1In any triangle, each side divided by the sine of its opposite angle gives the same value: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Side a is opposite angle A, so a side and the angle opposite it form a pair. The sine rule needs one complete pair plus one more side or angle. To find a length, the rule is written with the sides on top and rearranged: a = b x sin A / sin B.6
      11H.2.2.2Use the sine rule to find a missing side in a triangle that is not right-angled.6
      11H.2.2.3Find a missing side with the sine rule after finding the third angle from the angle sum, including in context.7
      11H.2.3.1To find an angle, the sine rule is written with the sines on top: sin A / a = sin B / b. This gives sin A, and then A = sin^-1 of that value. Because sin x = sin (180 - x), a value of sin A fits two angles, A and 180 - A. The obtuse angle is possible only if it leaves room for the other angles, so when the given angle is opposite the shorter given side there can be two triangles: the ambiguous case.7
      11H.2.3.2Use the sine rule to find a missing angle in a triangle that is not right-angled.7
      11H.2.3.3Decide whether the ambiguous case gives one or two possible triangles, and find both angles when two exist.8
      11H.2.4.1In any triangle, a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc cos A, where A is the angle between the sides b and c, and a is opposite it. The cosine rule is used when the given angle is enclosed by the two given sides, so no complete side-and-opposite-angle pair is known. When A = 90 degrees, cos A = 0 and the rule becomes Pythagoras. When A is obtuse, cos A is negative, so the last term is added and the opposite side is longer.7
      11H.2.4.2Use the cosine rule to find a missing side, given two sides and the angle between them.7
      11H.2.4.3Choose between the sine rule and the cosine rule for a given triangle, and use the one that fits.7
      11H.2.5.1Rearranged, the cosine rule finds an angle from three sides: cos A = (b^2 + c^2 - a^2) / (2bc), where a is the side opposite A. A negative value of cos A means that A is obtuse. The area of any triangle is 1/2 ab sin C, where C is the angle between the sides a and b. A given area can be used in the same formula to find a missing side or angle.7
      11H.2.5.2Use the cosine rule to find an angle, given all three sides.7
      11H.2.6.1A multi-step problem is split into triangles, each solved with the rule its given information fits. A side-and-opposite-angle pair calls for the sine rule; two sides and the angle between them, or three sides, call for the cosine rule; and two sides with the angle between them give the area by 1/2 ab sin C. A length or angle found in one triangle becomes given information in the next, kept to full calculator accuracy and rounded only at the end.8
      11H.2.6.2Solve problems on compound shapes that need two or more of the sine rule, the cosine rule and the area formula.8
      11H.2.6.3Solve trigonometry problems in context, including bearings, justifying the rule used at each step.8
      FM.7.1-7.2.3Use the sine rule to find an unknown side or angle, recognising the ambiguous case.8
      FM.7.3-7.4.1The cosine rule, a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc cos A (and its relabelled versions), applies when the sine rule cannot: given two sides and the included angle, or all three sides. Rearranged as cos A = (b^2 + c^2 - a^2) / (2bc), it finds an angle from three known sides. A triangle has only three independent measurements, so knowing any three unlocks the rest.7
      FM.7.3-7.4.2Use the cosine rule to find an unknown side or angle.7
      FM.7.3-7.4.3Decide which rule to apply from the information given, and combine both rules with bearings and angle facts.8

      11H.2.5.3Find the area of a triangle using 1/2 ab sin C, and find a missing side or angle from a given area.7
      FM.7.1-7.2.1The area of any triangle is half the product of two sides and the sine of the included angle - e.g. Area = 1/2 ab sin C. The sine rule, a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C (or its reciprocal sin A/a = sin B/b = sin C/c for finding an angle), follows from equating two area expressions for the same triangle; use the side-over-sine form to find a side, and the sine-over-side form to find an angle.7

      Vectors
      • Magnitude and direction
      • Vector notation

      5.1A(H)Magnitude and direction

      11H.8.1.1A vector has both a magnitude (its size) and a direction; a scalar has a size only. A vector can be written as a column vector, as vector AB from the point A to the point B, or as a single bold letter such as a, underlined when handwritten. In a column vector the top number is the move right (negative for left) and the bottom number is the move up (negative for down). Equal vectors have the same magnitude and the same direction wherever they are drawn, and vector BA = -vector AB. The magnitude of a column vector with components x and y is the square root of (x^2 + y^2), by Pythagoras.6
      11H.8.1.2Write the column vector from one point to another, and find the magnitude of a vector.6
      11H.8.1.3Find the direction of a vector as a bearing, using trigonometry.7

      5.1B(H)Vector notation

      5.1C(H)Scalar multiples

      11H.8.2.1Multiplying a vector by a scalar k multiplies each of its components by k. The vector ka is parallel to a and k times as long; when k is negative, ka points the opposite way to a. Two vectors are parallel exactly when one is a scalar multiple of the other: the vector with components 2 and 3 is parallel to the one with 6 and 9, but not to the one with 4 and 5. The scalar gives the ratio of the lengths: if vector PQ = 3 x vector AB, then PQ is three times as long as AB.7
      11H.8.2.2Multiply a vector by a scalar, and decide whether two vectors are parallel.7
      11H.8.2.3Find an unknown component that makes two vectors parallel, and state the ratio of their lengths.8

      5.1D(H)Adding vectors

      11H.8.3.1Vectors add head to tail: vector AB + vector BC = vector AC, which is called the resultant. Column vectors add and subtract component by component. Subtracting a vector adds its negative: a - b = a + (-b), where -b has the same length as b and points the other way. A route is reversed by changing every sign: vector CA = -vector AC. The magnitude of a resultant is found from its components, not by adding magnitudes.7
      11H.8.3.2Add and subtract column vectors, including scalar multiples such as 2a - 3b, and draw the resultant.6

      5.1E(H)Modulus of a vector

      11H.8.3.3Find the magnitude of a resultant, and solve a vector equation such as 2a + kb = c for an unknown scalar.7

      5.1F(H)Resultant vectors

      11H.8.4.1In a diagram, the vector between two points is found by a route along known vectors, adding each step: vector AC = vector AB + vector BC. A step taken against a vector's arrow takes a minus sign. Any route between the same two points gives the same vector, so the simplest route is chosen. With vector OA = a and vector OB = b, vector AB = -a + b = b - a. Opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal vectors, and a side parallel to a and twice as long is 2a.7
      11H.8.4.2Write vectors in a triangle or parallelogram in terms of a and b, choosing a route.7
      11H.8.4.3Write vectors in a shape whose sides are multiples of others, such as a trapezium with vector DC = 2 x vector AB, or a regular hexagon.8
      11H.8.5.1If M is the midpoint of AB, then vector AM = 1/2 vector AB. If P divides AB in the ratio m:n, then vector AP = m/(m + n) of vector AB, because the line is split into m + n equal parts. The vector to such a point from O is found by a route: vector OP = vector OA + vector AP. With vector OA = a and vector OB = b, vector AB = b - a, so vector OM = a + 1/2(b - a) = 1/2(a + b).8
      11H.8.5.2Find the vector to the midpoint of a line, such as vector OM, in terms of a and b.8
      11H.8.5.3Find the vector to a point dividing a line in a given ratio, such as AP:PB = 1:3, in terms of a and b.8
      11H.8.6.1A point on a line extended beyond B, such as C with AB:BC = 2:1, is reached by carrying on in the same direction, so vector BC = 1/2 vector AB. A point on a side of a shape is reached by a route along known vectors, using the fraction of that side. Every vector in a problem is written in terms of the same two non-parallel vectors, such as a and b, and simplified by collecting terms.8
      11H.8.6.2Find the vector to a point on a line extended beyond a vertex, given a ratio.8
      11H.8.6.3Find vectors in a shape that combine points given by ratios on two different sides.8
      Vectors
      • Vector proof

      5.1G(H)Vector proof

      11H.8.7.1To prove two lines are parallel, both vectors are written in terms of a and b, and one is shown to be a scalar multiple of the other. A common factor may need taking out first: 2a + 4b = 2(a + 2b), so it is parallel to a + 2b. The proof states the multiple and concludes in words: vector PQ = 2 x vector RS, so PQ is parallel to RS and twice as long. A quadrilateral is a parallelogram when both pairs of opposite sides are equal vectors, and a trapezium when one pair is parallel but not equal.9
      11H.8.7.2Prove that two line segments are parallel using vectors, and state the ratio of their lengths.9
      11H.8.7.3Prove that a quadrilateral is a parallelogram or a trapezium using vectors.9
      11H.8.8.1Three points A, B and C are collinear when vector AB is a scalar multiple of vector BC, or of vector AC, and the two vectors share the point B. Parallel alone is not enough: parallel vectors with no point in common lie on separate parallel lines. The scalar gives the ratio: vector AC = 3 x vector AB means AB:BC = 1:2. An unknown scalar k is found by making one vector a multiple of the other and comparing the coefficients of a and b, since a and b are not parallel.9
      11H.8.8.2Prove that three points are collinear using vectors, and state the ratio in which the middle point divides the line.9
      11H.8.8.3Find the value of an unknown scalar, such as k, that makes three points collinear or two lines parallel, by comparing coefficients.9

      7.12.1.2Classify data as discrete or continuous, primary or secondary.3
      7.12.1.3Write a testable hypothesis and identify which representation suits given data.4
      7.12.1.1The data handling cycle runs hypothesis, collect, represent, analyse, conclude, and can be repeated. A hypothesis is a statement the data can support or contradict. Discrete data takes separate fixed values; continuous data can take any value in a range. Primary data is collected first-hand; secondary data comes from someone else.3
      7.12.2.1A bar chart shows frequency by bar height, with equal bar widths and equal gaps for discrete data. The axes must be labelled and the frequency scale must go up in equal steps. A pictogram uses a repeated symbol with a key stating what one symbol represents. A part-symbol represents that fraction of the key value.2
      7.12.2.2Draw bar charts and pictograms accurately, with labelled axes, scale and key.2
      7.12.2.3Interpret bar charts and pictograms, including part-symbols and comparisons between categories.3
      10.23.1.1A bar chart shows the frequency of each category as the HEIGHT of a bar, and the bars are equal in width and separated by gaps. The vertical axis starts at zero and is labelled with what is being counted, or the chart misleads. A pictogram shows frequency with repeated symbols, and the key states how many items one whole symbol stands for. Part of a symbol stands for the matching fraction of that number, so half a symbol worth 10 is 5.1
      10.23.1.2Draw a bar chart from a frequency table with a sensible scale and labelled axes, and a pictogram using a stated key, including part symbols.1
      10.23.2.1A dual bar chart places two bars side by side for each category to compare two sets of data, and it needs a key. A composite bar chart stacks the two on top of each other, so the whole bar is the total and each part is a component. A dual chart compares the parts directly; a composite chart compares the totals directly. The question decides which is right.3
      10.23.2.2Draw a dual or composite bar chart from a two-way frequency table, with a key.3
      10.23.3.1A pie chart shows how a whole is shared out, so the whole circle is the total frequency and 360 degrees represents that total. The angle for a category is (frequency / total frequency) x 360 degrees, and the angles must sum to 360 degrees. A pie chart shows proportions, not amounts, so two pie charts cannot be compared unless both totals are known.3
      10.23.3.2Draw a pie chart from a frequency table by calculating each sector angle.3

      10.4.3.1A two-way table organises two characteristics of a group at once, one across the columns and one down the rows, with row and column totals and a grand total that must all be self-consistent.3
      10.4.3.2Complete a two-way table from partial information, using the row, column and grand totals to find missing values.4

      7.12.3.1Grouped data collects values into class intervals, each with its own frequency. The midpoint of a class interval is halfway between its endpoints and represents the whole class. A frequency polygon plots frequency against midpoint and joins the points with straight lines. The shape of the polygon shows where the data clusters and how spread out it is.4

      Probability
      • The probability scale

      6.3BThe probability scale

      7.17.1.1Probability measures how likely an outcome is, on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). An even chance is 0.5, and a probability can be written as a fraction, decimal or percentage. Outcomes are equally likely when there is no reason to expect one rather than another. For equally likely outcomes, the probability of an event is the number of favourable outcomes over the total number of outcomes.2
      7.17.1.2Place events on a 0-1 probability scale and describe likelihood in words.2
      10.23.4.1A probability is a number from 0 to 1, where 0 means impossible, 1 means certain and 1/2 means an even chance. When outcomes are equally likely, P(event) = (number of outcomes in the event) / (total number of outcomes). A sample space is the list of every possible outcome, and for two successive events it is listed systematically, for example in a grid, so that none is missed or counted twice. The probabilities of all the possible outcomes add up to 1, so P(not A) = 1 - P(A).1

      6.3FListing outcomes

      10.23.4.3List all the outcomes of two successive events systematically, such as two coins or a spinner and a dice, and use the sample space to find a probability.3
      11H.4.4.1The product rule for counting: if one choice can be made in m ways and a second in n ways, the two together can be made in m x n ways, and the rule extends to any number of choices. Choosing from the same list again multiplies by the same number when repeats are allowed, and by one fewer each time when they are not. A restriction is applied first to the place it controls, then the remaining places are counted from what is left. When every outcome is equally likely, a probability is the count of wanted outcomes over the count of all outcomes.6
      11H.4.4.2Use the product rule to count the outcomes of two or more choices, with and without repeats.6
      11H.4.4.3Count outcomes with a restriction, such as an even last digit, and use the counts to find a probability.7

      6.3GExperimental probability

      7.17.3.3Calculate experimental probability from results and compare it with theoretical probability, commenting on fairness.5
      10.23.5.1Relative frequency = (number of times the event happened) / (number of trials), and it estimates a probability from collected data. The more trials there are, the closer the relative frequency is likely to be to the true probability, so a large experiment gives a better estimate than a small one. Expected frequency = probability x number of trials, which is how many times the event should happen on average and not a guarantee. For mutually exclusive events, which cannot happen at the same time, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).3
      10.23.5.2Estimate a probability from experimental data as a relative frequency, and use a probability to calculate an expected frequency.3

      7.17.2.2Find the probability of a complement using P(not A) = 1 - P(A).4
      9.16.1.3Find the probability of a complement using P(not A) = 1 - P(A).2
      Probability
      • Expected frequency

      6.3JExpected frequency

      7.17.3.1The expected number of occurrences is the probability multiplied by the number of trials. An expected value is a prediction rather than a guarantee, so real results vary around it. Experimental probability (relative frequency) is the number of successes divided by the number of trials. Experimental probability approaches theoretical probability as the number of trials increases. A large gap between the two over many trials suggests the item is biased.4
      7.17.3.2Calculate expected outcomes for a given number of trials.4

      6.3DProbability from Venn diagrams

      7.17.4.2Complete a probability distribution table and find a missing probability.4
      7.17.4.3Find probabilities for two successive events, using sample space diagrams or multiplication.6
      9.16.4.3Find the probability of combined outcomes from a tree diagram.5

      10.4.2.1A probability read from a Venn diagram is the number of elements in a region divided by n(xi); because every element appears exactly once, the region counts add up to n(xi).4
      10.4.2.2Find probabilities from a completed Venn diagram, including for a union, intersection or complement.4
      10.4.2.3Solve a Venn diagram problem working backwards from a given probability to find a missing value or a missing region.5
      10.4.4.1The structure of a problem decides which representation to use: a Venn diagram suits overlapping categories, a two-way table suits two characteristics at once, and a tree diagram suits a sequence of events. Whichever is used, every representation must account for the whole sample space, so its probabilities sum to 1.4
      10.4.4.2Choose an appropriate representation (Venn diagram or two-way table) for a given probability problem and use it to find the probability asked for.4

      6.3IMutually exclusive events

      7.17.2.1The probabilities of all possible outcomes sum to 1. The complement of A is everything else, so P(not A) = 1 - P(A). Mutually exclusive events cannot both happen at the same time. The probability that one of several mutually exclusive events occurs is found by adding their probabilities.4
      7.17.2.3Identify mutually exclusive events and find the probability that one of them occurs.4
      9.16.1.1Two events are independent when one happening does not change the probability of the other. They are dependent when it does, as when an item is taken and not replaced. They are mutually exclusive when they cannot both happen at once. Mutually exclusive is not the same as independent: mutually exclusive events are strongly dependent, since one occurring makes the other impossible. The probabilities of all possible outcomes sum to 1, so P(not A) = 1 - P(A).4
      9.16.1.2Classify pairs of events as independent, dependent or mutually exclusive.5
      9.16.3.1For mutually exclusive events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). Where the events can both happen, the overlap has been counted twice, so P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). In set notation 'A or B' is the union, A union B, and the overlap is the intersection. 'And' multiplies and 'or' adds, which is the quickest way to tell which rule a question needs.5
      9.16.3.2Calculate the probability that one or other event occurs.5
      10.23.5.3Use the addition rule for mutually exclusive events, including finding a missing probability in a table whose probabilities sum to 1.3

      6.3B(H)Independent events

      7.17.4.1A probability distribution lists every outcome with its probability, and these must total 1. A missing probability is found by subtracting the others from 1. A sample space diagram lists every possible outcome of two events, so probabilities can be counted from it. Two events are independent when one does not affect the other. For independent events, the probability of both is found by multiplying their probabilities.5
      9.16.2.1For two independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B). Multiplying makes the answer smaller, which fits: both happening is less likely than either alone. The rule extends to more than two independent events by multiplying all of their probabilities. In set notation 'A and B' is the intersection, A intersect B.5
      9.16.2.2Calculate the probability of two independent events both occurring.5
      9.16.2.3Use set notation to describe combined events.5

      Probability
      • Tree diagrams

      6.3A(H)Tree diagrams

      9.16.4.1A tree diagram lists every possible outcome of a sequence of events, one branch per outcome. The probabilities on any one set of branches sum to 1. Probabilities multiply along a path, because a path is an 'and'. Probabilities add across paths, because separate paths are an 'or'. All the final path probabilities together sum to 1, which checks the diagram.5
      9.16.4.2Draw a tree diagram for two events and label every branch probability.5
      9.16.5.1With no replacement the first outcome changes what is left, so the second set of branch probabilities differs. Both the numerator and the denominator change: one fewer of the item taken, and one fewer in total. Each second-stage branch set has its own probabilities, depending on which first branch it follows. Each branch set still sums to 1, which is the check that the diagram is right.6
      9.16.5.2Draw and complete a tree diagram for dependent events, without replacement.6
      9.16.5.3Calculate probabilities for dependent events.6
      9.16.6.3Solve multi-step problems using tree diagrams.6

      Probability
      • Probability problems

      6.3D(H)Probability problems

      9.16.3.3Apply the and/or rules to problems stated in set notation.6
      9.16.6.1'At least one' covers every outcome except none at all. So P(at least one) = 1 - P(none), which is usually far quicker than adding the separate cases. P(none) is the product of the probabilities of it not happening at each stage. A multi-step problem may combine this with tree paths, adding the relevant path probabilities.6
      9.16.6.2Find the probability of at least one occurrence using the complement.6
      9.16.9.1The structure of a problem decides the tool: a two-way table, a tree diagram, a Venn diagram, or direct calculation. A tree suits a sequence of events, a Venn suits overlapping categories, and a table suits two characteristics at once. The and/or rules apply whichever representation is used, since the representation only organises the outcomes. Every representation must account for the whole sample space, so its probabilities sum to 1.6
      9.16.9.2Select and apply the appropriate representation for a probability problem.6
      9.16.9.3Solve multi-event problems combining several probability rules.7
      11H.4.5.1When a bag holds an unknown number of items, each probability is an algebraic fraction: with n sweets of which 6 are orange, P(orange) = 6/n. Without replacement both counts fall by one for the second pick, so P(two orange) = 6/n x 5/(n - 1); with replacement it is 6/n x 6/n. Setting the expression equal to the given probability makes an equation, which is cleared of fractions and is usually a quadratic. Only a positive whole number can be a count, so any other root is rejected.8
      11H.4.5.2Form an equation from a probability involving an unknown number of items, with or without replacement.8
      11H.4.5.3Solve the equation, reject any root that cannot be a count, and use the count to find a further probability.8
      11H.4.6.1The probabilities of all the outcomes of one event, or of one set of branches, sum to 1; when they are written with x, that sum is an equation. Adding or removing items changes the total as well as the count of one colour, so a new probability is written over the new total. Two items taken from two different bags are independent, so their probabilities multiply. The value of x is usually a step, not the answer: it is substituted back into the expression the question asks about, and a value that makes a probability negative or greater than 1 is rejected.8
      11H.4.6.2Use the fact that probabilities sum to 1 to find an unknown probability written with x.7
      11H.4.6.3Solve multi-step algebraic probability problems, such as items added to a bag or a choice from two bags.8
      Probability
      • Conditional probability

      6.3C(H)Conditional probability

      11H.4.1.1A sample space lists every equally likely outcome, in a two-way table or a grid such as the 36 outcomes of two dice. A probability is the count of wanted outcomes over the count of all possible outcomes. A conditional probability is a probability GIVEN that something is already known, and the known fact shrinks the possible outcomes to one row, column or part of the grid. So P(A given B) = (number in both A and B) / (number in B): the denominator is the restricted total, not the grand total.6
      11H.4.1.2Find a probability from a completed two-way table, including a conditional probability restricted to one row or column.4
      11H.4.1.3Find a conditional probability from a sample space diagram for two events, such as the scores on two dice.6
      11H.4.2.1On a Venn diagram, P(A given B) uses only the elements inside circle B, so P(A given B) = n(A and B) / n(B). The numerator is the overlap and the denominator is the whole of B: B only plus the overlap. P(A given B) and P(B given A) share a numerator but have different denominators, so they are usually different. When the Venn diagram holds probabilities instead of counts, the same rule applies: P(A given B) = P(A and B) / P(B).7
      11H.4.2.2Find a conditional probability from a Venn diagram of counts or of probabilities.7
      11H.4.2.3Find a missing value in a Venn diagram from a given conditional probability, and use it.7
      11H.4.3.1On a tree diagram the second set of branches carries conditional probabilities: each is the probability of the second event GIVEN the branch it follows. Multiplying along a path gives P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B given A). P(B) adds every path that ends in B. Reading a tree backwards, P(A given B) = P(A and B) / P(B), which is not on any branch. Without replacement the second-stage branches change, which is the commonest source of a conditional tree.7
      11H.4.3.3Work backwards on a tree diagram to find a reversed conditional probability, such as P(rain given late).7
      Set language and notation
      • Definition of a set

      1.5ADefinition of a set

      7.2.1.1A set is a collection of distinct elements; order does not matter and nothing is listed twice. A set takes a capital letter, with its elements in curly brackets: A = {2, 4, 6}. 'a in A' means a is an element of A; 'a not-in A' means it is not. The universal set (xi) is everything under consideration in the question. The empty set (empty, or {}) has no elements. n(A) is the number of elements in A.3
      10.4.1.1A set is a collection of distinct elements, written with a capital letter and curly brackets; the universal set (xi) is everything under consideration and the empty set (empty) has none. The complement A' is everything in xi not in A, so n(A) + n(A') = n(xi). B is a subset of A when every element of B is also in A.3
      Set language and notation
      • Set notation
      • Universal and empty sets

      1.5BSet notation

      7.2.3.1A union B is the elements in A, in B, or in both, each listed once. A intersect B is the elements in both; it is empty when the sets share nothing. n(A union B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A intersect B), since shared elements would otherwise count twice.4
      7.2.3.2List the elements of A union B and A intersect B given two sets.4
      7.2.3.3Use set notation (in, not-in, union, intersect, subset, complement) fluently to describe relationships between sets.5
      8.7.1.3Identify subsets and describe groups of numbers (integers, primes, multiples) using set notation.5
      8.7.2.3Shade the regions representing a simple union or intersection.4
      8.7.3.1A compound expression combines union, intersection and complement. It is read inside out: brackets first, then union and intersect, with the complement dash applying to whatever it follows. A' intersect B means in B but not in A; (A union B)' means in neither. Different expressions can describe the same region, so (A union B)' and A' intersect B' are the same set. With three sets the same reading applies, across eight regions rather than four.6
      10.4.1.2Use set notation (in, not-in, union, intersect, subset, complement) to describe relationships between sets, and identify subsets of a given universal set.4

      1.5CUniversal and empty sets

      7.2.1.2Identify elements of a set, and write/interpret the universal set (xi) and empty set (empty).4
      8.7.1.1A set is a collection of distinct elements, named with a capital letter and listed inside curly brackets. xi is the universal set, everything under consideration in the question; the empty set has no elements at all. 'in' means is an element of, and 'not-in' means is not. A' is the complement of A: everything in the universal set that is not in A. n(A) is the number of elements in A, and n(A) + n(A') = n(xi). B subset-of A means every element of B is also an element of A.4

      1.5DComplements and subsets

      7.2.2.1The complement A' is every element of the universal set not in A. Every element is in exactly one of A or A', so n(A) + n(A') = n(xi). B is a subset of A (B subset-of A) when every element of B is also in A. Every set is a subset of itself, and the empty set is a subset of every set. Groups of numbers (evens, primes, squares, multiples of n) are commonly used as sets, some subsets of others.5
      7.2.2.2Identify and write the complement of a given set.5
      7.2.2.3Determine whether one set is a subset of another.5

      7.2.1.3Find n(A), the number of elements in a set A.4

      Set language and notation
      • Venn diagrams

      1.5EVenn diagrams

      7.2.4.1Each set is a closed region inside a rectangle representing the universal set. Every element appears once, in the region matching all the sets it belongs to; elements in no set sit outside the circles but inside the rectangle. Two sets make four regions; three sets make eight. An Euler diagram shows only the relationships that occur, so it is used when sets share nothing or one lies inside another.4
      7.2.4.3Choose whether a Venn or Euler diagram best represents a given group of sets.5
      7.2.5.1A shaded region is the set of all elements the expression describes. Read a compound expression inside out: brackets, then union and intersect, with ' applying to whatever it follows. A' intersect B means 'in B but not A'; (A union B)' means 'in neither'. Different expressions can give the same region: (A union B)' = A' intersect B'.5
      7.2.5.2Shade the region representing a given set expression, including compound expressions.5
      8.7.2.1In a Venn diagram each set is a closed region inside a rectangle representing the universal set. Every element appears exactly once, in the region matching all the sets it belongs to. Elements in none of the sets sit inside the rectangle but outside every circle. Two sets create four regions and three sets create eight, each region corresponding to one set expression. An Euler diagram is used instead when the sets are nested or share no elements.4
      8.7.4.1A probability read from a Venn diagram is the number of elements in the region divided by n(xi). The region is identified from the set notation first, and its elements counted second. Because every element appears exactly once, the region counts add up to n(xi). A given probability works backwards: multiplying it by n(xi) gives the number of elements in that region.5
      8.7.4.2Find probabilities from a completed Venn diagram.5

      Statistical measures
      • Mean, median, mode and range

      6.2BMean, median, mode and range

      7.8.1.1The mean is the total of the values divided by how many there are, sharing the total equally. The median is the middle value once the data is in order; with an even number of values it is halfway between the middle two. The mode is the most frequent value, and there can be more than one or none at all. The range is the largest value minus the smallest, and measures spread rather than a typical value.2
      7.8.1.2Find the mode, median and range of listed data, including ordering data first.2
      7.8.1.3Calculate the mean of listed data.3
      7.8.2.2Find all four measures from a data set, including data with an even number of values and data containing negatives or decimals.3
      8.17.1.1The mean is the total of the values divided by how many there are. The median is the middle value once the data is ordered; with an even count it is halfway between the middle two. The mode is the most frequent value, and there may be more than one or none at all. The range is the largest value minus the smallest, and measures spread rather than a typical value. A stem-and-leaf diagram keeps every original value in order, so all four measures can be read straight from it.2
      8.17.1.2Find the mean, median, mode and range of listed data.3
      10.18.1.1The mean is the total of the values divided by how many values there are. The median is the middle value once the data are in order; with an even number of values it is the mean of the middle two. The mode is the most common value, and a data set may have more than one mode or none. The range is the largest value minus the smallest and measures spread, not average.2
      10.18.1.2Calculate the mean, median, mode and range of a discrete data set.2

      Statistical measures
      • Comparing data sets
      • Modal class
      • Frequency tables

      6.2AComparing data sets

      7.8.2.1The same data set can give three quite different averages. The mean uses every value, so one extreme value shifts it; the median depends only on position, so it resists extremes. Because the mean is the total divided by the count, the total can be recovered as mean x count. A missing value is found by subtracting the known values from that total.4
      7.8.3.1A fair comparison needs two measures: an average for the typical value and the range for consistency. A smaller range means more consistent data, not better data. A comparison is only complete when it is stated in the context of the data. The mode suits categories, the median suits data with extreme values, and the mean suits data without them.4
      7.8.3.2Compare two data sets using an average and the range, with statements in context.4
      7.12.4.1A diagram holds the same information as a list, so averages and range can be read from it directly. In a frequency table the mode is the value with the highest frequency, and the median is found by counting through the frequencies. The mean of a frequency table is the total of value x frequency, divided by the total frequency. Two data sets are compared using an average and the range, stated in context.4
      8.17.1.3Find averages from a stem-and-leaf diagram, and compare two data sets using an average and the range.4
      10.18.5.1Two data sets are compared on two things: an average, which locates the data, and the range, which measures how spread out they are. A comparison is only meaningful when the same average is used for both. A conclusion is stated in the context of the data, saying what the difference means and not only that one figure is larger.4
      10.18.5.2Compare two data sets using an average and the range, and state a conclusion in context.4
      10.18.5.3Decide which of two data sets is more consistent, and support the answer with a calculated measure of spread.5

      6.2DModal class

      8.17.3.2Identify the modal class and the class containing the median from grouped data.5
      9.16.7.2Identify the modal class and the class containing the median.5
      10.18.4.1The modal class is the class with the highest frequency, and it is a class, not a single value. With unequal class widths the highest frequency need not be the most densely populated class, so the modal class must be quoted with care. The class containing the median is found by counting through the frequencies to position (n + 1) / 2.4
      10.18.4.2Identify the modal class and the class containing the median from a grouped frequency table.3
      10.18.4.3Choose and justify the most appropriate average for a set of grouped data.4

      Frequency tables

      8.17.2.1In a frequency table each value occurs as many times as its frequency states. The mean is therefore the total of value x frequency, divided by the total frequency. The mode is the value with the highest frequency, not the frequency itself. The median is found by counting through the frequencies to the middle position, at (n + 1) / 2. A missing frequency is found by writing the mean formula as an equation and solving it.4
      8.17.2.2Find the mode, median and mean from a discrete frequency table.4
      10.18.2.1In a frequency table each value carries a frequency, so the total of the values is the sum of value x frequency, and the number of values is the total frequency. Mean = (sum of value x frequency) / (total frequency). The modal value is the one with the highest frequency, and the median is found by counting through the frequencies to position (n + 1) / 2.3

      Statistical measures
      • Estimated mean, grouped data

      6.2CEstimated mean, grouped data

      8.17.3.1Grouping data loses the individual values, so only the class each value fell into is known. The mean can therefore only be estimated, using the midpoint of each class to stand in for its values. The estimated mean is the total of midpoint x frequency, divided by the total frequency. The modal class is the class with the highest frequency, and the median is reported as the class containing the middle value. Both answers are classes rather than single values, which is why they are named rather than calculated.5
      8.17.3.3Estimate the mean from grouped discrete data using midpoints.5
      8.17.4.1Continuous data can take any value in a range, so its classes are written as inequalities rather than separate values. Inequality boundaries leave no gaps, so every possible value falls into exactly one class. The midpoint of a class is halfway between its two boundaries. Because the total is mean x count, the original total can always be recovered from a given mean. A value added, removed or corrected changes that total and possibly the count, and the new mean follows from both.6
      8.17.4.2Estimate the mean from grouped continuous data.6
      9.16.7.1Grouping data loses the individual values, so only the class each value fell into is known. The mean can therefore only be estimated, using each class midpoint to stand in for its values. The estimated mean is the total of midpoint x frequency, divided by the total frequency. The modal class is the class with the highest frequency, and the median is the class containing the middle value. Both are classes rather than single values, which is why they are named rather than calculated.5
      9.16.7.3Estimate the mean from grouped discrete data using midpoints.5
      9.16.8.1Continuous data can take any value in a range, so its classes are written as inequalities. Inequality boundaries leave no gaps, so every value falls into exactly one class. The midpoint of a class is halfway between its two boundaries. A conditional probability restricts the sample space to the outcomes where a known event has already happened. On a tree diagram that means using only the branches following the known outcome, rescaled so they sum to 1.6
      9.16.8.2Estimate the mean and identify the median and modal classes from grouped continuous data.6
      10.18.3.1When data are grouped the individual values are lost, so the mean can only be estimated. The midpoint of a class is taken as representative of every value in it, and midpoint = (lower bound + upper bound) / 2. Estimated mean = (sum of midpoint x frequency) / (total frequency). The estimate is not the true mean, and it would only be exact if the values in every class were symmetrically spread about its midpoint.4
